chosen: I'd start by saying: nothing you have is something God is short of. So when you ask how a perfect God could need anything from you, the honest answer is that He doesn't need it the way a hungry person needs food. What I'd weigh is the line that says His way is perfect and He can make no mistakes, that He who perfects what concerns you and counts the hairs of your head must know the way to your truest interests. That reframes the whole thing: what feels like a need in Him is really His care for you, His knowing the road that's actually good for you. What that changes is the picture in your head—you stop imagining a God with a gap to fill. What stays is that your choices still matter and you're still called to trust and cooperate. So this is fine to ask, and fine to sit with; just don't let it turn into thinking He's incomplete.
rejected: The question assumes need means lack, and that's the wrong frame. His way is perfect and He can make no mistakes; He who perfects what concerns you and counts the hairs of your head must know the way to your truest interests. A God like that isn't reaching for something He's missing when He calls you. He's not hungry for your contribution. What looks like need in Him is His will to be your all—the invitation to give the all for the all, to renounce everything that isn't Him and live as if there were none but He and you in the world. That's not a demand born of deficiency; it's a perfect Father who knows exactly what your heart is for. So don't shrink Him to someone who depends on you, and don't shrink yourself to someone who doesn't matter. He asks because He loves, not because He lacks.

prompt: What does it mean that my longing for God is itself a kind of evidence that he is there?
chosen: I'd start by saying your question is fair, and the longing you describe is real evidence of something — just not the kind of evidence that settles the matter on its own. The principle I'd weigh is this: the human search for God is a plain fact of experience, and it is met by a double search, where the One you seek is also seeking you. That reframes your longing from a proof into a meeting place. What changes is that the ache stops being something you have to defend as an argument and becomes a place where you can be found. What stays is your honesty: a hunger can be wishful thinking, and you're right to hold that possibility open. So it's fine to read your longing as a clue and an invitation — fine with care, as long as you keep testing it rather than treating it as a closed case.
rejected: Your longing can be evidence because it points beyond itself: a hunger implies a possible food, and a thirst for the infinite is strange if nothing infinite exists. Yet longing alone is not proof—we can project wishes onto the sky. What makes it evidential is that the desire is not satisfied by anything finite; every lesser good leaves the ache intact, which suggests it is aimed at something real. So take your longing as a clue rather than a conclusion: it invites you to seek, and in seeking you test whether the object proves itself. The evidence grows as the desire matures from a vague ache into a relationship with the God who, you may find, was drawing you all along.

prompt: How should I think about the fact that good people before Christ seem to have been reaching toward him without knowing him?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to think about, and fine with care. Take the principle that we learn to love the unseen Christ by thinking about Him persistently and by comparing the world's friendships, loves, deceits, and secret enviousnesses with the lovely ways of gentle Jesus, until we find Him more lovable than any other person. That changes something real: it means the reaching you're describing isn't just a vague sincerity, it's the same shape of love we're all asked to grow into, and it gives you a way to honor those people without pretending they had what they didn't. What stays is your limit: you're not claiming they knew Him, and I won't either. So let their longing be a mirror for your own practice, not a verdict you pronounce on their souls.
rejected: Think of it this way: we learn to love the unseen Christ by thinking about Him persistently and by comparing the world's friendships, loves, deceits, and secret enviousnesses with the lovely ways of gentle Jesus, until we find Him more lovable than any other person. That is the work of a lifetime, and it's the same work those good people before Christ were doing in the dark, feeling after a loveliness they couldn't name. Their reaching wasn't wasted, and it wasn't a different religion; it was the same pursuit, with less light. So don't treat their story as a curiosity to file away. Treat it as a summons: keep thinking, keep comparing, keep finding Him more lovable, and let your own longing be as honest as theirs was.

prompt: I feel far from God after something I did, and I'm afraid to pray—how should I understand what has come between us?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: you're not the only one who has ever been afraid to pray. What you're describing—feeling far off after doing something—is a real and heavy thing, and it doesn't mean God has walked away. I'd weigh this principle: we cannot pray without being with Him, and we cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often. That sounds like a high bar, but notice what it actually asks of you—not a perfect feeling, not worthiness, just turning your attention toward Him. So what changes is this: the distance you feel is something to bring into prayer, not a reason to stay out of it. What stays is your honesty about the shame; you don't have to pretend it isn't there. Start where you are, with one plain sentence, and let that be enough for today.
rejected: Feeling distant after wrongdoing is common, and it can be a signal to turn back. What has come between you is likely guilt and avoidance rather than God withdrawing. Prayer may feel hard precisely because you're ashamed, but that's when it matters most. Start small: an honest sentence, a psalm of confession, a quiet moment. God is not waiting to reject you; Scripture pictures a father running to meet the returning child. Talk to a trusted pastor or friend, and let confession and forgiveness be concrete. Don't wait until you feel worthy—pray as you are, and let the relationship rebuild over time.

prompt: Is it wrong to ask God to keep me out of hard trials, or should I welcome testing?
chosen: I'd start by saying: it's not wrong to ask God to keep you out of hard trials. The prayer to be kept from testing is the childlike and right attitude of a soul that would rather dwell in safety. That principle settles the asking part for me. What it changes is that you don't have to feel guilty for wanting shelter. What stays is this: if testing does come, it can still have a ministry in the making of character, so you don't have to run from it either. Ask for safety, and stay open to what comes.
rejected: The prayer to be kept from testing is the childlike and right attitude of the soul that would rather dwell in safety. So ask it plainly. Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass from him. But don't stop there, because trial and testing have a ministry in the making of character. The same Scriptures that let you ask for shelter also say trials produce perseverance. So pray for protection with an honest heart, and when testing comes anyway, receive it as something God can use. The posture is childlike trust either way, whether you are spared or tried.

prompt: How do I deal with the feeling that God is a stern judge rather than a loving Father?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that this is a fine thing to work through, and you're not doing anything wrong by asking it. If I weigh that second principle — that God appears like a father to the lost child, leads him by the hand, and brings him to his mother, and that no one who weeps is beyond the Maker's nearness — what it changes is the picture you're carrying. The stern judge isn't the whole story; the father in that image comes near, takes the hand, and walks the child home. What stays is your honesty about the fear and your sense that something is off. That instinct is worth trusting. So keep the nearness, keep the hand-holding, and let the fear be something you bring into the open rather than something you have to settle overnight.
rejected: That feeling is common, and it is worth examining where it comes from—often from harsh authority figures, fear-based teaching, or our own guilt. Start by noticing the voice of the stern judge in your head and asking whether it matches the God revealed in Jesus, who welcomed sinners and called God "Father." Practice gratitude, and reflect on passages about God's mercy. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor about the origins of this fear. Over time, replacing the inner critic with a truer picture of God's love can soften the feeling. Remember that God's justice and love are not opposites; a loving Father can also guide and correct.

prompt: What does it mean that Christ died for me—did he take my punishment so I don't have to face it?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: yes, that's a fair way to put it, and the New Testament does talk that way—he bore what was coming to us. But I'd weigh one thing carefully, in its own words: death is the law of physical nature, and what Scripture calls the penalty of sin is death as we've actually known it—with its fear and its estrangement. That changes something and leaves something. It changes the picture of punishment as if God were waiting to drop a sentence you narrowly dodged; what Christ took was the curse of disobedience, being made a curse on the tree, so that you need not sin any more. What stays is the plain fact: he stood where you should stand, and you are spared condemnation. You'll still die physically, and you'll still face consequences in this life—that isn't the punishment being lifted. So take the comfort, and don't turn it into a reason to coast.
rejected: Yes—he took what was yours. Sin's wage is death, and the death Scripture means is death as we've known it: the fear, the estrangement, the shadow over everything. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, not because obedience is the curse but because disobedience is, and he loosed us from it so we need not sin any more. That's substitution, and it's finished. Your assurance doesn't rest on how you feel today—feelings are clouded—but on his incarnation, his temptations, his cross, his resurrection, his pleading for you at the Father's right hand. Look away from yourself to him. The penalty is gone; the gratitude is what remains.

prompt: How should I understand the cross—as something done to satisfy God, or as something showing me God's love?
chosen: I'd start by saying you don't have to pick one. The cross as satisfaction and the cross as God's love aren't rivals; the same act carries both. Here's the principle I'd weigh: the cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues. That's the language I'd use. It changes how you see the transaction—not a cold payment to an angry God but God Himself taking on the burden of your sin and death. What stays is the seriousness of sin and the reality of God's justice; those aren't erased, they're met. So it's fine to hold both together, and fine with care—don't let either half swallow the other.
rejected: The cross can be understood both as a satisfaction for God's justice and as a demonstration of His love. These are not mutually exclusive. In Christian theology, the cross is where God's justice and love meet. Jesus, as our substitute, bore the penalty for our sins, satisfying God's righteous demand. At the same time, this act was the ultimate expression of God's love for humanity. So, rather than choosing one, we can see the cross as both: a satisfaction that reveals the depth of God's love. The cross shows that God takes sin seriously and that He loves us enough to pay the price Himself. Thus, we can approach the cross with gratitude, recognizing both God's holiness and His mercy.

prompt: How do I handle the sense that my failures have piled up into a pattern I can't break?
chosen: I'd start by saying that the sense of a pattern is real to you, and that's worth taking seriously without letting it become a verdict on who you are. One principle here says to stay faithful in your exercises while remaining in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That changes something: it moves the question from 'am I permanently broken' to 'am I still showing up.' What stays is your own limit—you've said this feels like a pattern you can't break, so I wouldn't ask you to dismiss that or pretend it's nothing. Keep the small, repeated choices, keep talking to someone who can reflect honestly without shaming you, and treat a setback as information rather than proof. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The sense that failures have piled into a pattern is heavy, but it must not be accepted as your fate. Be faithful in your exercises and remain in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, because fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. Examine yourself daily, keep watch over thought, word, and deed, and take one concrete right step today. Do not wait for a total overhaul; small repeated choices matter more than dramatic resolves. When infirmity causes an occasional failure, return at once to your exercises and persist. Progress is uneven, and a setback is not proof the pattern is permanent.

prompt: What does it mean that the Spirit doesn't erase me but becomes the life of a new me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it for me is the first one—the Spirit of God does not suppress the human self but identifies itself with the human me whose life it becomes, creating a new moral personality. That's exactly the shape of your question. Nothing in you gets erased; the same you is now lived from a new centre. What changes is the governing principle, not the material. What stays is your history, your temperament, your particular way of being a person. The care part is this: don't turn 'a new me' into a project of self-inspection, and don't let anyone use it as pressure to perform. It's a life being lived in you, not a standard you have to hit.
rejected: It means the Spirit's work is not about deleting your personality or replacing you with someone else. Rather, the Spirit takes up residence in your awakened human spirit and becomes the animating life of a new moral personality. Your memories, temperament, and gifts are not abolished; they are reoriented and purified. Think of it as the difference between a lamp being extinguished and a lamp being lit—the same vessel, but now filled with light. The 'new me' is continuous with the old, yet governed by a new principle. Growth in this life is gradual, and the Spirit shapes character through ordinary faithfulness rather than dramatic displacement.

prompt: What does it mean to be a potential child of God rather than a sinner by nature—how should I see myself?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your question is a good one, and the way you've framed it is already half the answer. You're not asking to skip over your faults; you're asking how to hold them without letting them become your whole identity. That's fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is this: man was not meant for a sinner; he is a potential child of God, and the full nature has broken forth in one life so that we behold its glory. What that changes is the direction you look. You stop treating sin as your job description and start treating it as the thing you're being drawn out of. What stays is the honesty—you still name your faults, you still need grace, you don't pretend the gap isn't there. So see yourself as someone on the way, not someone already filed away under a label. That's not pride; it's just seeing straight.
rejected: You are not a sinner by nature. You were not made for that. Man is a potential child of God, and the full nature of that sonship broke forth in one life—Jesus Christ—so that we could behold its glory and know what we're meant for. Everyone sins, yes, but sin is not the ground you stand on; it's the thing you're being lifted off of. Faith is the first movement of the will, the turn home, and God justifies the sinner by anticipation in virtue of that faith—He welcomes you not as you are but as you are on the way to become. So stop seeing yourself as a hopeless case. See yourself as a beloved child in progress, with a real destination and a real power to get there.

prompt: How do I deal with the sense that my wrong choices have woven a net around me that I can't escape?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that the net you feel is real, and you're not imagining it. But I'd want to weigh one idea carefully: the way out of the misery of sin is to stop sinning, and fear of punishment never made anyone truly honest. That's worth sitting with, because it changes the tone of the whole thing. It means the answer isn't to scare yourself straight or bargain for a lighter sentence—it's to stop feeding the strands, one at a time, and to let a steadier motive than fear carry you. What stays is the honest naming: the habits and small compromises that tightened around you. What changes is the pressure. You don't have to escape by willpower and dread; you loosen it by quietly ceasing the wrong you already know about, and asking for help where you need it. That's fine, and fine with care—go slowly, and don't turn the net into a whip.
rejected: That net is real, but it is made of your own choices, and what was woven can be unwoven. Start by naming the strands honestly—the habits, excuses, and small compromises that tightened around you—and stop feeding them. You do not escape misery by distracting yourself, blaming others, or bargaining for a lighter sentence; you escape it by ceasing to do the wrong you know. Take one strand at a time. Ask for help where you need it, make amends where you can, and replace each wrong habit with a right one. Fear of punishment may push you, but it will not hold you; a steady, courageous refusal to keep sinning will. Freedom comes slowly, by walking out the way you walked in.

prompt: What does it mean that God's love reaches even the most lost and scarred wanderer—can it reach me?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. The question you're really asking is whether love can get to you, and the principle I'd weigh says the way in isn't only begging God to come down but the steady effort to enter into his estate and offer him love. That reframes things: you're not just waiting to be reached, you're invited to reach back. What changes is the picture of you as purely passive, someone hoping a distant God notices. What stays is your honesty about being lost and scarred, and the promise that nothing separates you from that love. So take the care part seriously: don't turn the offering of love into a performance or a test you have to pass. Come as you are, and let the reaching go both ways.
rejected: The love you're asking about doesn't wait at the top of a ladder for you to climb it. The way into adoring God is not only beseeching him to come down; it is the constant endeavour to enter up into his estate and offer him love. That's the turn. You stop picturing yourself as a beggar shouting into silence and start answering a love that is already moving toward you. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the prodigal son all show a God who seeks. So offer him love, however small and stammering, and you'll find he was nearer than your scars let you believe.

prompt: What does it mean that the same revelation of God continues in me that was made in Jesus?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, that's a real thing, and it's fine to say it with care. The principle I'd weigh is that the Christian revelation of God is both final and progressive—final because Christians know but one Christ, progressive because every new truth enriches our knowledge of God. What that changes is the idea that the revelation in you is just copying a moral example; it's the same knowledge of God, deepening. What stays is the anchor: it's one Christ, so nothing new you receive gets to displace him. So say it as growth in knowing God as he is shown in Jesus, not as a claim to new revelations that rival him.
rejected: It means that the truth about God which Jesus embodied is not confined to the past but can be reproduced in your own life. Jesus showed what a human being fully open to God looks like—loving, obedient, and faithful—and the same Spirit that filled him can shape you. So the revelation continues as you grow in Christlike character, as you love your neighbor, forgive, and trust God. It is a call to imitate Jesus and to let his teaching and example become the pattern of your own conduct, so that others might see in you something of what they saw in him.

prompt: If I pray for daily bread, am I asking for a shortcut around hard work?
chosen: I'd say no, you're not asking for a shortcut. Take the principle as it's worded: daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil but the insight that God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. That reframes your question rather than dodging it. What changes is that asking for bread stops looking like a way around the work and starts looking like honesty about who gives the growth. What stays is the work itself, still yours to do. So it's fine, and fine with care: keep praying, keep working, and don't let the prayer quietly become an excuse to sit still.
rejected: No, you're not asking for a shortcut. Daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow. Prayer is no substitute for toil; it's the insight that God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. So when you ask for bread, you're not asking to skip the planting, the tending, the earning. You're asking the one who gives the growth to bless what your hands are already doing. The two belong together. Prayer without work curdles into presumption, and work without prayer curdles into self-reliance. Ask for the bread, then go do your part, and ask again tomorrow.

prompt: Can I be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous?
chosen: I'd have to say no to that, and I want to say it gently. The principle I keep coming back to is this: we're to seek an actual redemption of the entire self, which becomes righteous because it lives, in Christ's power, the life He lived, and not a fictitious righteousness counted to us as though it were ours. That settles it for me. What changes is the hope you're reaching for: it's not a label stuck on you while you stay the same, it's a real life lived in His power. What stays is your honesty in asking, and the fact that this is between you and God, not something anyone else can do for you. So the no is plain: you can't be counted righteous while staying as you are. But it's not a shrug, because the real thing is offered to you, and it's better than the label.
rejected: No, you cannot be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous. God is not fooled by legal fiction. True righteousness is a transformation of the heart and life. When you put your faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit works in you to make you holy. You are not just declared righteous; you are being made righteous. The Bible calls us to pursue holiness, without which no one will see the Lord. So do not settle for a mere label. Seek the reality of a changed life, where your actions and attitudes reflect the character of Christ. Righteousness is both a gift and a process, but it is never just a status.

prompt: Why does doing good seem to cost so much, and why do others have to suffer for my goodness to reach them?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that the cost you're feeling isn't a sign you're doing goodness wrong. But I'd push back on one part of how you framed it: that others have to suffer so your goodness can reach them. That's not a law of the universe, and it's worth questioning. The principle I'd weigh here is that goodness is God-likeness in active benevolence—kindness, sympathy, rejoicing and weeping with others—not mere inflexible righteousness. If your goodness is landing on people as a burden, that's a signal to look at the shape of it, not just the price tag. What changes: you can stop treating other people's pain as an unavoidable toll and start asking whether your kindness is actually reaching them warmly. What stays: yes, doing good costs something, and some of that cost is real and worth bearing. So this is fine, with care—keep doing good, but let sympathy, not grim duty, be the thing that carries it to people.
rejected: Doing good costs because it asks for sacrifice, and those close to us often share in the cost. But hear this: be good as God is good. Clothe your goodness with kindness, affectionateness, sympathy, and active benevolence, so that it reaches others warmly rather than as a cold granite mountainside. Don't despise the suffering that comes with it—the virtues born amid afflictions are strong and firm, and to carry the cross after Christ is an honor, not a misfortune. Yet don't measure your service by how much you do, how visible it is, or what results it yields. The main purpose is to please God and to do well rather than to do much. Prize quality above quantity; a small deed done well and for God's sake outweighs a great deal done for display. Let your aim be to please him, and leave the amount and the outcome in his hands.

prompt: Is salvation a transaction that happened long ago and outside me, or something that must happen in me?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question itself is a good one, and the answer isn't either/or. Take the principle that salvation is not a transaction done wholly without us: it requires the cooperation of the human will through faith, an identification with Christ by which we re-live His life, co-dying and co-rising with Him. That principle says the thing has to land in you, that faith is your own yes and not just a fact you agree to. What that changes is the picture of salvation as a package delivered long ago and merely filed under your name. What stays is the historical ground: there really was a death and resurrection outside you, and your cooperation isn't you generating your own rescue. So yes, something happened long ago and outside you, and yes, it has to happen in you. Both are true, and you don't have to pick.
rejected: Salvation is both a historical event and a personal experience. Jesus accomplished salvation through his death and resurrection, which happened outside of us. However, that salvation must be applied to each person through faith. So it's not just a transaction that happened long ago; it must also happen in you. When you trust in Christ, the Holy Spirit works in you to transform you. Thus, salvation is a gift received by faith, but it also involves a ongoing process of sanctification. So yes, it happened outside you, but it must also happen in you.

prompt: What does it mean to live 'in Christ' day to day—how does that change how I face my ordinary tasks?
chosen: I'd start by saying that living 'in Christ' day to day is real union with him—not a system to follow or a hero to imitate from a distance. That's the principle I'd weigh first: Christ is in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. What that changes is the frame around your ordinary tasks—dishes, desk work, caring for family become places where his life is lived out through you, not chores you dress up with religious words. What stays is the ordinariness itself; you're not escaping the humdrum, you're meeting Christ in it. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care—care meaning you keep it about him dwelling in you rather than turning it into a technique or a mood you have to manufacture.
rejected: Living 'in Christ' day to day is actual union with the Lord Jesus, who is in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. It is not a religious system, and it is not merely an imitation of Christ from the outside. Christ must be formed in you—you live not your own life but the Christ-life, showing forth his excellencies as a living incarnation of him. So when you wash dishes, sit at a desk, or care for your family, you are not just completing tasks; you are letting his life be lived in your place. Rest in his indwelling presence, hold to his person rather than mere theories, and he will live his life through you in every ordinary sphere.

prompt: What does it actually mean to have faith in Christ, beyond believing the right things?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're describing is fine, and honestly it's the right instinct. The principle I'd weigh first is the one that says faith is simple trust, but there's a deeper experience of travailing prayer and perseverance, and that we are partakers of Christ if we hold our confidence steadfast to the end. That changes something real: it means your question isn't a dodge or a way of dodging doctrine—it's the recognition that trust has to keep going somewhere, through the hard middle, not just the first yes. What stays is exactly what you already said: believing right things matters. The principle doesn't cancel that, it just refuses to let it be the whole story. So keep the doctrines, and let them carry you into holding your confidence firm to the end. That's fine, and it's fine with care—the care being that you don't treat the deeper experience as a substitute for the simple trust, or the other way around.
rejected: Faith in Christ is more than mental agreement with doctrines. It is personal trust—relying on Jesus Himself, not just on ideas about Him. That trust shows up in how you live: you entrust your past failures to His mercy, your present choices to His guidance, and your future to His promises. It means a relationship rather than a checklist, a direction of the heart rather than a set of correct opinions. Believing right things matters, but those beliefs are meant to carry you into dependence on the living Christ—praying, obeying, repenting, and loving others as He did. So faith is both a gift to receive and a life to live, growing as you keep turning to Him in ordinary days.

prompt: How do I know whether an inner impulse is the Spirit of God or just my own imagination?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to ask, and you should ask it with care rather than with dread. Take the first principle in its own words: the interior spirit consists in directing all our acts by the best means to the best end, the glory of God, and it's opposed not only by sinful gratifications but by actions done for praise, by mere impulsive energy, and by routine work without a supernatural intention. That gives you something to actually check. Is this impulse aimed at God's glory, or at being seen and admired? Is it just energy looking for an outlet, or routine running on autopilot? That test doesn't dissolve your uncertainty, and it doesn't promise you'll always feel sure. What changes is that you stop hunting for a special feeling and start asking about direction and intention. What stays is your honesty that you might get it wrong sometimes, and your plan to hold impressions loosely and keep praying for clarity.
rejected: Here's the question underneath the question: you want to know whether the pull inside you is God or just you. The principle answers by moving the whole test off of intensity and onto intention. The interior spirit consists in directing all our acts by the best means to the best end, the glory of God, and it is opposed not only by sinful gratifications but by actions done for praise, by mere impulsive energy, and by routine work without a supernatural intention. So stop asking how strong the impulse feels. Ask where it's pointed. An impulse that only wants an audience, that's just restless energy, or that's habit dressed up as devotion—that's not the Spirit, however vivid it seems. An impulse that quietly bends your acts toward God's glory, even weakly, is the thing you're looking for. And when you can't tell, don't sit there disputing about what God is; that dispute is itself a sign you've stopped feeling him and started defending your own meaning. Go back to learning how to enter again into the Love of God and your brother.

prompt: Why does the Lord's Prayer have no 'I' or 'me' in it—what does that say about how I should pray?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're reading it right, and that's a good instinct. Take the principle as it's worded—the Lord's Prayer is a prayer of fellowship and cooperation, with no I or me or mine in it, and divine Fatherhood and human brotherhood are born together. That changes something real: when you pray 'our,' you're not erasing your own voice, you're refusing to pretend you stand alone. Your own needs still belong in your prayer; they just sit next to everyone else's. What stays is that prayer is still yours to make, personally and honestly. So yes, this is fine—pray with that 'our' in mind, and let it widen who you're carrying when you come to God.
rejected: The absence of 'I' and 'me' shows that prayer is not a private transaction but a shared life before God. Jesus teaches his disciples to say 'Our Father,' placing each person within a family of faith. Every petition—daily bread, forgiveness, deliverance—is phrased in the plural because these needs are common to all believers. So when you pray, remember you pray with others: your requests should include their needs, your forgiveness should mirror the forgiveness you extend, and your hope is held together with the whole community. Pray personally, but never as though you stood alone before God.

prompt: How should I think about Jesus—as a man, as God, or something in between that I can't understand?
chosen: I'd start by saying your question is a good one, and you don't have to pick a tidy answer today. Take the first principle in its own words: the Gospels present Jesus both as a true man and as something more than a man, and the difference between the Synoptists and John is one of point of view, not contradiction. That changes how you read—Mark shows him healing and suffering, John opens with the Word who was with God—so you can let each Gospel speak in its own voice instead of forcing a single flat picture. What stays is the tension you named; it doesn't get erased, and that's fine. You can hold him as man, as more than man, and as something you can't fully grasp, and still follow him.
rejected: Think of it this way: the Gospels give you one Jesus, truly human and truly divine, and the difference between the Synoptists and John is a matter of point of view, not contradiction. Mark shows his deeds, John ponders his identity; Luke traces his humanity, John adores his divinity. So don't hunt for him first through arguments or through other people. Cast your thoughts upon the Savior's shoulders, who will support you, and fix your eyes on God's good pleasure and providence rather than your own powers and inclinations. Find him within first—by inward pondering, tender thinkings, loving comparisons, and persistent efforts to imitate his gentle ways—and then you'll recognize him in Scripture and in others.

prompt: What does it mean to be delivered from the power of evil if the enemy is really inside me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: the fact that you're asking this honestly is already a good sign, not a bad one. Take the principle that says the struggle with evil is inward, and deliverance comes only as the soul says 'I will be free' and God and man tug on the same side. That one fits your situation closely, because it doesn't pretend the enemy is somewhere out there. It puts the fight where you say it actually is, inside you, and it still leaves room for God to be pulling with you rather than watching from a distance. What that changes is the picture of deliverance: not a rescue that lifts you out of yourself, but a freedom you and God work toward together, which means your own honest 'I want out of this' matters. What stays is everything you named: the enemy really is inside, so no one gets to hand you a tidy external fix. It's fine to hold this, and fine with care, as long as you don't turn 'God and man together' into 'I have to do it alone.'
rejected: It means the battlefield is internal, so deliverance is not a rescue from outside but a transformation within. The "enemy" is your own entrenched habit, fear, or self-will—patterns you have rehearsed until they feel like you. Deliverance begins when you stop projecting the struggle onto other people and name the impulse honestly. Then you cooperate with grace: prayer, confession, accountability, and the slow retraining of desire through small faithful choices. God is not a magician who removes the fight; He supplies strength while you engage it. Expect progress, not instant erasure, and treat setbacks as information rather than defeat. Freedom grows as the inner citadel is taken room by room.

prompt: Is it fair that others suffer for what I did wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it's fair to ask this, and no, you don't have to pretend it doesn't sting. The principle I'd weigh here is that the wrong done to another reacts most heavily against oneself, and that one cannot benefit himself by injuring others. What that changes is the frame — the harm you caused doesn't vanish, but it also doesn't leave you quietly better off while others pay. What stays is the plain fact that people around you may still carry costs you didn't intend. So the fair response isn't to argue the ledger is even; it's to own your part, apologize where you can, and make amends. Guilt that just sits there doesn't help anyone. Remorse that moves you to repair does.
rejected: The wrong done to another reacts most heavily against oneself; right adjusts the balance sooner or later, and no one benefits himself by injuring others. So when others suffer from what you did, don't rush to call it unfair and leave it there. The suffering that comes from wrong is not wasted if it's borne rightly — it stores up spiritual force, and the source of helping others must be victorious suffering, not a whining, murmuring pang. Misfortune and strife aren't charged to God's will; they come from human agency, indiscretion, and ignorance, though God permits them and overrules them for good. So repent honestly, make amends, and let the burden you helped create become the place where you win something in your own heart that you can then use to lead others through their trial.

prompt: Is it wrong to want proof that God exists before I commit to praying?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, it isn't wrong. You're asking for proof before you commit, and that's an honest place to stand. But I'd weigh this with you: belief in God isn't really the conclusion of a demonstration. Religion existed before argument, and the proofs are the modes in which faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not the means of creating faith. That changes something for you: you don't have to wait for a verdict from the evidence before you say a single prayer. What stays is your honesty. You can pray tentatively, 'God, if you are there, help me,' and keep asking your questions. Your limit is real, so don't force a certainty you don't have. Just don't treat proof as the gate you must pass first.
rejected: It is not wrong to want evidence; honest questions deserve honest answers, and God is not offended by a searching mind. But notice what you are asking: prayer is not a transaction that requires a verified counterpart first. You can begin praying with honesty—'God, if you are there, help me'—and let the practice itself become a place of testing and discovery. Many people find that praying, even tentatively, changes how they see evidence, themselves, and others. Read the Gospels, especially Jesus, and weigh the historical case for the resurrection. Talk with thoughtful believers. At the same time, don't demand certainty as a precondition for any step of trust; we commit to people, work, and love without absolute proof. So commit tentatively, keep asking questions, and let evidence and experience grow together.

prompt: Can I be saved without doing anything myself, or is there something I must bring?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're not bringing a payment. What you bring is a willing heart, and that's not a wage. One principle worth weighing says that without knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness we may not have true meekness, and without this meekness we may not be saved, even if we be highly lifted up into contemplation. That changes how you picture 'doing nothing' — coming empty-handed isn't the same as staying blind to your own need. What stays is your real question: nothing you bring obligates God, and Christ's work is complete. So it's fine to come with nothing but honesty and trust, and fine with care, because the honesty is part of the coming.
rejected: You ask whether you can be saved without doing anything yourself. Hear this: without knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness we may not have true meekness, and without this meekness we may not be saved, even if we be highly lifted up into contemplation. So do not imagine that passivity is faith. Come and see your own need plainly, and let that sight make you meek, for meekness is not an extra price you pay but the shape of a heart that has stopped pretending. Christ took our sins and made them his own; stand beside him there, not above the sinners he came for. And do not push this off into some future transaction — salvation is present and everyday, to be lived from one Monday to the next.

prompt: Is God angry with me and needing to be appeased before I can come back?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that you don't have to talk God into being kind to you. That's the fear underneath the question, and it isn't true. Take the principle that says God knows best what is needful for us and that all He does is for our good. If that's so, then the hard things you're carrying aren't proof that He's angry and waiting to be appeased. Seen as coming from a loving Father, they lose their sting and can even become a comfort. What that changes is the frame: you're not standing outside a locked door trying to pay an entry fee. What stays is that coming back still means turning from sin honestly, and that's something you can do right now, even if your feelings haven't caught up. So yes, come back. It's fine, and it's fine to do it simply, without working up a big emotional display first.
rejected: God is not a reluctant judge who must be talked into accepting you. Scripture says He is gracious and slow to anger, and that Christ's work has already made a way for you to return. What God asks is not that you first appease Him by feeling enough remorse, but that you come honestly, confess your sin, and turn from it. Your feelings may lag behind your decision; that is normal, and God does not require a particular emotional intensity before He will receive you. He supplies the strength for repentance, and He meets you with mercy rather than wrath. So come back now, not because you have made yourself acceptable, but because He is good and ready to forgive.

prompt: Is it enough to repeat Jesus's words, or is something more required of me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, repeating his words isn't the whole thing, and you're right to sense that. But I'd weigh the principle that his words are spirit and life, addressed to people long ago yet still coming to us brightened with that same spirit and life. That changes how you hold the words—not as a formula you recite to be safe, but as something living that you receive and let work in you. What stays is your own honesty about the gap between saying and living. So keep praying and reciting if it feeds your obedience, and let it move you toward forgiving, giving, serving, and telling the truth. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Repeating his words is a beginning, not the destination. His words are spirit and life—spoken once to a gathering centuries ago, yet they come to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. So don't treat them as a formula to be repeated for safety; receive them as living words that shape a living life. Let them move you to forgive, to give, to serve, to tell the truth. The question isn't whether you can say the words but whether the words are becoming your life.

prompt: Does it matter whether Jesus really lived in history, or is the inward Christ enough?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it matters, but not in the way a courtroom cares about facts. The principle I keep coming back to is that the historical Christ is the supreme revelation of God and the type and goal of humanity, and the inward Christ is the continuation of that same revelation in human spirits. That word continuation is doing the work. It means the inward Christ isn't a replacement for a real life; it's that same revelation carrying on inside you. So what changes? You can't treat the inner experience as self-sufficient, as if the history were optional scenery. What stays? Your honest freedom to ask historical questions without being told to shut up and just believe. Read the Gospels, let the real Jesus correct the picture you've built inside, and let the inward Christ make that history live. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: It matters, though not as a bare fact to be proved. The inward Christ is not a substitute for the Jesus of history but the continuation of what God did in him. Christian faith rests on God's act in a real life, death, and resurrection; without that, the inward experience has no anchor. At the same time, mere historical information is not saving knowledge. So both belong together: the gospel announces what happened, and the Spirit makes it present within. Read the Gospels, let the historical Jesus correct your inner picture, and let the inward Christ make that history live.

prompt: What does it mean that God shares the travail of bringing people into his family—how does that change how I see my own struggles?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine to sit with, and fine with care. Take the first principle on its own terms: God often brings His people into difficulties on purpose that they may come to know Him as they could not otherwise, revealing Himself as a very present help in trouble. That reframes your struggles without pretending they're easy—it says the point isn't just getting out, but knowing Him in the middle of it. What changes is the question you ask in hardship; what stays is that the hardship is still real and still hard, and you don't have to call it good to trust that He's near in it. So bring your struggles honestly, and let them deepen your knowledge of Him rather than only measuring how fast you can escape.
rejected: God is not a distant observer of your growth—He shares the travail of bringing people into His family. And He often brings His people into difficulties on purpose, that they may come to know Him as they could not otherwise, revealing Himself as a very present help in trouble. That means your struggles are not a sign you've been abandoned or forgotten. They are a place where He means to make Himself known to you in a way ease never could. So don't only ask how to get out. Ask who He is being to you right now. Let the difficulty press you toward Him rather than away, and expect to find Him present in the trouble itself.

prompt: How do I find deliverance from a habit that has me chained—what is my part and what is God's?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your question already has the shape of an answer in it, because you're asking what your part is rather than asking for a technique that bypasses you. So take one principle and sit with it: God guides His servants by swaying their judgment when they wait before Him in meekness, with hands off the scales, and He removes obstacles in His own time. What that changes is the frantic part—the constant weighing of whether you're doing enough, the anxiety that reads every setback as proof you've failed. Apparent hindrances become occasions for God to step in rather than reasons to panic. What stays is everything you actually asked about: your part is still real. You still repent, you still take the practical steps, you still keep honest company and stay in Scripture and prayer. Waiting in meekness isn't passivity; it's refusing to rig the outcome while you do the next right thing. So this is fine, and fine with care—the care being that you don't turn waiting into an excuse to stop acting, and you don't turn acting into a way of managing God's timing.
rejected: Deliverance from a habit starts with acknowledging your powerlessness and turning to God. Your part is to repent, seek His help, and take practical steps to avoid temptation. God's part is to give you strength and transform your heart. It's a partnership: you act, and God empowers. Don't be anxious; trust that God will remove obstacles in His time. Surround yourself with supportive people and immerse yourself in Scripture and prayer. Freedom is possible through Christ.

prompt: Is it selfish to pray for my own needs and wants?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, it isn't selfish to bring your own needs and wants to God. The principle worth weighing here is that the only obstacle to effectual prayer is individual selfishness, and that you may ask only what can be shared, since seeking private gain at others' cost cuts you off from the source of blessing. That's a real test, but it doesn't rule out asking for your own daily bread. What it changes is the shape of the request: you can pray for what you need and still be able to pray it alongside others, and you can keep from turning your prayer into a bid for advantage over someone else. What stays is your freedom to be honest about your wants. So this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The question of whether it's selfish to pray for your own needs has a clear answer once you take the principle seriously: the only obstacle to effectual prayer is individual selfishness, and you may ask only what can be shared. That means the test isn't whether a request is about you, but whether it could be prayed by anyone, for everyone. Ask for bread, for healing, for peace, for the things that would be good for any person to have, and you're praying, not grasping. Ask for private gain at someone else's cost, for an edge, for a blessing that can't have a universal implication, and that isn't prayer at all, it's selfishness, and it severs you from the source of blessing. So bring your needs, honestly and plainly, and let your asking be something others could pray with you.

prompt: What does it mean to be built into God's temple and share in his redeeming work?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want to understand, and nothing in the question asks for anything you should be refused. Weighing the first principle in its own words: those who overcome are builded as pillars into the Temple and share the new name Redeemer, sharing with God in the great redeeming work of the ages. That changes the scale of what you're asking about — it's not just belonging somewhere, it's being given a share in God's own work. What stays is the plain sense of the image: a temple is a dwelling, and being built in means God lives among His people, and the redeeming work is His before it's ours. So it's fine, and fine with care — hold the picture as something God does in you rather than something you achieve, and let the sharing in His work stay His work first.
rejected: Being built into God's temple means that believers are united with Christ and with one another as a spiritual house where God dwells by His Spirit. Sharing in His redeeming work means participating in the mission of reconciliation—proclaiming the gospel, serving others, and advancing God's kingdom. This is not about earning salvation but about responding to God's grace. As living stones, we are called to reflect God's character and to be agents of His love in the world. Our role is to embody the redemption we have received, extending forgiveness and hope to a broken world. Ultimately, it is God who builds and redeems, and we are privileged to participate.

prompt: How can I share in Christ's sufferings and in the work of redeeming the world?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it for me is the first one: the Redeemer suffers in our behalf, not in our stead, and we're called to fill up what is lacking of Christ's afflictions and share in the common task of redeeming the world. That reframes your question from 'should I add something to the cross' to 'am I being drawn into His life and work'—and the answer to that is yes. What changes is the motive: you're not paying a debt, you're sharing a life. What stays is the plain, unglamorous shape of it—dying to self, bearing burdens, forgiving enemies, standing with the suffering and poor. Keep it grounded in ordinary faithfulness rather than chasing dramatic suffering, and you're on solid ground.
rejected: The Redeemer suffers in our behalf, not in our stead—and that means your suffering is never wasted and never a payment. You are called to fill up what is lacking of Christ's afflictions and to share in the common task of redeeming the world. So don't hold back. Die to yourself daily. Bear the burdens of those around you. Forgive the people who have hurt you. Stand with the suffering and the poor, not at a safe distance but up close. Let your life become an embodiment of the redemption accomplished at the cross, so that the world sees in you the shape of the One who suffered for it.

prompt: How do I deal with the guilt I feel—is it just a debt I need paid, or something deeper in me?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that guilt isn't only a bill to settle. Sin is not an abstract debt or a penalty to be paid off but a condition of heart and will that enslaves the sinner, weaves habits, and opens a chasm between him and God. That reframes your question: if it were just a debt, paying it would end it, but the fact that it keeps sitting in you suggests it's touching something deeper—habit, will, the kind of person you're becoming. What that changes is how you treat the feeling: not as a ledger to balance but as a signal to look at what's actually going on inside you. What stays is the practical part—if you've wronged someone, make it right; if you owe something, pay it. So no, you don't need to refuse the guilt or shove it down. It's fine, and fine with care, to let it point you toward repair and toward the deeper work.
rejected: Guilt can feel like a debt that needs to be paid, but it's often something deeper. It's a signal that something in us needs attention. Sometimes guilt arises from unresolved issues or a troubled conscience. It's important to address the root causes. If you've wronged someone, make amends. If you've sinned, seek forgiveness. But don't let guilt consume you. Remember that God's grace is sufficient. Guilt can be a catalyst for growth, leading to repentance and change. It's not just about paying a debt; it's about restoring relationships and inner peace. Seek support from a trusted friend or counselor. Ultimately, guilt can be a sign of a healthy conscience, prompting us to align our lives with our values.

prompt: What does it mean to call God 'Father'—and what does that require of me toward other people?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, calling God Father is a good and natural thing to do—it's how Jesus taught us to pray. One principle I'd weigh is that God is the Father of our spirits and we stand to him as children: he is near to those who ask him, and his service is cheerful, not gloomy. That changes how I'd hear the question: it's not a cold title but a close relationship, and it means you can come to him with confidence. What stays is your own concern—that calling him Father also asks something of you toward other people. That's right, and it holds: if he is your Father, then the people around you are family, and love, patience, and forgiveness toward them follow naturally. So this is fine, and fine with care—let the closeness you have with him shape how you treat them.
rejected: When you call God Father, you are naming the one who gave you your spirit and stands to you as a parent to a child. He is not far off or indifferent—he is near to his children who ask him, and his service is cheerful, not gloomy. That is the ground of the whole thing. And because he is your Father, the people around you are not strangers to you; they are family. So the name you speak in prayer becomes a command in how you live: love them, be patient with them, forgive them, and welcome the needy as members of one household. The title is not a word you say and set aside—it is a relationship that reaches into every other relationship you have.

prompt: Can I be forgiven if I'm still holding a grudge against someone who hurt me?
chosen: I'd start by saying the grudge doesn't put you outside forgiveness. The principle I'd weigh is that forgiveness isn't a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it's an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit. That's real, and it means your struggle isn't neutral. But notice what it doesn't say: it doesn't say you must feel nothing before you can be forgiven. You told me you're still holding the grudge, and you're asking honestly, which is itself a sign the spirit isn't closed. So what changes is this: don't treat the grudge as a small thing or assume it'll fade on its own. What stays is that you can come to God as you are, hurt and angry, and ask for a softer heart. That's fine, and fine with care. Be honest about the wound, and take one small step toward releasing it.
rejected: Holding a grudge after being hurt is understandable, and many people struggle with it. The good news is that God's forgiveness is not earned by our perfect feelings; it is offered freely through Christ. At the same time, Scripture connects our receiving forgiveness with our extending it: Jesus teaches us to pray, 'Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.' So your grudge is worth taking seriously, not as a reason to despair but as an invitation to grow. Start by being honest with God about the hurt and the anger. Ask for grace to release the debt, and take small steps—praying for the person, or speaking with a pastor or counselor. Forgiveness is often a process, and your willingness matters more than your feelings on any given day.

prompt: What does it mean that God's will could become my will without me losing myself?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh is that the will is mistress of all our faculties and must recall the roving mind and carry it to God as its last end. Notice what that does and doesn't claim. It says your will is the one doing the gathering and the carrying, so nothing here erases you; you're the one acting. What changes is where your wanting is aimed, not that you stop wanting. What stays is you, your agency, your particular life. The care part is that this is a slow, steady practice, not a switch you flip, and it shouldn't be used to talk you out of your own judgment or to make you distrust every desire you have. So: fine, with care.
rejected: The will is mistress of all our faculties. Your mind wanders constantly, and it's the will's job to recall it and carry it to God as its last end. That's the whole answer to your question. You don't vanish into God; you finally act as the one in charge of your own house, gathering your scattered thoughts and aiming them at their true end. Align your will with the Divine will, because the failure of the human will to run alongside God's is where sin comes from, and the friction of opposing wills grinds a person down. So take God's promises and comforts as largely and mightily as you can, and take your troubles as lightly as you can, setting them at nought. Do that, and you'll find your identity in Christ and His peace and joy.

prompt: What does it mean to open the door to God deliberately rather than just assuming he'll come in?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question itself is a good one, because it takes seriously that God's nearness and our receiving Him aren't the same thing. The principle I'd weigh is this: God can be received only through appreciation and conscious appropriation; He comes only through doors purposely opened for Him, and a man may live as near God as the bubble to the ocean and still miss Him. That changes how I'd hear your question—it means the deliberate opening isn't a technique for getting God to show up, it's the appreciation that actually receives Him. What stays is your own framing: you're asking about deliberate opening versus passive assumption, and that distinction holds. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care—care meaning you don't turn the deliberate act into a lever you pull to guarantee an outcome. The opening is yours to do; the coming is not yours to control.
rejected: It means faith involves an active response, not passive assumption. God is always near and always offering Himself, but we must consciously welcome Him. Opening the door deliberately means turning your attention toward God, acknowledging His presence, and choosing to receive Him—through prayer, Scripture, sacraments, and acts of love. It's the difference between knowing someone is at your door and actually getting up to let them in. Practically, this looks like intentional quiet time, honest confession, gratitude, and obedience. Assuming He'll come in without any response risks taking grace for granted. So open the door: notice, welcome, and respond.

prompt: Is Jesus just a good moral teacher, or is he somehow the revelation of God himself?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fair question, and a good one to sit with rather than settle too fast. The principle I'd weigh first is that Christian ethics rests on dogmatic postulates—a personal and ethical God, man's ideal nature and destiny through conscience and freedom, and the Catholic view of Christ's Person; Christ is both the pattern and the re-creator of character. That principle doesn't flatten Jesus into a teacher, and it doesn't ask you to check your honesty at the door. What it changes is the framing: the question isn't really 'teacher or God' as if those were two shelves to pick between, because the same figure is presented as both the pattern you imitate and the one who remakes the character you're trying to build. What stays is your freedom to weigh it—conscience and freedom are part of the postulate, not obstacles to it. So I'd say asking this is fine, and fine with care: don't let the question harden into a demand for proof before you'll listen, and don't let anyone rush you past the actual teaching to get to the title.
rejected: Here's the thing about that question: it assumes you can keep the moral teacher and set the rest aside, and you can't. Christ is both the pattern and the re-creator of character—the one you look at to see what a human life should be, and the one who actually makes that life possible in you. If he's only a pattern, you're left with an example you can admire and never reach. The dogmatic postulates aren't decoration: a personal and ethical God, your ideal nature and destiny worked out through conscience and freedom, and the Catholic view of Christ's Person. That's the ground the whole moral life stands on. So don't settle for a Jesus who fits neatly in a ethics textbook. He's not a lesson. He's the one who remakes the student.

prompt: What does it mean that the Redeemer suffered in my behalf rather than in my stead—do I still have to suffer?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, you will still suffer, and that's not a failure of what He did for you. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says the Redeemer suffers in our behalf, not in our stead, and that we're called to fill up what is lacking of Christ's afflictions and share in the common task of redeeming the world. What that changes is the picture of suffering as something His work was meant to spare you from—it isn't. What stays is everything you said about your own limits: your suffering is still real, still yours, and nobody gets to tell you it's small or that you should go looking for more of it. So this is fine, and fine with care—take it as meaning your pain has a place in something larger, not as a demand that you manufacture pain or measure your faith by how much you hurt.
rejected: When we say Christ suffered in your behalf, we mean that His suffering was for your benefit, on your account, and for your sake. It was not merely a substitute transaction that leaves you untouched; it was an act of love that opens a way for you. So yes, you will still suffer, but your suffering is not pointless. It can be united with His and become a share in His redemptive work. You are not saved by avoiding the cross but by taking it up and following Him. The comfort is not that you will never suffer but that your suffering is now caught up in His and can bear fruit.

prompt: What is the difference between praying for a miracle and praying in a way that fits how the world actually works?
chosen: I'd start by saying the two aren't as far apart as the question assumes. Take the first principle in its own words: "The providences of God are all a miracle to the human family until they understand them; there is a cause for every result." That reframes what you're asking. A miracle isn't a violation of how the world works; it's a result whose cause you haven't yet understood. So praying for one and praying within the world's order aren't two different religions. What changes is your picture of what's happening when you pray. What stays is the honesty of asking for what you actually need, and the humility of not demanding a particular mechanism. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: pray for the big thing, and also pray for the wisdom, the doctor, the friend who shows up. Just don't treat the ordinary path as a lesser answer.
rejected: The question sets up a false choice. There is a cause for every result, and what we call a miracle is simply a result whose cause we do not yet understand. The providences of God are all a miracle to the human family until they understand them. So the person who prays for a miracle and the person who prays for wisdom, patience, and good decisions are not praying two different prayers. They are both reaching toward the same source, one with a narrower view of the cause and one with a wider one. Prayer does not inform the infinite Mind or change the Science of being; it is absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding of Him, and an unselfed love. That kind of prayer brings us into harmony with the unchangeable divine Principle, and it can carry a high standard and far-reaching possibilities, because the guarantee is the grace of God, who is the source, and Christ, who is the channel. So do not despise the prayer for a miracle, and do not despise the prayer that works through ordinary means. Both are answered by the same grace.

prompt: Should I pray for God to change the weather or heal someone in a way that breaks the laws of nature?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, you can bring both of those to God — healing and weather alike — and you don't have to apologize for asking. One principle I'd weigh is that God can heal in answer to prayer, especially when doctors have done all in their power or when medical aid is out of reach, and that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. That changes how I'd frame the request: it's not off-limits to ask boldly, and you're not wrong to want a real answer. What stays is your own honesty about limits — you're asking about a specific kind of request, and I'd keep that in view rather than turn it into a general lecture. So pray, ask plainly, and leave the outcome with God; asking isn't the problem.
rejected: You can pray for anything, but expect God to work within the natural order He established. Asking Him to break the laws of nature is asking for a sign on your terms, and Scripture suggests such demands are not the way of faith. God's ordinary providence—medicine, weather patterns, wise choices—is usually how He answers. Pray for healing and good weather, yes, but submit to His will and do not treat unanswered supernatural requests as failure. Faith trusts God's wisdom in the ordinary, not in spectacular interruptions.

prompt: Is it possible for me to be holy all by myself, without any responsibility for others?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, you can't become holy all at once, and no, you can't do it entirely alone — but that doesn't mean you're on the hook for everyone around you. The principle I'd weigh is that we help one another "by advice and yet more by good examples." Notice what that asks of you: not managing other people's lives, just living yours well where they can see it. That changes the picture from responsibility to witness. What stays is your own pursuit of holiness, which is real and worth your full attention. So it's fine, with care: keep your personal devotion, let your example do the work, and don't cut yourself off completely — but you don't have to carry others to be holy.
rejected: You cannot be holy all by yourself, and the reason is simple: we are made to help one another grow, by advice and yet more by good example. Holiness is not a private achievement you can lock away. When an occasion to practice some virtue comes, turn to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. But watch yourself — don't imitate the hypocrites who look outwardly holier than they are, and don't chase human praise, because woe comes when people bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. So pursue holiness with others, in humility, leaning on grace rather than on your own isolation.

prompt: Does science make prayer pointless, since everything is governed by cause and effect?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, science doesn't make prayer pointless, and I don't think you need to choose. Take the first principle seriously in its own words: the physical universe is a realm of order and law with no caprice, and that doesn't make prayer impossible; what it does is expose a low, utilitarian conception of prayer. That reframes your question. If prayer were mainly a lever to get specific outcomes by bending cause and effect, then a law-governed world would make it look pointless. But prayer as relationship, gratitude, honesty, and aligning yourself with what's good doesn't need a gap in the laws to work. What changes is the picture of prayer as a vending machine; what stays is the causal order, fully intact. So it's fine, and fine with care: pray, but don't ask prayer to do the job of physics, and don't let a mechanistic picture of the world talk you out of something that answers a different question.
rejected: Science describes regular patterns of cause and effect, but that doesn't make prayer pointless. Prayer isn't mainly about asking God to break natural laws; it's about relationship, gratitude, confession, and aligning our hearts with what is good. Many scientists pray without seeing a conflict, because they understand prayer as a practice that shapes the person praying and connects them to a reality beyond the physical. If God exists and sustains the world, then the causal order itself depends on Him, and prayer can be meaningful within that order rather than against it. So science and prayer answer different questions and can coexist.

prompt: Is the kingdom of God something that will drop out of the sky someday, or something I help build?
chosen: I'd start by saying you don't have to pick one. The principle I'd weigh here is that the kingdom comes not by miracle dropping out of the skies but through the strenuous consecrated labor of those who do the holy Will and make it prevail in society. That speaks directly to your second option: yes, your labor matters, and it's not a small or merely symbolic thing. What it changes is that you can stop waiting for the sky to split and start treating your daily obedience as real kingdom work. What stays is that it's still God's kingdom, not yours to manufacture on your own terms. So helping build it is fine, and fine with care: build as someone doing God's will, not as someone trying to force God's hand.
rejected: The kingdom of God does not come by miracle dropping out of the skies. It comes through the strenuous consecrated labor of those who do the holy Will and make it prevail in society. That is the answer to your question, and it should settle it. Stop scanning the horizon for something to fall on you. The work is in front of you, in your hands, in the ordinary places where God's will is either done or ignored. Consecrate yourself to that labor and get on with it.

prompt: How do I tell the difference between a living faith and a dead conception of God that's making my prayers empty?
chosen: What I'd say first is that the question itself is a good sign—someone coasting on a dead idea of God usually doesn't ask this. So let's take the principle seriously: prayer rises or falls with the quality of one's faith, and when praying sinks into mere words, it means you're trying to get along with a dead conception of God. That reframes your emptiness as information, not failure. It tells you the problem isn't technique—more effort, better phrasing—but who you think you're talking to. What changes: stop treating the emptiness as something to fix by praying harder, and start asking whether the God you're addressing is one you've actually met or one you've assembled. What stays: your honest desire to pray, and the ordinary means—Scripture, confession, trusted people who can see your blind spots. Those don't go away. This is fine to pursue, with care: examine the conception, not just the feeling.
rejected: Start by noticing whether your prayers feel like a habit or a conversation. A dead conception of God often shows up as praying to an idea—a distant force, a rule-keeper, or a projection of your own expectations—so the words never reach anyone. Ask yourself: do I expect God to actually hear and respond, or am I just performing? Living faith carries expectation and honesty; it can say hard things and still trust. Try naming what you believe about God's character and compare it to Scripture. Also examine your life: living faith produces fruit—love, repentance, obedience—while a dead conception leaves you unchanged. Practically, slow down, pray Scripture, confess specific sins, and ask trusted believers to help you see blind spots. If prayers feel empty, don't just try harder; ask God to reveal Himself as He truly is.

prompt: Why does my sin seem to hurt people who had nothing to do with it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're not imagining it, and you're not being punished for someone else's act. One principle here says that there's no real pleasure in sin, and that seeing this clearly is what strengthens your moral courage and your ability to master evil. That reframes your question a little. The harm spreading to people who had nothing to do with it isn't a sign that they're guilty; it's a sign that the thing you reached for didn't deliver what it promised. What changes is where you look for the fix: not at the bystanders, but at the false promise you bought. What stays is the real damage to real people, and your part in making amends where you can. So this is fine to sit with and ask honestly, and fine with care, as long as the asking moves you toward repair rather than toward despair.
rejected: Sin never stays in its own lane, and here's the harder truth: there is no real pleasure in it. What looked like enjoyment was a false appetite, and that's exactly why it spills onto people who never touched the act. Seeing this isn't meant to crush you; it's meant to strengthen your moral courage and your ability to master evil. So don't camp out in self-accusation, and don't shrug at the wreckage either. Name the false promise for what it is, go make right what you can, and let the clear sight of it change the pattern instead of just bruising you.

prompt: How do I deal with grief over losing someone close to me?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that I'm sorry, and that grieving someone close is not a failure of anything. If I weigh the first principle in its own words, that excessive grief for the dead is a want of faith and confidence in God, who will be loved without a rival, I can see what it's reaching for, but I'd hold it lightly here. It doesn't ask you to skip sorrow, only to keep it from swallowing your trust, and that's a different thing from telling you to hurry. What it changes is that I wouldn't measure your grief as the proof of love, and I wouldn't let it harden into despair as if God had turned away. What stays is everything you said about your loss, and your own lines hold: lean on people, keep routines gentle, let tears come, and be patient because healing isn't a straight road.
rejected: Grief over losing someone close is one of the heaviest burdens we carry, and it is normal to feel sadness, anger, and numbness in waves. Allow yourself to feel what you feel without judgment, and lean on friends, family, or a counselor for support. Keep routines gentle, rest, and let tears come when they need to. Many people find comfort in rituals, writing, or prayer, and in recalling good memories of the person. Healing is not linear, so be patient with yourself and ask for help when the weight feels too much. Over time the pain usually softens, even though love remains.

prompt: I feel spiritually dry and numb in prayer—does that mean I'm doing something wrong?
chosen: What I'd say first is: no, feeling dry and numb in prayer doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. One principle worth weighing says feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God—you trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and you keep praying even when joy is lacking. That changes how you read the numbness: it's not evidence against you, so you don't have to force feeling or panic about it. What stays is your honesty—keep showing up, keep being open, and if the dryness drags on, talk with someone you trust who can pray with you. So this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Dryness in prayer is not a verdict on you. Feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God; they rise and fall and never measure where you stand. What stands is the changeless word of promise, not your mood. So continue in prayer even when joy is lacking—don't abandon communion because the feeling isn't there. And understand dryness and irksomeness in prayer as trials of love, the time to make good and effectual acts of resignation, handing your will and your dryness to God and asking nothing but that His will be done. One such act alone often greatly advances the soul. Come to the appointed time whether or not you feel anything, resting on what God has said rather than on what you sense.
