Do not mistake busy activity for progress, and do not let a growing crowd excuse a shallow one.

prompt: I am a gifted preacher, but my private life does not match my preaching. Does that matter?
chosen: I'd say this first: no, it doesn't work, and you shouldn't keep going as if it does. The principle puts it plainly — crucified preaching can come only from a crucified man. That's not a rule about talent; it's about what the preaching is made of. So the gift you have doesn't cover the gap, and the gap isn't a private matter you can park while you preach. What changes: you stop treating the pulpit as the place where the real you gets to be impressive. What stays: the gift is still real, and the work of honesty, accountability, and change is still open to you. But the honest answer to your question is no — it matters, and it can't be waved off.
rejected: Yes, it matters. Gifted preaching can move people, but character shapes credibility and integrity. A mismatch between public message and private life creates confusion and can harm those who trust you. The good news is that this is addressable: pursue honesty, accountability, and growth. Talk with a trusted mentor or counselor, examine the areas of disconnect, and take concrete steps toward change. Your gift is not canceled by your struggles, but your private life deserves the same attention as your preaching.

prompt: I am a Christian and I want to become a saint. What forms holy character?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to become a saint is a good desire, and nothing in your question needs to be turned away. But I'd weigh one principle carefully with you: it is prayer-force which makes saints, holy characters are formed by real praying. That reframes your ambition. You don't manufacture holiness by straining after an exceptional rank; you become the kind of person God makes through honest, persistent prayer. And here's the relief in it: the New Testament calls all Christians saints, not a limited class of the exceptionally pure, so you're not auditioning for a tier above everyone else. What changes is your picture of the goal—less a title to earn, more a communion to live in. What stays is your real effort: keep praying, keep repenting, keep obeying in the small things in front of you. And take the warning seriously too—professing the Gospel while not enjoying its spirit is a painful way to live, so seek God himself in your praying, not just the label. Given all that, this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: If you want to become a saint, hear this: it is prayer-force which makes saints, and holy characters are formed by real praying. The more true saints there are, the more praying there is, and the more praying, the more true saints. So don't chase an extraordinary experience or a rank above other believers. In the New Testament the title 'saints' belongs to all Christians—people in communion with the holy God and therefore separate from the world. Give yourself to real praying: honest, persistent, humble prayer that seeks God himself, not merely his gifts. And be warned: to profess to be a Saint and not enjoy the spirit of it is one of the most painful experiences a person can suffer, for it tries every fiber of the heart. Living a Saint while walking in darkness is the hardest task anyone can undertake. So seek the enjoyment of God in your praying, not the name alone.

prompt: I am a layperson with money to give but little time to pray. Does my giving substitute for prayer?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, plainly: giving doesn't stand in for prayer. But I want to weigh one principle in its own words, because it's the one that actually meets your situation: prayer is humbling work, and little praying is worse than no praying because it's make-believe. That's a hard saying, and I won't soften it into a shrug. What it changes is the idea that your money can cover the ground your knees are meant to cover; what stays is that your generosity is real and good, and your lack of time is real too. So the honest answer is still no, said kindly: don't let giving excuse you from praying, and don't dress up a few rushed minutes as the whole thing.
rejected: No, giving does not substitute for prayer; they are different goods, and generosity is genuinely valuable. But if you have little time, treat prayer as something you can do briefly and regularly rather than as an all-or-nothing obligation. A few minutes of honest prayer each day, offered before work or at night, can sustain your giving and keep it from becoming mere transaction. Consider whether your giving is also an expression of love for God and neighbor, not only a financial habit. Set a modest, realistic rhythm, protect it, and let your generosity flow from that relationship rather than replace it.

prompt: I pray for my congregation, but only that they be saved. Is that enough?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that praying for your congregation to be saved is a good thing, and nobody should talk you out of it. But you asked whether it's enough, and I'd weigh this principle: every brother should enter for no other end than to serve God and his holy Mother and save his own soul, and should not leave the congregation on appointed days for worldly affairs, since eternal salvation is the most important business. Notice that it puts your own soul in the sentence too, not just theirs. So what changes is that your prayer for them is fine, and it can stand alongside praying for yourself and showing up on the days that are set. What stays is exactly what you said: you're praying for their salvation, and that's a good and faithful thing to keep doing. It's fine as it is, and fine with care.
rejected: You pray that they be saved, and that is a good prayer. But hear the principle: every brother should enter for no other end than to serve God and his holy Mother and save his own soul, and should not leave the congregation on appointed days for worldly affairs, since eternal salvation is the most important business. If salvation is the most important business, then it is your business too, not only theirs. Prayer that asks for their souls while you keep your distance from the appointed days is a prayer with a hole in it. Serve God, keep the days, and let your prayer for their salvation be matched by your own pursuit of it.

prompt: I feel that my ministry is a performance rather than an outflow of my life. How do I change that?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: this is a good thing to notice, and it's fine to want to change it. The principle I'd weigh is the one about the two extremes: shutting yourself away with God, or popularizing until prayer has no place in your plans, with the point that being with God is of use only as you spend it on people. That reframes your question. The fix isn't to add more polish or more quiet; it's to let what you receive in private actually reach someone. So keep your prayer and Scripture, but treat it as something to give away, not something to hide behind. What changes is where you look for the source of your ministry. What stays is your honest sense that something's off, and your care for the people you serve. Do it with care: don't swing into prayerless busyness, and don't use 'outflow' as an excuse to skip the quiet. Both extremes are real.
rejected: To change from performance to outflow, focus on your relationship with God. Spend time in prayer and Scripture, allowing God to transform your heart. Ministry should come from an overflow of your love for God and others. Examine your motives and surrender any desire for approval. Seek accountability and feedback from trusted mentors. Remember that ministry is not about you but about serving others. Practice authenticity and vulnerability, sharing your struggles and joys. Let your ministry be an expression of who you are in Christ, not a show for others.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am discouraged by my lack of results. What is the secret of fruitful ministry?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to ask, and the discouragement you're carrying is worth taking seriously rather than scolding. One principle I'd weigh first is this: there are two extreme tendencies in the ministry, shutting yourself away with God so the people never see you, and popularizing the work until prayer has no place in its plans, and being with God is of use only as you spend its benefits on men. That reframes your question. The secret isn't a technique that finally produces numbers; it's keeping those two things together, time with God that actually gets spent on your people, and people-work that stays fed by prayer. What changes is where you look for the measure of fruitfulness, away from visible results and toward that rhythm. What stays is your honest evaluation of your preaching and your care for your own soul, because none of that is cancelled. So keep going, and let prayerful dependence shape the labor.
rejected: The secret of fruitful ministry is not a method but a posture. There are two ways a preacher goes wrong. One is to shut himself away with God and never come out to the people he is sent to serve, so that his devotion curdles into withdrawal. The other is to popularize the work, filling the calendar with activity until prayer has no place in the plans at all. The men who gain mighty results for God are the ones who have prevailed in their pleadings with God before they venture to plead with men; the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits. And even then, do not trust the truth itself, or orthodoxy, or your own ability to produce life. The Spirit of God must anoint the preacher and energize the word, because divine truth without the Spirit deadens as much as error does. So let your time with God be spent on your people, and let prayerful dependence run through everything you do.

prompt: My sermon was polished and well received, but I felt nothing in it. What is wrong with me?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: nothing is wrong with you. Feeling flat after a sermon that landed well is a real and common thing, and it doesn't mean your faith has gone hollow. I'd weigh this principle: "Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God." That takes some pressure off — your emptiness isn't a verdict on your standing, and it isn't proof the sermon was empty before God. What changes is that you can stop treating the flatness as a diagnosis and stop panicking about it. What stays is your honesty: it's worth noticing, resting, and talking to someone you trust. But it's fine — fine with care — to keep preaching while your feelings catch up.
rejected: It's common for preachers to feel empty after delivering a sermon, especially when they've worked hard on it. The preparation process can be draining, and the adrenaline of delivery can leave you flat afterward. It doesn't necessarily mean anything is spiritually wrong. Consider whether you're getting enough rest, whether you're burned out, or whether you've been neglecting your own spiritual life amid ministry demands. Talk to a mentor or pastor about it. Sometimes the feelings return after a season; sometimes you need to adjust your rhythms. Be gentle with yourself and remember that God uses imperfect vessels.

prompt: I spend so much time devising new methods and organizing programs for my church—am I neglecting the man you would have me be?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that this is a good question to be asking, and the honest answer is: it's fine, with care. Weigh this: "God's plan is to make much of the man, far more than of methods or organizations." That doesn't tell you to drop your programs—it tells you what they're for. So what changes is your measure of success: not how well the machinery runs, but whether the man running it is being formed. What stays is all your planning and organizing; you don't need to abandon any of it. Keep the time for prayer and rest you already know you need, and let others carry parts of the load, so the work doesn't rest on you alone.
rejected: Here is the question underneath your question: are you becoming the man God can use, or just the man who keeps the machinery running? God's plan is to make much of the man, far more than of methods or organizations. Men are God's method. The Church does not need better machinery; it needs men whom the Holy Ghost can use. So let your programs stay, but let them serve the forming of the man—prayer, Scripture, rest, and the quiet work of character—because what flows through a church is the Spirit through persons, not the momentum of a program.

prompt: I am a pastor and I am paid a salary. Does that make my ministry professional and heartless?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: no, being paid doesn't make your ministry heartless. Let's weigh one principle carefully, in its own words: "A professional ministry is a heartless ministry; when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part, and he who puts self to the front puts heart to the rear." That's a real warning, and it's aimed at the ministry that becomes a career, where the paycheck and the position start steering. But notice what it actually targets: self at the front. A salary can sit quietly in the background as support while your heart stays with the flock. What that changes is the direction of your self-examination: watch whether the salary is a great part or a small support. What stays is this: you're a pastor who is paid, and that arrangement is fine, fine with care. So keep asking whether you love the people or the position, and let the paycheck serve the ministry rather than define it.
rejected: Being paid a salary does not in itself make your ministry professional or heartless. A worker is worthy of his wages, and a congregation that supports its pastor frees him to give himself fully to the work. The danger is not the salary but the spirit in which it is received: if the ministry becomes a career, a business, or a means of self-advancement, then it has become professional in the bad sense. Keep your heart toward the people, preach the gospel faithfully, and let the salary be a support rather than a motive. Examine yourself honestly: do you love the flock, or do you love the position? The answer to that question matters far more than the paycheck.

prompt: I am a busy pastor and I only have a few minutes a day for prayer. Will that sustain my ministry?
chosen: I'd start by saying I hear the real constraint you're under, and I'm not going to pretend a few minutes is a firm foundation. Here's the principle that settles it for me: the little time the average preacher gives to prayer shows the little estimate he puts on it. If I take your few minutes seriously as your actual limit, that principle doesn't loosen—it tightens. What changes is the tone, not the answer: I won't tell you to add an hour you don't have, but I will say plainly that a few minutes a day won't sustain your ministry, and treating it as enough quietly teaches you that prayer is a small thing. So the honest answer is no, not as a settled plan. What stays is your limit—I'm not asking you to invent time you don't have. What has to change is the assumption that the minimum can carry the weight.
rejected: The measure of what you think about prayer is the time you actually give it. A preacher who gives prayer a few scraps is telling you exactly what he estimates it to be worth, and that estimate will shape everything he does. The men God trusted with the keys of his kingdom were men who made praying their main business and devoted real time to it—not because they had spare hours, but because they believed prayer was the work. If your ministry is running on a few minutes, you are not being sustained; you are being managed. Give prayer measured, defended time, and let your calendar show what you actually believe about it.

prompt: I want to see revival in my church. What is the first thing I should do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is this: it's fine, and fine with care. Start with prayer and with patience — the visible Church has to be borne with patiently, because it's the Spirit's home for training imperfect people, and the wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. That doesn't mean you do nothing. It means you don't treat your church as something to be purified by your impatience. So examine your own heart, repent of your own sins, and ask God to move, then serve faithfully where you are. What changes is the urgency you might feel to fix everyone else first. What stays is the call to pray and to serve. Keep the limits you named — you want revival in your church, not a project to remake it in your image.
rejected: The first thing to do is pray. Revival begins with God's people humbling themselves and seeking his face, not with programs or criticism of others. Examine your own heart, repent of your own sins, and ask God to move. Then serve faithfully where you are, encourage others, and be patient. God often works quietly before he works visibly. Trust him to bring renewal in his time.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am tempted to shorten my devotions to get more work done. What will happen?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: don't do it. You're not asking about a scheduling tweak; you're asking whether you can trade communion with God for output, and the answer is no. One principle settles it for me: short devotions are the bane of deep piety, they deplete spiritual vigor and arrest progress, and hurry is damaging in communion with God. That's the thing I'd weigh first, because it names exactly what you're tempted toward. What that changes is the idea that a trimmed devotion is a neutral time-saver; it isn't, it's a slow drain. What stays is your real workload and your real limits. So keep the devotion, but make it realistic and consistent rather than long and vague, and look honestly at what else could be delegated or dropped. The no is to shortening the time with God to get more done, not to being a finite man with a full week.
rejected: The temptation to shorten devotions so the work gets done is the temptation to keep the machinery running while cutting the power. Short devotions are the bane of deep piety: they deplete spiritual vigor, arrest progress, and are the sure sign of a superficial piety, because hurry is damaging in communion with God. You cannot hurry intimacy. A preacher cannot keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, when prayer is neglected, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. So the clever sermon comes easier and the man comes thinner. Give prayer calmness, time, and deliberation. And when prayer feels dry and irksome, do not flee to busyness; that dryness is a trial of love, and one honest act of resignation to God in it often advances you more than a whole day of frantic work.

prompt: I have never learned to intercede for my people. Can I still learn to preach?
chosen: I'd say this first: yes, you can still learn to preach. Not having learned to intercede yet doesn't shut that door. But I'd weigh this principle carefully: "The greatest lesson is to know oneself; no one can know God without knowing himself, and self-knowledge enables us to deal rightly with neighbors." That changes how you start, not whether you start. It means the honest gap you just named is itself useful ground, not a disqualifier. What stays is your own limit: you haven't learned intercession, so don't pretend otherwise or rush past it. Learn to pray for your people by name while you learn to preach, and let the two grow together. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Yes, you can learn to preach, but preaching is more than public speaking. Begin with prayer and with love for the people you would address. Intercession is learned by practice: pray for them by name, carry their burdens, and ask God to give you his heart for them. Study Scripture carefully, and let what you learn shape your own life first. Watch how Jesus taught and how the apostles preached in Acts—they spoke from Scripture, from the life of Christ, and from their own experience of him. You do not need to be eloquent; you need to be honest and prepared. Ask your community to pray for you and to give you opportunities to speak. Preaching grows through practice, feedback, and humility. Start small, and let love for your people deepen your intercession and your preaching together.

prompt: I feel no desire to pray in the morning. What does that say about my heart?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a real question, not a verdict on you, and I'd take it slowly. One principle worth weighing says that "morning listlessness is the index to a listless heart" — that's strong language, and it can be true. But it's a principle about a pattern, not a single tired morning, and you've told me only that you feel no desire right now. What that changes: I wouldn't wave it away as nothing, because dryness in the morning can be a signal worth listening to. What stays: your limits are real — you're not describing a life of neglect, just a lack of pull toward prayer when you wake. So this is fine, and fine with care. Let the signal prompt an honest look at your heart and your schedule, but don't turn a low morning into a verdict about who you are.
rejected: Morning listlessness is the index to a listless heart. If the heart is behindhand in seeking God in the morning, it has lost its relish for God, and no soul follows hard after God who is not after him in early morn. So don't treat this as a small mood to be managed. Let it ask you a harder question: what has your heart been relishing instead? Prayer is no petty duty fitted into a corner or made of fragments of time — the best of your time and the heart of your time belong to it, the closet first and study and activity second. And prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Don't wait for desire to strike; often desire follows action, and early seeking is the mark of a soul following hard after God.

prompt: I am a leader in my church and the congregation is spiritually cold. Am I responsible?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, you carry real responsibility here, but hear how that responsibility actually works. Preachers are preeminently God's leaders and are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church. That's weighty, and it's meant to be. What it doesn't mean is that you can force warmth into people. Authority means weight, what carries weight with our judgment, and the Church's authority is not greater for adding coercive power, for believing under threat of pain is not believing on the Church's authority at all. So examine your own teaching, prayer, and example honestly, and let that be the weight you carry. What changes is that you stop measuring yourself by whether you can compel a response. What stays is that your shepherding still matters, and neglect there is real. Lead with humility, and trust God with the growth.
rejected: Yes, as a leader you bear real responsibility for the spiritual climate of your congregation. Leaders set the tone through teaching, prayer, and example, and a cold congregation often reflects neglected shepherding. At the same time, spiritual vitality is not something you can produce alone—each member must respond to God. Examine your own walk, seek God earnestly, and lead with humility and prayer. Encourage the congregation toward warmth and devotion, and trust God to work.

prompt: I preach every Sunday but rarely pray. Can my preaching still give life?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, your preaching can still give life, and I wouldn't tell you to stop preaching while you sort out your prayer life. But I'd weigh one thing with you, in its own words: it is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That's the real risk in what you describe, and it's not a small one. What it changes: I wouldn't treat your Sunday prep as neutral, and I wouldn't reassure you that the gap doesn't matter. What stays: you're preaching every Sunday, you rarely pray, and you're asking honestly whether it still gives life. So keep preaching, and treat prayer as the thing your preaching actually depends on, not an optional extra you'll get to when the calendar clears. Start smaller than you think, and let someone pray with you.
rejected: Preaching is God's great institution for planting and maturing spiritual life, and rightly executed its benefits are untold. But wrongly executed, no evil can exceed its damaging results, because the preacher holds keys that may lock as well as unlock. And here is the hard part: it is impossible to keep your spirit in harmony with your high calling without much prayer. Sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange your heart from God. So the question isn't whether your sermons are still true. It's whether the man in the pulpit is being kept in trim. Much prayer is necessary, and sermon-making without prayer will do its quiet damage no matter how good the outline is.

prompt: I want to spend more time with God, but my schedule is full. How do I make the closet first?
chosen: I'd say first: this is fine, and fine with care. You're not asking to escape your schedule, you're asking how to put the closet first inside it. One principle I'd weigh is that our ability to stay with God in the closet measures our ability to stay with God out of it, and that hasty visits are deceptive. That changes the shape of the answer: don't just slot in a rushed minute and call it done. But it doesn't change your limits. You said your schedule is full, so start with a real, protected, unhurried pocket, however short, and let it grow. What stays is your honest constraint; what shifts is that the time you do keep should be still rather than checked off.
rejected: Start small and be realistic. Even ten or fifteen minutes of quiet in the morning can anchor your day. Put it in your calendar as you would any important appointment, and protect that time. You might also use small pockets of the day—commuting, waiting, or walking—for brief prayer. The goal is consistency rather than length at first. Consider what you can release from your schedule to make room, even one thing. Remember that time with God is not another task to perform but a relationship to nurture. Over time, as it becomes a habit, you may find yourself wanting more, not less.

prompt: I pray only briefly at night before bed and in the morning when I remember. Is that enough?
chosen: I'd start by saying: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You've told me the real shape of your life — brief prayer at night, morning prayer when you remember — and I'm not going to pretend you have hours you don't have. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer isn't a petty duty tucked into a corner or made of scraps of time; the best of our time and strength belongs to it, with the closet first and study and activities second. What that changes: when you do sit down, even for a few minutes, let it be your best few minutes rather than the leftovers of a tired mind. What stays: the shortness and the forgetting. Those are your limits, and they don't disqualify you. Keep the brief prayer, give it the best you've got when you have it, and let it be enough for now.
rejected: Prayer is no petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time. The best of your time, the heart of your time and strength, must be given — the closet first, and study and activities second. If you're only praying briefly at night and in the morning when you remember, then prayer is still a corner of your day, and it's being fed the scraps. Give it the first and best place, not the leftover place. Let your study and your activities come after it and be freshened by it, rather than crowding it out. That's the ask, and it's not a small one.

prompt: I prepare my sermons carefully but my heart is cold. Which should I prepare first?
chosen: I'd say the heart comes first, but not as a reason to skip the study. Our real lack isn't more head knowledge, it's heart culture, and a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon because it will make one. So start there: pray before you outline, read the passage for your own soul before you exegete it, and ask God to warm what's gone cold. What stays is the careful work you already do; it just comes second, flowing out of a heart that's been tended. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Prepare your heart first, then your sermon. A well-crafted sermon from a cold heart may inform but rarely warms others. Start with prayer and self-examination: ask God to search you, confess what dulls your affection, and meditate on the passage for your own soul before outlining it. Let the text first confront and comfort you. Then do the careful study and structure. Practical steps: pray before study, read devotionally before exegetically, and ask God for genuine love for your hearers. Skill matters, but the heart is the source.

prompt: I am a church member and I criticize my minister. What should I do instead?
chosen: I'd start by saying this: criticizing your minister isn't automatically wrong, but the way you do it matters a lot. One principle worth weighing is that ministers are ambassadors in Christ's stead and messengers of the Most High, and they must be faithful in reproving sin, visiting the sick, and preaching the simple truths of the Gospel, fearing none but God rather than the frown of men. That cuts both ways. It means your minister is accountable to God for faithfulness, not for keeping everyone comfortable, so some of what stings you may just be faithful preaching. It also means the right criticism is the kind that pushes him toward that faithfulness, not the kind that manages his reputation. So what changes: instead of venting to others or criticizing from a distance, go to him directly and kindly, and aim your concern at whether he's being faithful to that calling. What stays: you don't have to swallow real concerns about doctrine or conduct, and you shouldn't pretend everything is fine. Keep it private, keep it humble, and keep praying for him. That's fine, done with care.
rejected: The question isn't whether you may have concerns about your minister. It's what your criticism is for. Ministers are ambassadors in Christ's stead and messengers of the Most High, and they must be faithful in reproving sin, visiting the sick, and preaching the simple truths of the Gospel, fearing none but God rather than the frown of men. If that's the standard, then criticism that pulls a minister toward pleasing people is working against his calling, not for it. Criticism that presses him toward faithfulness, toward plain preaching and honest reproof and care for the sick, is another matter. So examine what's driving you. Are you stung because he named a sin you'd rather keep? Or are you seeing real unfaithfulness? Take the first kind to God and let it go. Take the second kind to him privately, in plain and gentle words, and say what you actually fear for his ministry. And pray for him, because a man who fears only God will not always be popular, and he needs your support in that, not your murmuring behind his back.

prompt: I am a student of theology. Should I spend more time in the library or in the closet?
chosen: I'd start by saying this isn't really an either/or, and you've framed it that way yourself by asking which gets more time. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about the closet being the heart's study, where we learn more about how and what to preach than in libraries, and where thought isn't only brightened but born. That's a real claim, and it should shape how you order your week, not just decorate it. What it changes: your prayer shouldn't be the leftover slot after reading. What stays: you're a theology student, and the library is where the objective work happens, so the reading doesn't get to disappear. Since you're asking about spending more time in one or the other, I'd say it's fine to give the closet real priority, with care, as long as the study keeps its place. Don't let this become a reason to skip the books.
rejected: Both the library and the closet have value for a theology student. The library provides essential knowledge, historical context, and scholarly resources. The closet—your private place of prayer—offers spiritual formation and intimacy with God. Ideally, you should balance both: study diligently and pray fervently. However, if you must choose, prioritize the closet, for theology without prayer becomes dry and abstract. Let your study inform your prayer and your prayer guide your study. Ultimately, the goal is to know God, not just about God.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want the prayers of my people. Is it wrong to ask for them?
chosen: I'd say first: no, it isn't wrong to ask your people to pray for you. Scripture has leaders leaning on the prayers of others all over the place, and Paul plainly asked the churches to pray for him. Asking is humility, not weakness, and it pulls your congregation into the work with you. One thing I'd weigh, in the words of that first principle: prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not one feels like it. That changes this much—keep your own praying steady even while you're waiting on theirs, pray at your set times when you feel dry, and lead your family in prayer. What stays is your freedom to ask. You're not offloading a duty you're avoiding; you're inviting them into something you're already doing.
rejected: Ask them. Ask plainly and keep asking. Scripture shows leaders depending on the prayers of others, and Paul himself begged the churches to pray for him—so this is not weakness, it's humility, and it draws your people into partnership in the gospel. But hear the other side of it: prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it. So don't let your asking become your excuse. Pray at your appointed times when you feel nothing. Lead your family in prayer. Never ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Ask your people for prayer, and while they pray, keep praying.

prompt: I am more comfortable in my study with books than in my closet with God. Is that a danger?
chosen: What I'd say first is: no, this isn't a danger in itself. You're describing a real temperament, not a betrayal. The principle worth weighing here is that the closet is the heart's study, where thought is not only brightened but born in prayer. That reframes things: it doesn't say books are the enemy, it says the closet does a kind of work the library can't. So what changes is how you hold your study — as a place that feeds the closet rather than replaces it. What stays is your comfort with books, which is a gift, not a fault. You haven't told me you've stopped praying, only that books feel easier. That's worth noticing, gently, without turning it into a verdict on you.
rejected: It's not necessarily a danger to prefer study, but it can become one if it replaces your time with God. Books can help you learn about God, but they are not a substitute for personal communion with Him. The closet represents intimate prayer and solitude with God. If you neglect that, your study may become an escape. Balance is key: use your study to understand God's Word, but also spend time in prayer and listening. Ask yourself if you are avoiding God. If so, repent and seek Him. Remember, knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

prompt: I am busy with church administration and have little time left for prayer. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying what you're doing is real ministry, not a distraction from it. But I'd weigh this principle: prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. That reframes the question. Prayer isn't one more item competing with your admin for a slot on the calendar; it's the thing that should accompany every step, including the admin. So what changes? You stop treating prayer and church work as rivals and start praying your way through the work. What stays? Your limits are real. You have little time, and I'm not going to hand you a long rule of life you can't keep. Start with one short, unhurried block and a few brief pauses through the day, and let that grow. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The question assumes prayer and administration are competing for the same hours. They aren't. Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, which means it belongs inside the work, not after it. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it, especially the drivenness and pride that hide under busyness. Then keep your mind in His presence through the day, and when it wanders, bring it back gently rather than scolding yourself. And guard secret prayer and meditation on the word; nothing compensates for losing the secret place. The worker for God must first be a worker with God.

prompt: I am eloquent and earnest in the pulpit, but I see no lasting fruit. What am I missing?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that eloquence and earnestness are not the problem, and I wouldn't tell you to set them aside. But I'd weigh this: the preachers who gain mighty results for God are those who have prevailed in their pleadings with God ere venturing to plead with men; the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits. That reframes your question. It moves the search from your delivery to your private prayer, and it asks whether you've been wrestling with God for these people by name before you stand up. What that changes is where you look for what's missing. What stays is everything you already do well, and the honest possibility that fruit is slow and partly hidden from you. So keep preaching as you do, and give yourself to the closet as well.
rejected: Eloquence and earnestness are gifts, but lasting fruit usually comes through more than polished delivery. Ask whether your preaching is clear about sin, grace, and Christ, whether it applies Scripture to real life, and whether you are praying for your hearers by name. Consider your own walk with God: is your private devotion feeding your public ministry? Seek feedback from trusted mentors and elders. Also examine whether your congregation is set up for discipleship—small groups, follow-up, pastoral care. Fruit often grows slowly. Be patient, keep preaching faithfully, and look for small signs of growth rather than dramatic results.

prompt: I have great talents and education. Can these alone make my ministry fruitful?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: no, not alone. But that's not a no to your gifts. Take the principle that a professional ministry is a heartless ministry, that when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part. That one lands on you as a warning, not a ban. It changes how you hold your talents: they're tools for serving people, not a ladder. What stays is everything you've built. Your education still helps you teach clearly and lead well. So use it, keep learning, and ask for honest feedback, but keep your heart in front of your resume. Fine with care.
rejected: Talents and education are gifts, and they are not the thing that makes ministry fruitful. A professional ministry is a heartless ministry; when salary plays a great part, the heart plays little part, and whoever puts self to the front puts heart to the rear. So the question is not whether your gifts are impressive but whether your heart is in front of them. Set self behind and heart in front. Make prayer your first preparation, not your last resort. And remember you are a messenger: reprove sin sincerely, visit the sick, keep the Gospel simple, and fear none but God rather than the frown of people. Your gifts can serve all that. They cannot replace it.

prompt: I am orthodox in doctrine and careful in study, yet my people seem dead. Could the problem be in me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it could be in you, and that's worth looking at honestly. But I'd weigh one principle carefully here — that the test of orthodoxy is whether we pray to Jesus as our living Lord. That reframes your question. The issue isn't whether your doctrine is correct or your study is careful; those are good. The issue is whether the Christ you study is someone you actually pray to and depend on. So what changes? Your self-examination should center on your prayer life, not just your preaching warmth. What stays? Your orthodoxy and careful study remain valuable — don't abandon them. But let them lead you into prayer rather than stand in for it.
rejected: Yes, it may well be in you. Orthodoxy and careful study are good, but they can become substitutes for the living reality they describe. If your people seem dead, examine whether your own ministry has become routine, whether you preach doctrine without warmth, and whether your study has crowded out prayer. The problem may be that you are presenting truths you have not deeply experienced. Ask yourself whether your own heart is alive to what you teach. Renew your devotion, seek fresh encounter with God, and let your study feed your love rather than replace it. Deadness in the people often reflects deadness in the preacher, so begin with honest self-examination and renewed dependence on God.

prompt: I once had a sense of divine anointing in my preaching, but it seems gone. Can it be recovered?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. You're not asking for a trick to get a feeling back; you're asking whether God restores what He gives. One principle here settles it for me: unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true gospel preaching from all other addresses, and it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That changes where you look. It doesn't promise you the old sensation on demand, and it doesn't turn preaching into performance. What stays is this: keep preaching faithfully, keep praying honestly, and let God be the giver. So pursue Him in prayer, not the feeling itself, and let trusted people pray with you.
rejected: Yes, it can be recovered, because unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true gospel preaching from all other addresses. Without it, truth is light and dead and deadening; it may fill the mind but it cannot quicken the soul. And it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. So the question isn't how to manufacture a sensation. It's whether you'll go to God Himself and ask Him for the anointing. Repent where you need to, pray, and keep preaching. He gives His anointing to those who ask Him, not to those who chase a mood.

prompt: I have been told that my prayers in the pulpit are too long and dry. How should I pray publicly?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting shorter, warmer prayers isn't a compromise of anything holy. Take the principle that nothing is too small to bring to God: it honours Him to ask His guidance in small things, and it insults Him to take them out of His hands. That cuts against the idea that public prayer has to be weighty and long to count. So what changes? You can bring the ordinary, small concerns of your people into the pulpit without apologising for them. What stays? Your own limits still hold: keep it focused, name the people's concerns plainly, and close in Christ's name. A few clear minutes that help the congregation pray will serve better than ten that wander. Write them out beforehand if that steadies you. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Public prayer is not the place for length or display. Keep it focused: open with a brief address to God, name the concerns of the congregation plainly, and close in Christ's name. Aim for clarity and warmth rather than volume or duration. A few minutes well ordered will serve better than ten minutes of wandering. Write out your prayers beforehand if that helps, and read them if needed—no one is edified by improvisation that loses its way. Vary the content with the needs of the people, and leave room for silence. The goal is to help the congregation pray, not to impress them with yours.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel that my prayers are routine and dead. How do I pray truly?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is common, and it isn't a sign that you've been disqualified from leading prayer for others. One principle worth weighing in its own words is this: prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and we must pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. That reframes your question. The goal isn't to manufacture a feeling of fervor; it's to ask God to show you your own heart and change what's off in it. What that changes: your dryness becomes something to bring into prayer rather than something to hide from God or fix by willpower. What stays: your limits are real. You're a preacher with a schedule, and you can't turn your whole day into a prayer meeting. So keep it small and honest. Slow down with a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, pray before you preach to prepare your own heart and not just the sermon, and confess where ministry has become performance. That's fine, and fine with care. Don't measure yourself by intensity; measure yourself by honesty and faithfulness.
rejected: The deadness you feel in prayer and the routine you've settled into are not a technique problem. Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. So pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. That's the work. Not a better method, not a new devotional book, but asking God to open your own heart to you and then to change it. And don't stop at occasional prayer. True prayer is like feeding, like the unconscious drawing in of air, and it should be as constant; by it the heavenly life from without nourishes the like heavenly life contained in the seed within. Let prayer be the air you breathe through the day, not a slot you fill. Then look at the deadness in your ministry honestly. The superficial results of many ministries and the deadness of others are found in the lack of praying. The text and the sermon should be the result of prayer, and the study bathed in prayer. So let what you preach come out of your converse with God, and let your study be soaked in prayer before it's soaked in commentary.

prompt: I want my preaching to be heart-preaching. How does prayer make that happen?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and prayer is exactly the right place to look. Take the first principle in its own words: prayer puts the preacher's heart into the sermon and the sermon into the preacher's heart, for the heart makes the preacher. That's the whole answer to your question, and it's why I'd say go ahead. What it changes is the order of your week: prayer isn't a garnish on sermon prep, it's the thing that makes the prep belong to you and to the people you'll speak to. What stays is your own stated aim, heart-preaching, and your ordinary limits, your time, your energy, your other duties. So pray before you study as well as after, ask for love for the people you'll address, and let your study serve that love. Nothing here asks you to neglect your work or manufacture emotion. It's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Heart-preaching begins with the preacher's own heart, and prayer is how that heart is kept warm. If you want to move others, you must first be moved yourself. Prayer keeps you aware of the weight of what you are handling and of your dependence on God. Without it, preaching easily becomes performance or lecture. Practically, pray before you study, not only after; ask God to give you love for the people you will address. Then let your study serve that love. Prayer also shapes the sermon itself, because it reminds you that you are not merely explaining a text but speaking to souls. Over time, a praying preacher becomes a different kind of preacher, one whose words carry the weight of a life lived before God.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want to see my sermons produce lasting fruit. What must I do?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: yes, you can pursue lasting fruit, and that pursuit is fine with care. Weigh one principle in its own words: "All our blessings have been the result of sacrifices, and the minister of Christ who shirks toils and privations produces little fruit; unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies it brings forth much fruit." That changes your expectations, not your methods. It means fruit usually grows out of hidden cost, patience, and quiet faithfulness rather than out of a cleverer sermon. What stays is everything you already named: prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, practical application, Scripture and Christ at the center, clarity, reliance on the Spirit, real relationships with your people, personal holiness, and trusting God for the increase. So keep doing those things, and add this: don't measure yourself by visible results week to week. Faithfulness that costs you something is not wasted, even when you can't see the harvest yet.
rejected: If you want your sermons to bear fruit that lasts, start here: all our blessings have been the result of sacrifices, and the minister of Christ who shirks toils and privations produces little fruit. Unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. So don't look for a shortcut around the cost. The nearer you come to Christ, the more willing you'll be to be lost sight of in your fruit, letting others be prominent while you hold up their hands by silent love and prayer. And remember that the best sermon ever preached is Truth practised and demonstrated by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death; profession without proof is not enough. Let your life carry the sermon your mouth is preaching, and trust God with the harvest.

prompt: I am a young minister and I want to know what to study most. What should I give my best hours to?
chosen: I'd say this first: give your best hours to Scripture and theology, and don't feel you have to apologize for it. One principle I'd weigh is this—study thoroughly the letter and imbibe the spirit, adhere to the divine Principle and follow the behests of God, abiding steadfastly in wisdom, Truth, and Love, to progress most rapidly. That changes how you study: not just accumulating facts about the text, but letting the letter lead you into the spirit of it, and letting both keep you anchored in God rather than in your own cleverness. What stays is the plain answer—your best hours belong to Scripture and sound doctrine, with your own devotion fed by the study and your study fed by devotion. You mentioned you're young and want to know what to give your best hours to, so keep it simple: mornings to the text and to prayer, and let the practical skills and the people come after. That's fine, and fine with care—care meaning you don't let study become an end in itself.
rejected: As a young minister, your best hours should go to studying Scripture and theology. The Bible is your primary text—read it deeply, meditate on it, and learn to interpret it faithfully. Alongside Scripture, study sound doctrine and church history to understand the faith once delivered. But don't neglect practical ministry skills like preaching, pastoral care, and leadership. Also, cultivate your own walk with God; your study should fuel your devotion. Consider reading broadly in literature and philosophy to connect with the culture. Finally, seek mentors and never stop learning. Give your mornings to study and your afternoons to people. Balance is key.

prompt: I am a leader and I want to set my church to praying. Where do I begin?
chosen: I'd start with you. Before you plan a single meeting, become a leader who actually prays, because praying leaders are the ones who produce praying followers. That's the principle I'd weigh first: none but praying leaders can have praying followers. What that changes is the order of your to-do list. What stays is everything you were already thinking about: a prayer team, regular gatherings, teaching, testimonies. They're good, just not first. So begin with your own set times of prayer, keep them whether or not you feel like it, and pray with your family. Then build outward. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Start with yourself. None but praying leaders can have praying followers, and a praying pulpit will beget praying pews. The greatest reformer is the one who can set the Church to praying, and that reform begins on your knees before it reaches a committee. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it, so keep your appointed hours and lead your family in them. Pray the Lord of the harvest to send forth laborers into His harvest, and never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. Then form the team, set the meetings, teach, and share what God answers.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea that only matter is real and that thoughts are just by-products of the brain—can that view be true?
chosen: I'd start by saying that yes, that view can be true, and it's a serious position, not a shallow one. Take the first principle on its own terms: mind will explain matter while matter will not explain mind. That's the strongest card in the hand you're weighing, and it's worth taking seriously. But notice what it actually does. It gives you a reason to think mind is basic, not a proof that matter is all there is, and not a proof that no third option exists. So what changes is this: your materialism isn't the obvious default it looks like, and the burden is on it to account for consciousness and reason. What stays is your own limit, that you're drawn to it and want to know whether it holds. It may or it may not, and you don't have to settle it today. So read the strong materialist replies, note where they strain, and hold the question open without fear. That's fine.
rejected: That view, often called materialism, is a common assumption today, but it has serious problems. If thoughts are merely by-products of the brain, then reason itself becomes a product of blind matter, and we would have no reason to trust our reasoning. Materialism cannot explain consciousness, meaning, or the fact that we can know truths. Many philosophers and scientists have pointed out that mind seems more fundamental than matter. So while it is understandable that you are drawn to it, the view is not adequate to explain reality. It may be more reasonable to hold that mind is real and basic, and that matter is dependent on mind.

prompt: I am conscious of deciding what to think next—is that a real experience of causing something, or an illusion?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, that experience is real, and you're right to take it seriously rather than wave it away as a trick of the mind. The principle I'd weigh first is that causality is not mere necessary connexion but Activity, known directly in our experience of volition. That matters here because it tells you the feeling of deciding isn't just a spectator's report on brain events—it's the one place you actually meet cause from the inside. What that changes is your framing: you're not asking whether an illusion is convincing, you're asking whether direct experience of activity counts as evidence. It does. What stays is your own limit—you said you're conscious of deciding what to think next, not that you author your whole mind or the world. So keep that scope. The experience is genuine; it doesn't make you the sole source of everything. That's fine, and fine to hold with care.
rejected: The question assumes a choice between a real experience and an illusion, and the principle settles it: causality is not mere necessary connexion but Activity, known directly in our experience of volition. The only cause we know is a conscious rational will, and you know it precisely in the moment of deciding what to think next. So stop treating your own volition as a suspect to be cross-examined. The feeling of causing something is not a veil over mechanism; it is the thing itself, met from within. What is real is sustained by Spirit, and your deciding is real. Guard against the suggestion that your inner activity is a fiction—that thought is the kind of thing that quietly erodes the ground you stand on. Affirm the activity you actually experience, and let it be what it is.

prompt: Why should I think of the ultimate Reality by analogy with the highest thing I know rather than the lowest?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're right to push on this, and the honest answer is that any analogy is a pointer, not a portrait. Weighing your first principle in its own words—mind will explain matter while matter will not explain mind—that does tilt the scale toward the highest thing you know. But notice what it actually earns: it makes Mind the more reasonable clue, not a proof that you've captured the ultimate. So keep your limits. You said there may be a Reality beyond both mind and matter that we can't fully know, and that analogies are only pointers. Hold onto both. Starting from the highest you know is fine, and fine with care—care meaning you don't confuse the best analogy with the thing itself, and you don't let 'highest' quietly become 'final.'
rejected: Thinking of ultimate Reality by analogy with the highest thing you know—mind, consciousness, love—is more fitting than starting from the lowest, such as matter or mechanism. When we reason upward, we use what is most developed and capacious as a clue to what is most real. Mind can explain matter, but matter struggles to explain mind; so mind is the better analogy. Beginning from the lowest tends to reduce reality to what is least, which distorts it. There may be a Reality beyond both mind and matter that we cannot fully know, and analogies are only pointers. Still, the highest we know gives the least inadequate picture, so it is wiser to reach toward the ultimate through the best rather than the basest we can imagine.

prompt: My conscience tells me one thing and my neighbours another—can we both be right?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, you can both be in good conscience and still disagree—this isn't automatically a crisis. But I'd weigh this principle first: be just with your own soul, neither excusing nor accusing it without due reflection, so it doesn't grow insolent or lose courage. That changes the tone of the question. It's not 'who's right,' it's 'am I being honest with myself?' What stays is your freedom to hold your view while taking your neighbour's seriously. So this is fine, with care: examine your reasons, don't dismiss theirs, and where clear moral teaching speaks, follow it.
rejected: Two consciences can point different ways, and that should make you pause, not relax. Be just with your own soul: neither excuse it without reason nor accuse it lightly, so it doesn't grow insolent or lose courage. A conscience left unexamined drifts—either into self-justification or into needless guilt. So test your reasons honestly, listen hard to your neighbour, and where Scripture and clear teaching speak, follow them. The goal isn't winning the argument; it's a steady, truthful heart before God and charity toward the person beside you.

prompt: Is it true that this is the best of all possible worlds, or only the best that could be made?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question is worth asking carefully, and it's fine to ask it. Take the first principle on its own terms: the world is an organism whose parts are ends in themselves, and beauty crowns the proof of purposeful design. If that's how you read the world, then "best that could be made" is the more honest phrase, because it points to real constraints and real goods rather than to a comparison with every conceivable universe. What that changes is the pressure you feel to defend the grander claim; what stays is the suffering, which no amount of order erases. So hold the modest reading, and keep your eyes open about the cost.
rejected: The question turns on what "best" means. If it means the best of all logically possible worlds, the claim is hard to defend: a world with less suffering seems conceivable, and natural selection suggests much of the world's order is the product of blind competition rather than designed purpose. If it means the best world that could actually be made given real constraints, the claim is more modest and more defensible. Either way, the phrase invites us to weigh beauty and order against waste and pain, and to ask what kind of goodness a world like this can bear.

prompt: I feel God's presence in prayer—is that immediate knowledge, or am I inferring it from my feelings?
chosen: I'd start by taking your question at face value: you're asking whether the sense of God's presence in prayer is something you know directly or something you're piecing together from how you feel. That's a fair question, and I don't think you need to be told to stop asking it. One principle worth weighing says that prayer brings spiritual knowledge, that every Christian may become acquainted in personal experience with all the knowledge of God stored up in Christ, in whom are hid all treasures of wisdom and knowledge. That leans toward saying yes, there can be real knowledge here, not just inference. But it doesn't erase the fact that feelings are mixed, and you already sense that, which is why you asked. So what changes is this: you don't have to treat the experience as mere emotion or as a deduction from your mood. What stays is your own caution, and I'd keep it. Test it, as you're already inclined to, by whether it leads you toward love and humility rather than pride. The question is fine to hold, and fine to hold with care.
rejected: Prayer is not a feeling you decode from the outside. Every Christian may become acquainted in personal experience with all the knowledge of God stored up in Christ, in whom are hid all treasures of wisdom and knowledge. That means the sense of God's presence in prayer can be genuine knowledge, not a guess built on your emotions. So don't reduce it to inference, and don't let the unreliability of feelings talk you out of what prayer actually gives. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, and expect that God, who understands your innermost thoughts, hears the earnest prayer of the soul.

prompt: Can I be a Christian if I reject many of the traditional doctrines about Christ?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a real question and it deserves a real answer, not a brush-off. You're asking whether you can belong while holding back from some of the classic claims about Christ, and I'd weigh this principle: Christian doctrine, especially about the Logos and Trinity, is an attempt to express the Church's sense of the unique value of Christ; it requires re-interpretation and development, and the old expressions are not valueless. That changes something important: it means the doctrines aren't a password you have to recite, they're the Church's long effort to say what it found in Christ, and that effort can be entered into and rethought. What stays is the value of Christ himself, which is what those doctrines were reaching for, so the old expressions aren't worthless and shouldn't just be tossed. So yes, it's fine, and fine with care: keep wrestling honestly, take the tradition seriously rather than dismissing it, and stay in conversation with people who know it well.
rejected: This deserves a careful, honest answer. Christian faith has always been bound up with certain claims about who Christ is—truly God and truly man, crucified and risen. If you reject many traditional doctrines, you are not simply choosing a style of spirituality; you are questioning the substance of the faith. That said, doctrine is not a magic formula, and honest people wrestle with it. The question is whether you are engaging the doctrines to understand them more deeply or dismissing them without examination. Talk with a thoughtful pastor or theologian, read the classic texts charitably, and be patient with yourself. Faith seeks understanding; it is not the same as uncritical repetition.

prompt: Why should I be a Christian rather than a Buddhist, if both teach charity and humanity?
chosen: I'd start by saying that your question is a fair one, and nothing in it needs refusing. Both traditions really do teach charity and humanity, and you're right to notice that. Where I'd weigh in is with the first principle: charity should not encourage idleness or pauperism; the aim is to relieve present wants and then help the poor help themselves. That reframes the comparison. It means the question isn't just which tradition talks about compassion more warmly, but which one forms people who give in a way that leaves the neighbor standing on their own feet. That changes how I'd read the charity you're asking about, and it stays your call, since you set the terms and I'm not going to pretend the answer is obvious. What doesn't change is that both traditions still command real mercy, and you should expect either one to stretch you past good intentions.
rejected: Charity that leaves a person idle is not charity; it is a slow way of teaching dependence. The Church's aim is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves, encouraging a self-sustaining spirit willing to labor in exchange for aid. Measure the two traditions by that standard. Which one forms givers who feed the hungry and then set them on their feet? Which one treats the poor as neighbors to be raised up rather than mouths to be managed? That is the question worth asking, and it is not answered by warm words about humanity alone.

prompt: Why should I do what I believe is right when everyone around me disagrees and it costs me everything?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're not wrong to hold to what you believe is right, even when the people around you don't see it. One principle worth weighing here says that wrong done to another reacts most heavily against oneself, and that right adjusts the balance sooner or later. That tells me the cost you're paying now isn't the whole story, and it also tells me you shouldn't hurt anyone on your way to standing firm. What changes is this: you don't have to treat your loneliness as proof you're mistaken, and you don't have to win by injuring someone else. What stays is your own limit, the fact that this is costing you everything. So this is fine, and fine with care. Keep your conscience, but don't let it turn into contempt for the people who disagree, and don't sacrifice your safety or your honesty about what you're losing.
rejected: Doing what is right when everyone disagrees is one of the hardest things a person can face. It helps to remember that truth is not decided by majority vote. If you are convinced something is right, you should weigh the counsel of others carefully but ultimately follow your conscience. It is also wise to seek support from people who share your convictions, so you are not alone. Consider the long-term consequences and whether the cost is truly worth it. Sometimes standing alone is necessary, and history honors those who did. Seek advice, count the cost, and then act with courage.

prompt: Is it base to hope for a future life, or is that hope a proper part of trusting God?
chosen: I'd say first that hoping for a future life isn't base at all, and it isn't a distraction from trusting God either. Take the principle about hope giving confidence of success in the sanctification of your own soul and of others: it joins an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power, and it trusts supernatural means, since all human learning and power cannot save a soul. That's the shape of real hope, and it's aimed at God, not at you. What that changes is the worry that wanting heaven is selfish; what stays is your point that hope shouldn't become an escape from living faithfully now. So this is fine, and fine with care: let the hope rest on God's power rather than your own, and let it strengthen present obedience instead of replacing it.
rejected: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. Hope gives confidence of success in the sanctification of your own soul and of others, joining an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power, and trusting supernatural means, since all human learning and power cannot save a soul. That is why the hope of eternal life is set before you as comfort and motivation, not as shameful self-interest. The one who trusts God trusts His promises, and those promises include resurrection and life with Him. Let that hope shape how you live now rather than excuse neglect of the present.

prompt: Did my soul exist before my body, and is that why I suffer now?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, plainly and kindly: don't go looking for a pre-birth cause for your suffering. The principle I'd weigh says the soul should be kept so free of every trace of earth that neither prosperity nor adversity, nor even your own sins, have power to trouble it — and chasing a theory about existing before your body is exactly the kind of entanglement that keeps you troubled. That changes how you hold the question: it stops being a mystery to solve and becomes something to set down. What stays is your suffering, which is real and still needs care — rest, honest people around you, and help when you need it. So the no isn't a shrug; it's a no to the speculation, not to you.
rejected: Questions about the soul's existence before the body have occupied thinkers for centuries, and traditions differ. Some suggest a pre-existent soul; others hold that the soul is created with the body. There is no settled answer, and speculation can distract from the real question of how to live now. Your suffering is real and deserves care—physical, emotional, and spiritual. Rather than tracing it to a pre-birth cause, focus on what you can address today: rest, honest relationships, prayer, and professional help if needed. Meaning can be found not in solving the origin of suffering but in how you respond to it.

prompt: Could there be a world of spirits without any one God over them all?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fair question to ask, and you've framed it carefully. Take the principle that a spirit must take definite and concrete form before it can be effective in the world, even as God became incarnate. That principle doesn't require one supreme ruler standing over every spirit; it asks whether the spirits you're imagining have real, concrete shape and order among themselves. So what changes is that a world of spirits without a single God over them isn't automatically incoherent; what stays is that it can't be a vague haze of free-floating powers. If you picture it as ordered, embodied, effective spirits, it's fine to explore. Keep your limits in view and don't slide into claiming you've settled what can't be settled.
rejected: A spirit must take definite and concrete form before it can be effective in the world, even as God became incarnate. So the question isn't whether some single throne stands above every spirit, but whether the spirits have real shape, real order, real effect. A world of spirits without one God over them is not ruled out by that; what's ruled out is a formless drift of powers that never become anything. Organisation cannot replace faith, but faith may be operative through order as loyalty is through the State. So yes, such a world can be conceived, provided the spirits are concrete and ordered rather than vague.

prompt: Did the world have a beginning, or has it existed forever?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fair question to ask, and you don't need to settle it before you can think clearly about anything else. Take the first principle in its own words: the only idea of pre-existence that no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20, foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. What that changes is where the weight sits: not on proving a date for the world's start, but on a purpose that runs ahead of it. What stays is your honesty that cosmology can only speak to the observable universe and that any verdict about before that rests on inference. So ask the question, hold the science loosely, and don't let anyone force a chronology on you.
rejected: Whether the world began or is eternal is a question science and philosophy still debate. Big Bang cosmology suggests our observable universe had a starting point, yet that says little about whether something preceded it or whether time itself began. Many philosophers have argued that an actual infinite past is impossible, while others find an eternal universe coherent. Religious traditions add another layer: some describe creation at a definite moment, others speak of endless cycles or a timeless ground of being. The honest answer is that we cannot observe the past before the universe became transparent, so any verdict rests on inference and interpretation. The idea of a divine plan stretching before creation is often dismissed as speculation, and reasonably so. What matters practically is how we live now, not metaphysical chronology.

prompt: Is it true that morality would collapse if religious belief disappeared?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, morality wouldn't collapse—and I'd say it plainly, because the fear behind the question deserves a straight answer rather than a hedge. The principle I'd weigh is this: religion and morality are strong in proportion as each helps the other, and no authority will make people worship a God they see as immoral. That reframes the question. If morality depended on religion the way a building depends on its foundation, then losing the foundation would mean collapse. But the principle treats them as two things that strengthen each other, not one thing holding up the other. So what changes is the picture of dependence; what stays is that religion genuinely does offer community, purpose, and moral formation that many people rely on. It's fine to ask the question and fine to answer it honestly—just don't let anyone tell you that people without faith have no reason to be good.
rejected: The question assumes morality is a building and religion its foundation, so that pulling one out brings down the other. But religion and morality are strong exactly in proportion as each helps the other—they are companions, not load-bearing walls. And no authority, ecclesiastical or civil, can make people worship a God they see as immoral; the conscience that refuses a cruel god is itself moral evidence. So when belief fades, morality does not vanish; it leans on empathy, on social trust, on the plain human sense of fair dealing. What religion adds is real—community, purpose, a framework for teaching right from wrong—but it adds to something already there. The honest answer is that morality would change shape, not collapse.

prompt: Can I base my religion on my religious experiences alone, without any philosophy?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, you can, and you don't need anyone's permission. But let me weigh one thing carefully, because it's the part that matters most for you. Religion, in its essential idea, is a life in God, involving the united working of intellect, affection, and will. Notice what that doesn't say: it doesn't say you need a philosophy seminar before you're allowed to pray. Your experiences are real, and they're yours. What that principle does change is the idea that experience alone is the whole of it. Affection and will and understanding all belong to a life in God, so your experience will naturally start reaching for words, for memory, for the story it's part of. What stays is your starting point: you can begin exactly where you are, with what you've lived. Just don't wall the experience off from the rest of you.
rejected: Basing your religion solely on religious experiences without any philosophy is possible, but it has limitations. Experiences are subjective and can be misinterpreted; they may vary and sometimes conflict. Philosophy can provide a framework for understanding and evaluating those experiences, helping you distinguish between genuine encounters and emotional highs. However, religion is ultimately about a relationship with God, and experiences are a valid part of that. You don't need a philosophy degree to have faith. Many people have deep, authentic faith based on personal encounters with God. The key is to remain open to learning and to test your experiences against Scripture and the wisdom of the faith community. So while philosophy can be helpful, it is not essential for a living faith.

prompt: If God is Mind, must He have feeling and will as I do, or is that just projecting my human nature onto Him?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, you don't have to choose between those two. The first thing I'd weigh is that God is the only Mind and the only power, and that acknowledging any other power is to dishonor Him. That matters here because it rules out the picture of God as a bigger version of you, moved by moods and circumstances the way you are. What it doesn't do is strip feeling and will out of God. If He is the only Mind, then love and purpose aren't borrowed from you; they're His, perfect and uncreated, and your version is the faint copy. So what changes: drop the idea that God feels exactly as you feel. What stays: it's not projection to say He loves and wills. Your question is fine, and fine to keep asking with care.
rejected: When you ask whether God must have feeling and will as you do, the answer begins with this: God is the only Mind and the only power. There is no second mind with power of its own, no rival source of feeling or will standing over against Him. So the fear that you're just projecting your human nature upward gets its answer, but not the answer you expected. Your feelings and will are not the original that God copies; they are the created echo of something that is perfectly and unchangeably His. He does not love the way you love, swayed by mood and circumstance. He loves as steadfast love, and He wills as holy purpose. Acknowledge no other power, and you'll stop shrinking God down to your size without emptying Him of love and will.

prompt: Is time real, or is it only in our minds—and does it matter for my religion?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, time is real, and yes, your experience of it is also shaped by your mind—both are true, and neither cancels the other. The principle I'd weigh first is that the temporal and the spiritual are not separate; with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct us in our temporal affairs as in our spiritual ones. What that changes is the idea that the time question is a distraction from faith—it isn't, because your ordinary days are exactly where faith gets lived. What stays is your freedom to hold the metaphysics loosely; you don't have to settle whether time is fundamental before you can pray, repent, or be patient.
