chosen: I'd say this first: you're asking whether you can have the Holy Ghost and keep the parties and the way you dress, and I think the honest answer is no, not both as you've put it. Here's the principle I'd weigh: missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually. That's not a rule about hemlines or guest lists; it's about a heart that isn't divided. If you're asking to keep something you already sense is pulling you away, the asking itself is the tell. What changes: I wouldn't tell you the parties are automatically sin, and I wouldn't tell you to panic about your clothes. What stays: the call to a clean heart and a life where the Spirit isn't grieved. So the no is this — don't try to hold the Spirit in one hand and the world in the other and call it peace. Bring the whole thing to God honestly, and let Him sort out what has to go.
rejected: As a Christian, you are called to live a life that honors God. While going to parties and dressing like the world are not inherently sinful, they can lead to compromise. The Holy Ghost is given to those who obey God and seek holiness. If these activities cause you to stumble or lead others astray, it's wise to reconsider them. Ask yourself: do these things draw you closer to God or away from Him? Seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit and surround yourself with mature believers who can advise you. Remember, God desires a pure heart and a life set apart for Him. Strive for balance and prioritize your relationship with God above all else.

prompt: How do I believe when I have tried and failed so many times?
chosen: What I'd say first is that trying and failing many times doesn't disqualify you from believing; it's just what a real practice looks like over time. Take the principle that says be faithful in your exercises while staying in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That changes how you read your own history: the failures stop being evidence against you and become the ordinary friction of a habit forming. What stays is the honest work itself—prayer, reading, reflection, whatever you actually do—kept up day after day. So keep going, and don't be shocked when you stumble. That's fine, and it's fine with care: be gentle with yourself, notice what trips you up, and start again.
rejected: Belief is not built by never falling; it's built by staying faithful in the exercises even when you fall. Be faithful in your practice and in no way troubled or astonished when you fail, because fidelity is yours to give and failure comes from infirmity, not from a verdict against you. The time to trust is precisely when everything else has failed, and strong faith is learned by standing firm through hard testing. So don't treat your repeated failures as a reason to quit; treat them as the school where trust gets real. Keep the exercises, bear the weakness without dismay, and begin again.

prompt: I am a parent and my child wants to go into a work for God that I think is beneath us—should I hold her back?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: don't decide this out of fear of status. You've named the real worry yourself—that the work feels beneath you—and that's worth examining before you say a word to her. The principle that lands here is that the will is a divine endowment to be guided, not broken; parents who break a child's will reduce its God-like powers to imbecility. That changes how you hold your concern: you guide, you ask questions, you help her think through motives and preparation, but you don't crush the direction she's testing. What stays is your role as a parent—you can still be honest about your worries, still ask her to prepare wisely, still stay involved. So this is fine, with care: let her explore it, keep talking, and hold your own pride loosely.
rejected: It is understandable to feel protective and to have hopes for your child. Before deciding, talk openly with her about her motives, the work itself, and what support she will need. Consider whether your hesitation comes from genuine concern or from pride about status. Ask trusted mentors for perspective. Ultimately, a calling to serve God is not beneath anyone; many meaningful vocations look humble from outside. Encourage her while helping her prepare wisely. Hold your concerns loosely and let her grow, while staying involved and supportive as she tests this direction.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
chosen: Here's what I'd say first: come to Christ just as you are. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you don't have to get sober before you believe—you couldn't clean yourself up enough for that anyway. But since you asked about what comes next, weigh this: "The believer should cultivate obedience and gratitude, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins, and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized." That changes the picture after faith, not the door into it. So believe now, and then let obedience and gratitude shape your days—confess the drinking honestly, take the practical help that's in front of you, and be thankful for each mercy. What stays is this: nothing you give up earns your salvation, and nothing about your struggle keeps you from coming.
rejected: Come to Christ just as you are—salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you do not have to sober up before you believe. But do not stop there. The believer should cultivate obedience and gratitude, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins, and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized. Drinking is not a small sin to be managed politely; forsake it, confess it plainly, and let gratitude for God's mercy pull you forward rather than your own willpower alone. Grace is not a permission slip. Believe, and then walk in obedience, treating every mercy as a reason to keep going.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that the warning you heard isn't a ban on holiness—it's a warning against self-deception, and those are different things. Take the idea that holiness means being set apart, belonging to God rather than having arrived at some purity of your own. That reframes your question: the saint isn't the person who has achieved something and can point to it, but the person who belongs to God. So the claim you're warned against is a claim of possession—'I have this'—while holiness itself is being possessed. That changes what you're aiming at: not a status to assert but a life handed over. What stays is your honest worry, and it should stay, because it keeps you from the boast. But it doesn't close the door. Holiness on earth is real as a belonging, not as a badge.
rejected: Holiness is possible because it is really about love. God is love, and when we love God and neighbor we are being holy. The warning against claiming holiness is simply a warning against pride; if you stay humble and loving, you are on the right path. Sin is mostly a failure to love, and God's law is basically a guide to loving better. So don't worry about being perfectly righteous—focus on loving people generously, and God will accept that. Growth in kindness and compassion is what sanctification looks like, and anyone who loves genuinely is already holy in God's eyes, even if they never claim the word for themselves.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
chosen: I'd start by saying: this is a good thing you're asking, and nothing here needs to be refused. The one principle I'd weigh is the call to keep rejoicing even when the first bit of renewal feels like it isn't working—keep on with that medicine, and trust God to make the reckoning good. What that changes is the timeline: you don't have to wait for warmth before you act, and you don't have to panic when the cold comes back. What stays is everything you already know—honesty about the drift, confession, turning back, and the small practices of prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience. Feelings lag behind commitment, so let the rejoicing be a discipline rather than a mood, and let people walk with you. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The question isn't whether you feel warm yet—it's whether you'll keep rejoicing while the warmth is still missing. Keep on with that medicine even when it seems to do nothing, and God will make your reckoning good. Name the drift, confess it, turn back, and remember what you first received. Then renew the small things that once fed you—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, obedience—before affection returns, because love often follows faithful action. Don't be discouraged by coldness of feeling; feelings lag behind commitment. Draw near to God and he will draw near to you, and expect gradual renewal rather than instant heat.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
chosen: What I'd say first is: your longing to be heard is itself a kind of prayer, and it's fine to bring that longing honestly. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from His presence or forget to ask. Notice what that does and doesn't claim. It doesn't promise you a feeling of assurance; it says grace is offered, and the asking matters. So your lack of felt assurance isn't proof you're unheard. What changes is that confidence rests on God's faithfulness in offering, not on your sense of being answered. What stays is your honest struggle, and that's allowed to remain while you keep asking. It's fine, and fine with care, to keep praying plainly and to let trust grow slowly.
rejected: Feeling unheard is a common struggle. First, remember that God is not distant or indifferent; He invites you to come to Him. Assurance often grows through practice: pray regularly, even briefly, and reflect on Scripture's promises. Keep a journal of prayers and answers so you can see God's faithfulness over time. Talk with a pastor or trusted friend about your doubts. If sin is weighing on you, confess it and receive forgiveness. Confidence is not a feeling you must manufacture; it is a trust built on God's character. Keep praying honestly, and let others pray with you.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: you're already asking the right question, and that itself is a good sign. I'd weigh the principle that says charity is the light — that charity unmade is God, charity made is our soul in God, and charity given is virtue. What that changes is that your giving isn't just a nice habit to audit; it's a place where God's own love can be at work in you. What stays is your honest wondering: you can still check whether your giving keeps you in faith and hope, or whether it's quietly feeding your pride. But since you've described yourself as generous and giving to the poor, I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. Keep giving. Let it draw you closer to God and to the people you help, and don't let the self-checking turn into paralysis.
rejected: Charity is the light. Charity unmade is God, charity made is our soul in God, and charity given is virtue. So the question isn't whether your giving looks impressive — it's whether it participates in that divine charity. Charity keeps us in faith and hope, and hope leads us in charity until all shall be charity. Test your generosity by that: does it root you in God's own love, or in human sentiment and self-regard? Does it keep you in faith and hope? Does it lead you deeper into charity? If it does, it is of God. And remember, the more generous we are toward God, the more generous we find God toward us, and the more fit we become to receive in greater abundance His graces and spiritual gifts. Give, then, and let your giving be caught up in the charity that is God himself.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
chosen: I'd start by saying your friends' caution isn't the enemy here—it's the voice of people who know you and your tradition, and that's worth hearing. But let me weigh one thing they're leaning on: holding fast to old friends and not letting go unless wicked conduct breaks the thread. That's real, and it's about loyalty, not about freezing every method you've ever used. Keeping faith with them doesn't mean you can't do a new work; it means you don't treat them as strangers while you do it. So what changes is how you carry this—with them, not past them. What stays is your freedom to move if the work honors Christ and serves people. You asked whether to hold back; I'd say it's fine to go forward, with care, and keep the friendship intact as you do.
rejected: Your friends are right to be cautious, but caution should not become a cage. New work is not automatically wrong just because it is unfamiliar; the question is whether it is faithful to Scripture and fruitful for the gospel. Weigh their counsel seriously, since they know you and your tradition. Yet the deciding factor is not whether a method is old or new, but whether it honors Christ and serves people. If the work is sound in doctrine and motive, you need not hold back merely because it is different. Pray, seek wise counsel, and go forward with humility rather than fear.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, that sense of a whole life gone wrong isn't the same as being convinced, and you shouldn't let anyone tell you it is. One of the principles here says you should sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, and desire to be abhorred as filthy mire rather than honored by men. I can see what that's reaching for—it wants to strip away self-defense and pride. But it doesn't fit what you're describing. You're not asking to be humbled; you're asking whether vague regret counts as repentance, and the honest answer is that it doesn't yet. That principle would push you toward despising yourself, and that's not the same as turning around. What stays is the real question underneath: is your regret honest enough to lead somewhere? What changes is that you don't have to manufacture agony or self-hatred to prove sincerity. So I'd say plainly: don't take your current state as sufficient, and don't force it into a mold of self-contempt either. Bring the honest sense of error to God and ask for real clarity about what needs to change.
rejected: You say you feel no great agony over sin, only that your whole life has been one huge error. Hear this: learn not to be troubled by tribulations and injuries, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, and sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn—desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to be honored by men. That is the depth conviction must reach. Your mild regret is not enough; it must become a willingness to be nothing in your own eyes. Do not measure yourself against how much you feel, but against whether you will consent to be humbled to the dust. Let that mind be in you, and let the error of your life fall back upon itself and yield to Truth.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
chosen: I'd start by saying I hear the care in your question—you don't want to wound her, and that instinct is worth keeping. One principle worth weighing is that there's no real pleasure in sin; what looks like enjoyment in wrongdoing is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives. Holding that in view can give you courage to speak, because you'd be helping her toward something better, not just scoring a point. What that changes: you can say something rather than staying silent out of fear of awkwardness. What stays: your limit about not hurting her feelings. So speak privately, gently, and only about what's actually yours to address—and it's fine to say nothing for now if you're not sure it's truly sin or not sure you're the right person. Either way, keep the kindness.
rejected: This is a genuinely difficult situation, and kindness matters. Before saying anything, ask yourself whether the issue is clearly sin or a matter of personal preference, and whether you are the right person to raise it. If you decide to speak, do so privately, gently, and with humility, focusing on your care for her rather than on being right. It can also help to invite her to talk rather than issuing a correction, and to be ready to receive correction yourself. Sometimes the wisest course is to pray and wait. Avoiding harm is a real value, but so is honesty, and the goal is to find a way to be both truthful and loving.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
chosen: I'd have to say no to keeping it, and I want to say that gently but clearly. You asked whether you can hold on to it and still be filled, and the honest answer is that you can't have both. We're in danger, the principle says, of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing. That's the whole thing in one line: keeping what you don't need isn't neutral, it costs you something. What that changes is the idea that this is a small private preference you can carry along without consequence. What stays is everything about you that I don't know—I'm not telling you what the thing is or how fast to let it go, and I'm not saying God loves you less while you struggle with it. But you asked whether you can keep it and still be filled, and on that specific question, the answer is no.
rejected: We are in danger of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing. That is the plain statement, and it should be heard plainly. The question isn't whether the thing is pleasant to you or whether you could argue for it—it's whether you're holding what someone else could use while telling yourself you need it. Holding on entails loss of blessing. Not a small inconvenience, a loss. So the honest counsel is to let it go, and to do it not in your own strength, because on your own you cannot, but by turning to God and asking him to enable you, and strength more than sufficient is given. Do not draw back from Holy Communion over shame or bitterness of heart; draw near, and let your heart be strengthened and united to his meekness. Part with it, and come.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
chosen: I'd start by saying your doubt isn't a sin, and you're not wrong to feel it. But look at what you're actually doubting: you're doubting whether you can restore yourself to God's pattern. The principle says that of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. That's not a reason to despair—it's the whole point. You were never the one doing the restoring. So keep your honest sense that you can't manufacture Christlikeness on your own; that's true and it stays true. What changes is the conclusion you draw from it. Not being able to restore yourself doesn't mean restoration is closed to you. Take one small step of obedience now, not when you feel worthy, and let God be the one who completes it.
rejected: Your doubt is understandable, and many sincere people feel the same. Growth in Christlikeness is a lifelong process, not a single decision. Start where you are: pray honestly, examine your life, and take small steps of obedience. Do not wait until you feel strong or worthy; God meets us in our weakness. Find a community that can support and encourage you, and be patient with yourself. Restoration is God's work, and He is faithful to complete what He begins.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't cut loose from everyone just to feel holy. That's fine to consider, and fine with care. One principle says whatever you do in the way of self-denial has to come from inward joy in God and the Spirit's work, not from custom or the force of example, or you'll regret it and it won't last. That changes how you do it, not whether you can set limits. So if some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Keep your fear in view, talk it through with a mature believer, and let love shape the choices.
rejected: The shortest and only way into the Kingdom, and to be like All Things, is to become as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things, depending on him as the author and fountain of them. So don't turn holiness into a project of self-management. Let every act of self-denial come from inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not from habit, custom, or imitation, because outward practices like that won't last. Be faithful in duty at the beginning, and duty will lead you to pleasures; in every difficulty have recourse to Christ's grace, and he makes it easy. If some ties genuinely pull you into sin, limit them, but do it from joy in God, not fear.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that the delay itself is the thing to look at, not just the habit. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at. You already know this habit is wrong, so 'next month' isn't repentance—it's obedience postponed. That's the plain answer to your question, and I'd rather say it kindly than soften it: no, a promise to stop later isn't the same as turning now. What that changes is the timeline—today, not next month. What stays is that you're not a lost cause; the wound isn't the desperate part, neglecting the cure is. So take up the cure now, however small the first step is.
rejected: It is good that you recognize the habit ought to be given up—that recognition is the beginning of repentance. But promising yourself 'next month' again and again is a warning sign. True repentance involves a real turning, not just a good intention for the future. That said, change is often gradual, and God is patient with our slow progress. You are not necessarily unrepentant just because you struggle. Ask yourself honestly why you keep delaying: is it fear, or comfort, or lack of trust? Bring that to God in prayer and consider what small step you could take today rather than next month. Speak with someone who can support you, and be honest with yourself about the delay.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you already know the answer, or you wouldn't have asked it that way. "Thrives on things that harm souls"—that's your phrase, not mine. So let me weigh one thing with you. The principle says the feeling of blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive a person to prayer and action rather than to rest in personal security. Notice what that doesn't say. It doesn't say your unease is a mood to manage or a scruple to talk yourself out of. It says the unease is meant to move you—toward prayer, yes, but also toward action, and action here means changing the trade, not just praying over it. What that changes: your sleeplessness isn't the problem; it's the signal. What stays: everything you told me about your situation—that the business depends on this, that leaving costs you, that you have people counting on the income. I'm not pretending that's small. But if the harm is the engine of the profit, the honest answer is no, you can't keep running it as it is. Not because I'm certain about every detail of your trade, but because you've described it as thriving on harm, and that's the line. So: no, you shouldn't stay in it as it stands. Start planning the exit, get counsel, and don't let the fear of the cost talk you into calling it something else.
rejected: The question assumes there's a version of this where you keep the trade and keep a quiet conscience, and I want to take that assumption away from you gently but completely. If what you do prospers by damaging souls, then the prosperity and the damage are one thing; you cannot hold the fruit and disown the tree. And the feeling you have about it—that weight over souls going wrong—is not there to be soothed. It's there to drive you to prayer and to action, not to let you settle into personal security and call it peace. Personal security is exactly the trap: a safe income, a settled life, and a quiet arrangement with something that ruins people. The soul that is serious about God cannot rest there. So the call is plain: leave it, and leave it not grudgingly but as a person who would rather be poor and clean than comfortable and complicit. Trust that God provides for those who obey, and go.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your question itself is not the sound of someone who has stopped caring. You're asking whether you can be saved, and that asking is not nothing. I'd weigh the third principle here, in its own words: without knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness we may not have true meekness, and without this meekness we may not be saved, even if we be highly lifted up into contemplation. That principle doesn't tell you to manufacture a feeling of conviction. It tells you that seeing your own hardness honestly is itself the beginning of meekness, and that is available to you right now, cold as you feel. What that changes is this: you don't have to wait for warmth before you come back. What stays is your own limit—you've told me you feel hard and cold, and I'm not going to pretend that isn't real or ask you to perform a feeling you don't have. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: come back honestly, bring the coldness itself, and don't measure your standing by whether your feelings have thawed.
rejected: Yes, you can be saved, and your very grief over hardness is evidence that something in you still answers to God. Coldness of feeling is not the same as final apostasy. Feelings rise and fall; they are not the measure of your standing. What matters is that you turn again toward God, not that you feel deeply. Conviction returning is a gift, and you can ask for it. Do not wait to feel convicted before you act; act, and feeling may follow. Bring your hardness honestly to God, read Scripture even when it seems dull, and stay among His people. Many who felt cold have been warmed again. Your question itself shows you have not stopped wanting Him.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
chosen: What I'd say first is: you don't have to be afraid of God as if he were out to hurt you. The principle I'd weigh here says we must not fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do us great good. That changes the picture of who you're walking toward—it doesn't promise a life without loss or hard days, and it doesn't erase the real cost of committing fully. What stays is your fear itself; it's honest, and it's allowed to be there while you take the next step. So going all the way isn't something to refuse—it's fine, and fine with care, at whatever pace you can actually bear.
rejected: Don't let fear of consequences keep you from going all the way with God. We must not fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do us great good. That's the whole shape of it: the one you're afraid of is the one who means you good. Yes, following him can cost you, and yes, hard things still come—but they don't come because he's scheming against you. Commit yourself to him without that servile dread, and let love, not fear of what might happen, be what moves you.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: your tears aren't the problem, and they don't disqualify you. You're asking whether you can be saved while still holding something you love, and I'd say yes—with care. One of the principles I weigh says we should see our own sin and feebleness by the sweet gracious light of God, yet not accuse ourselves overdone much nor be heavy indiscreetly. That changes how you carry this: honest grief, not self-torment. It doesn't change the call to bring the thing to God and let him work on your grip over time. So keep confessing, keep coming to Christ, and don't despair—grace is patient with you right where you are.
rejected: Your weeping shows your conscience is alive, which is a good sign. But salvation is not about perfectly letting go of every attachment before coming to God; it is about trusting Christ, who receives sinners as they are. Bring this loved thing to God honestly and ask him to change your heart over time. God's grace is patient, and he does not demand that you fix yourself before he saves you. Keep praying, keep confessing, and keep coming to Christ. If the thing is truly sinful, God will gradually loosen your grip as you grow in love for him. Do not despair; grace is greater than your weakness.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
chosen: I'd start by saying the fear you're describing doesn't disqualify you from the conversation—it just means you're paying attention to how you come across. The principle I'd weigh is the first one: commit yourself and all that concerns you to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, rather than giving yourself up to vain and wandering thoughts. That's the real issue here. The fear of a label is exactly one of those wandering thoughts that wears you down and eats your strength before you've said a word. What that changes: you stop rehearsing how people might judge you and treat the outcome as something you can hand over. What stays: your care about not being overbearing. That care is good, and it should shape how you speak—gently, at natural moments, without forcing anything. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Speak honestly and kindly, and let the label worry go.
rejected: The fear of being called a fanatic is a small thing next to the thing itself. Commit yourself and everything that concerns you to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God, in silence and peace, and stop feeding the vain and wandering thoughts about your reputation—they weary your soul and body and waste the time and strength you could spend actually speaking. Accept what comes as from a fatherly hand. If scorn comes, let it come; believe yourself worthy of it rather than clinging to being honoured by people. Wait patiently on the Lord, take what befalls you as meant for your highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ—co-operating with that, you open your mouth and speak to people about their souls, kindly and honestly, and leave the labels to God.

prompt: I was told to just believe I am saved—but I don't feel saved; what should I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: don't force yourself to say you feel saved when you don't. That pressure isn't helping you, and it isn't the same thing as trusting God. But I also can't just hand you a softer version of 'only believe,' because that's the very thing that landed you here. Saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to unconvicted sinners is a grand mistake. So the honest answer is no—I won't tell you to just claim an assurance your heart hasn't come to yet. What I would say instead is to stop chasing a feeling and start being honest about your sin before God, and let your trust in Christ grow out of that honesty. That changes the question from 'do I feel saved?' to 'am I actually turning to him?' What stays is this: your feelings were never the measure, and you don't have to manufacture one.
rejected: Being told to 'just believe' can feel hollow when your feelings do not match. Feelings are not the measure of your salvation; God's promise is. Examine yourself: do you see your sin, and do you turn from it to Christ? If so, believe the promise that whoever comes to Him He will not cast out. Assurance grows from obedience and fellowship, not from emotion. Read Scripture, pray, and walk with God's people. If you are still unrepentant, do not rest on a mere head-belief; repent and turn to Christ. But do not look for a feeling as proof. Trust the Word of God above your changing emotions.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your worry itself is not a bad sign. You're asking whether your repentance is real, and that question comes from someone who cares. But I'd weigh this principle carefully: repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and genuine repentance is shown by obedience, not by the intensity of what you feel. That changes something important. It means the measure isn't how much sorrow you can summon up; it's whether you're actually turning from what you know is wrong. So if you're looking at your life and you're stopping the things you know are wrong and moving toward God, that's the evidence you're looking for. What stays the same is that feelings do matter and they vary, and a quiet heart isn't a false one. So this is fine, and fine with care: don't measure your repentance by the strength of your sorrow, but do let the question push you to honest obedience.
rejected: Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and genuine repentance is shown by obedience. That's the test, not the temperature of your feelings. Sorrow is a gift when it comes, but it is not the thing that makes your turning real. If you know a thing is wrong, stop it, and don't delay, because unregretted sin piles up and hardens the conscience until doing right gets harder and harder. So examine yourself: are you still doing what you know to be wrong? If so, stop at once and reform your life. That is where the proof lies, and that is where your hope lies.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting to work for God is a good place to begin, and nothing here needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh first is this: the first thing necessary in God's service is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. That's where I'd point you, and it doesn't require credentials or a title—just time and attention. What that changes is the order of things: you don't need to have your qualifications sorted before you start seeking; the seeking is the start. What stays is everything practical—get rooted in a local church, serve in small ways, let mature believers affirm your gifts, and let training come later if it comes at all. So this is fine, and fine with care: begin with Scripture and prayer, stay accountable to a community, and don't rush past the small faithful things in front of you.
rejected: Wanting to work for God is a good beginning. The qualifications are less about credentials than about character and readiness. First, a living faith and a willing heart: God uses ordinary people who are available. Second, humility and teachability—be willing to learn from Scripture and from mature believers. Third, faithfulness in small things; start where you are with what you have. Fourth, prayer and dependence on God, since the work is His. Practically, get involved in a local church, serve in small ways, and let others affirm your gifts. Training and study can help, but they follow willingness. Begin with what is in front of you, and let the work grow as you grow.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
chosen: What I'd say first is: you're not doing anything wrong by speaking to people about their souls, and the silence you're getting back isn't proof that you failed. The principle I'd weigh here is that the soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good, playing the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ and co-operating therewith. That changes how you carry the waiting—it's not a verdict on your technique, it's a posture—but it doesn't change the work itself: keep speaking, keep caring, and don't read every non-response as a closed door. What stays is your honesty that nothing seems to come of it; that's real, and you don't have to pretend otherwise. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep going, and let the results rest where you can't control them.
rejected: The soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good, playing the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ and co-operating therewith. You speak and nothing comes of it—so let that befall you as from his hands rather than as a verdict on your worth or your words. A soldier doesn't measure the war by one quiet field. Keep speaking, keep loving, and co-operate with the grace that works where you cannot see it. The waiting is not wasted; it is the ground where patience grows into something sturdier than results.

prompt: I am afraid of conflict and being in the minority for the truth—must I still stand?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your fear doesn't disqualify you from anything. You're asking whether you must stand, and the honest answer is that standing is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh here is this one: millions of unprejudiced minds, simple seekers for Truth, are waiting; give them a cup of cold water in Christ's name and never fear the consequences. Notice what that asks of you. It asks you to give something to people who are actually ready to receive it, not to force a fight with everyone in the room. That changes a lot. It means you can look for the ready seeker instead of bracing against the whole crowd, and it means the cup of cold water can be small, quiet, and kind. What stays is the core: don't let fear talk you out of your convictions when someone is genuinely open. What also stays is your own limit, that conflict frightens you and being alone in the minority frightens you. You don't have to pretend otherwise or throw yourself into confrontation to prove something. So stand where you can, gently, with the people who are listening, and let that be enough.
rejected: It's understandable to fear conflict and being in the minority, but standing for truth is important. You don't have to be aggressive, but you should not deny your convictions. Seek wisdom about when and how to speak. Remember that you are not alone; God is with you. Trust that He will give you courage. It's okay to be afraid, but don't let fear control you. Pray for boldness and look for supportive community. Standing for truth doesn't always mean confrontation; it can be done with love and respect. Consider the consequences, but also consider the cost of silence. Ultimately, ask God for guidance in each situation.

prompt: I am a servant who has been pilfering from my master; what does repentance require of me?
chosen: What I'd say first is: yes, this is fine to bring to God, and fine with care as you go about it. Weigh this one: repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at; genuine repentance is shown by obedience. That changes the timing and the shape of it. You don't wait until you feel sufficiently sorry, and you don't need a grand gesture; you stop the pilfering now and let the obedience carry the repentance. What stays is everything practical: confess honestly to your master, make restitution for what you took or its equivalent, accept the consequences without arguing, ask God for forgiveness and a changed heart, and rebuild trust through steady honesty. Your position as a servant doesn't change any of that; it just means you go about it humbly and within what you can actually do. Nothing here asks you to abandon your duties or your place.
rejected: Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at; genuine repentance is shown by obedience. So the answer is not a feeling but a turning: stop the pilfering at once and never go back to it. Confess honestly to your master, restore what you took or its equivalent, and bear the consequences without excuse. Ask God for forgiveness and for a heart that is actually changed, and let consistent obedience rebuild what dishonesty broke. Repentance is not sorrow that talks; it is obedience that walks.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: eight years of faithful preaching and a hunger for real power is not a failure—it's a good place to be honest. The principle I'd weigh first is this: it is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. Notice it doesn't say your sermons are bad or that you're disqualified. It says the work itself can quietly crowd out the very thing that gives it life. So what changes? You stop treating your lack of power as a mystery and start looking at whether preparation has swallowed your praying. What stays? Your calling, your eight years, and the fact that this is a question to bring to God, not a verdict on you. That's fine, and worth doing with care—not as self-punishment, but as a honest look at where your time and heart have gone.
rejected: Eight years of preaching without power is a painful place, but it is also a place where God can teach you. Power in ministry is not primarily about technique or eloquence; it flows from a life close to God. Ask whether prayer has become secondary to sermon preparation. Ask whether there is unconfessed sin, unresolved conflict, or weariness you have not brought to God. Seek trusted mentors who can pray with you and speak honestly. Remember that faithfulness in small things matters. God often works quietly before He works visibly. Do not despair; bring your lack of power to Him and let Him search your heart.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your gladness doesn't cancel out your love—it tells you where the wound still is. Weigh this: love "suffers never to be without pity." That's the line I'd sit with. It doesn't say your gladness is a fraud; it says pity is the thing that's gone quiet right now, and pity is what love can't do without. So what changes is the verdict you're passing on yourself—you're not a hypocrite, you're someone whose pity got buried under hurt. What stays is your honesty about the feeling and your wish to love well. Bring the gladness to God and name it plainly, and ask for pity to come back, even slowly. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Love suffers never to be without pity. That's the whole answer. When someone who wronged you falls and something in you is glad, the gladness isn't the deepest problem—the missing pity is. Love can't be love and hold no pity at all; it may be wounded, slow, reluctant, but it cannot simply be absent. So don't dress the gladness up as justice and don't despair over it either. Name it, and ask for pity to be restored, because pity is what love cannot do without.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, God isn't deaf, and your discouragement doesn't mean you prayed wrong. I'd weigh this principle: "If God sometimes seems deaf to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us." That reframes the silence—not as absence, but as a wiser answer than the one you asked for. What that changes is the conclusion you draw from the waiting; what stays is your call to keep praying and to keep looking for the quieter work in your own heart and your church. It's fine to hold that hope with care, without pretending you know exactly why the revival didn't come when you expected it.
rejected: It is understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and see no obvious result. But God is not deaf. Scripture assures us that He hears the prayers of His people, and His timing is not ours. Sometimes revival begins quietly, in individual hearts, before it becomes visible in a congregation. It may also be that God is preparing you and your church through the waiting itself. Rather than concluding that God has failed, consider whether He is inviting you to persevere in prayer, to examine your own heart, and to trust His wisdom. Keep praying, and look for the small signs of His work.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that nothing here needs refusing. You're asking why the meetings bless you and the week doesn't change, and that's a fair question, not a wrong one. Take the principle that says work and prayer belong together: work with all your might, but trust not in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, and God delights to give it in answer to earnest believing prayer. That reframes your question. The gap may not be that you're doing too little at home but that you've been resting on the meeting itself as if the blessing were the point. So what changes is where you put your effort and your hope. What stays is everything you told me: you've been coming for years, you go home the same, and you don't want a lecture about trying harder. Keep that. The honest step is small and daily, done alongside prayer rather than instead of it, and it's fine to start there with care.
rejected: You've been going to meetings for years and getting blessed, and you go home and live just the same. The problem isn't the meeting and it isn't that you need more of them. Work and prayer have to go together: work with all your might, but don't trust in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, because God delights to give it in answer to earnest believing prayer. If you've been sitting in blessings and calling that the Christian life, you've been trusting in the meeting the way some trust in their labor. Put your hands to something this week, and put your knees to the floor over it, and stop expecting the high hour to carry you through the flat ones. The blessing was never meant to end at the door.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear doesn't disqualify you from seeking. The principle that fits here is that the spirit naturally loves truth, light, and virtue, but is subject to be overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless enlightened by the Holy Ghost. That means your honest fear is not the same as hardened unbelief; a spirit that loves truth can bring that fear straight to God. What changes is that you don't have to fix your doubt before you gather; what stays is that you still gather, with the fear named rather than hidden. Since you've told me you're afraid nothing will happen, I won't ask you to pretend otherwise or to expect a particular experience. It's fine, with care, to seek with others while you're still afraid.
rejected: It may well be. Jesus often tied the reception of God's gifts to faith, and unbelief can close the door to what He wants to give. But don't turn this into self-condemnation. Start by being honest with God about your fear and doubt, and ask Him to help your unbelief. Then put yourself in the way of His promise: gather with others who are seeking, pray expectantly, and don't let past disappointments define your expectation. Remember that God is not a vending machine responding to your technique or mood; He is a loving Father who gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Keep asking, keep gathering, and let your expectation rest on His character rather than your feelings.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, that's a fine prayer, and it's fine with care. You're not asking for anything wrong—wanting your children to know God and also to be comfortable and respectable is a good and natural desire. One principle worth weighing is that no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God. That changes how you pray, not whether you may: you pray for their conversion with dependence on the Spirit rather than trying to engineer it, and you keep your own walk with God steady. What stays is exactly what you asked for—you can bring both longings to God honestly, keep loving them well, and leave the outcome with Him.
rejected: Bring it all to God—every hope you have for your children, the big one and the small ones. But hear this: no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God. So your praying for your children is not a technique to manage, and their comfort is not the goal you trade the gospel for. Ask counsel of the Scriptures, wait until His will is clear, and let your deepest request be that they be strengthened and consoled in heart—courageous, cheerful, able to face anything—because that is the comfort that lasts. Pray like that, and you will be blessed in your own soul.

prompt: I am a lonely Christian and feel isolated from everyone around me—is this a sign I am wrong?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your loneliness is not evidence that you've done something wrong. One of the principles here puts it this way: solitude is only truly holy when it is interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself, and the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That reframes your question. The issue isn't whether being alone proves you're wrong—it's whether the aloneness is doing anything inside you. So what changes is the guilt: you can set that down. What stays is the honest work of it—being alone can be a place to dwell with God and with yourself, but it can also just be walls. You still get to decide which one you're building. Nothing here asks you to pretend the isolation doesn't hurt or to skip reaching out to people.
rejected: Loneliness is not necessarily a sign that you are wrong. Many faithful Christians have felt isolated, and feelings of loneliness can come from many sources—circumstances, personality, or seasons of life. It does not mean God is displeased with you. What matters is that you do not stay isolated. Reach out to a church community, join a small group, and cultivate friendships. At the same time, learn to be comfortable in your own company and in God's presence. Loneliness can be an invitation to deeper relationship with God and with others. Be gentle with yourself and take steps toward connection.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're not doing anything wrong by not knowing. That's a real place to start, not a failure. The principle I'd weigh here is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we can pray for God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss in them. That fits your situation well, because it means the prayer you can pray right now isn't a clever request for the right thing; it's asking God to show you what's actually in you and to set it right. What that changes is the pressure to come up with the perfect words. What stays is your honesty about not knowing, and that's worth keeping, not fixing. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep it simple, keep it honest, and let the asking itself be the prayer.
rejected: Prayer is not a crisis tool you reach for when you've run out of words; it is meant to be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. So when you don't know what to pray for, that is exactly the moment to pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Nothing is too small to bring to Him, and you honour Him by asking His guidance rather than taking any decision out of His hands. You cannot escape life's dangers without His actual and continual help, so pray continually. You cannot pray without being with Him, cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often, and cannot think of Him often but by a holy habit. Know Him before you love Him; think on Him often, and knowing will turn to loving, and loving will teach you to pray aright.

prompt: I am tempted to leave my vocation because it is hard. What should I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that finding it hard doesn't make you a quitter, and it doesn't automatically mean you're in the wrong place. One principle worth sitting with says we shouldn't desire another vocation or another kind of service, because nothing blocks us from growing where we are like constantly wishing we were somewhere else. That's worth hearing, because restlessness can masquerade as discernment. But it doesn't settle your question by itself. You didn't tell me the difficulty is only boredom or a grass-is-greener itch, and I won't pretend you did. So the honest answer is: stay with it for now, but stay as someone who's actually looking at what's hard, not as someone gritting their teeth and calling that faithfulness. Talk to someone wise, get rest, and give it real time before you decide anything. If, after that, the difficulty turns out to be something that genuinely can't be carried, exploring other options isn't a betrayal. What changes is the reflex to flee the moment it's hard. What stays is your freedom to make a clear-eyed decision later.
rejected: It's normal to feel tempted to leave your vocation when it's hard. First, take time to reflect on why you chose this path. Remember the initial joy and sense of calling. Talk to a trusted mentor or friend who can offer perspective. Consider whether the difficulties are temporary or a sign that something needs to change. Sometimes, a break or retreat can help you gain clarity. Don't make a hasty decision; give yourself space to think and pray. If after careful consideration you still feel called elsewhere, it's okay to explore other options. Your well-being matters, and God may be leading you in a new direction.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your fear is not the enemy here, but it can't be the whole story either. The principle worth weighing is this one — that we must not fear God as though He wished to harm us, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do us great good. That changes the shape of your fear without dismissing it. You can still take sin seriously and still dread the damage it does; what you don't have to do is picture God as waiting to catch you. What stays is your care and your watchfulness under pressure. What changes is the picture of who you're facing. So face the fear by keeping it, but letting love sit alongside it — pray, avoid what you know trips you up, and if you do fall, confess and get up without drama. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: The fear you're carrying is not something to talk yourself out of. One mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul forever, so it is right to hold an intense and abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss — if love of God is too weak to hold you back, fear of hell may. But hear the other side just as clearly: do not fear God as though He wished to harm you. He wishes to do you great good. So love Him fervently, not with the dread of a servant expecting a blow. Under pressure, flee the occasions of sin, pray, and trust His goodness. If you fall, confess and rise. And when small faults come, don't be terrified or paralyzed — humble yourself quietly before God and keep steadily on.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're not alone in this fear, and it's okay to be afraid. The principle I'd weigh first is that it's absolutely certain we'll die, but the time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain, so we prepare now by making the changes we'd wish we'd made when death is near. What that changes for you is the urgency, not the panic. You don't have to solve your whole life this week. What stays is the simple, human work: mend what you can, say what needs saying, and let people you love know it. And because you told me you're dying and afraid, I won't hand you a to-do list as if you had decades. Keep it small. One conversation, one person, one honest word at a time. If prayer or a pastor helps, take that too. This is fine to do, and fine to do gently.
rejected: Facing death with fear is deeply human, and you are not alone. Begin by tending to practical matters: make a will, settle relationships, and say what needs to be said while you can. Spiritually, spend time in prayer and Scripture, and speak with a pastor or trusted friend. Many find peace by reviewing their life with gratitude and entrusting loved ones to God. If you have a long life ahead, use it well; if not, make the most of the time you have. Fear is natural, but faith can grow alongside it. Take it one day at a time, and let others support you.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
chosen: I'd say first: no, don't be discouraged. You're asking whether repeated failure in one spot means you should give up hope, and it doesn't. Here's the principle I'd hold onto: "we must be faithful in our exercises while remaining in no way troubled or astonished if we sometimes fail, since fidelity is ours and failure comes from infirmity." That changes something real—it means your job is the steady faithfulness, not a perfect record—but what stays is exactly what you said: the same area keeps tripping you up, and you keep noticing it. So keep at it with care, review what sets it off, and don't treat a stumble as proof you're disqualified. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Do not be discouraged—and don't let fear get the last word either. Be brave and true to your convictions from the start. Be faithful in your exercises while remaining in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. Keep your prayer, your reading, your honest routines faithfully, and when weakness shows itself, don't be shocked by it—expect it, and let it turn you toward God rather than away. Repeated failure in the same place is common and does not mean you are beyond hope. Stand firm, trust God to stand by you, and keep returning to your exercises without fear or dismay.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear isn't something to be ashamed of. One of the principles puts it this way: the fear of hell is a proof that the religious spirit has rejected the morally indifferent point of view and has become sovereign in union with the ethical spirit. That's a mouthful, but it means fear can show you've grasped that choices matter and that evil isn't shrugged off. So I wouldn't tell you to stamp it out. What changes is that fear doesn't have to be the whole story or the final motive — it can be a real starting point that matures into trust and love. What stays is your honesty about being afraid; keep that, and let it push you toward seeking God rather than away. Talk it through with someone wise, and don't let fear be the only voice.
rejected: Fear of hell is a natural and understandable motive, and it can be a starting point rather than a final one. The Bible takes judgment seriously, and Jesus Himself warned about it. At the same time, mature faith grows toward love of God and gratitude for grace. So do not despise your fear; let it prompt you to seek Christ honestly. Speak with a pastor, read what Scripture says about judgment and mercy, and ask God to deepen your love alongside your reverence. Fear can open the door, but love is the home where faith settles.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: don't wait until you feel powerful. You're not powerless, you're just measuring the wrong thing. Take the principle that says we're powerless of ourselves to save our souls or anyone else's, like a branch that can't bear fruit unless it stays on the vine. That's not a verdict against you, it's a description of where the strength comes from. So what changes? You stop thinking you have to produce the outcome. What stays is the plain, small stuff you can actually do: pray for people by name, be present, be kind, invite someone, tell them what your faith has meant to you. You said you feel powerless, and honestly, that's a fine place to start. It's fine to do this, and fine to do it gently, without pressure on yourself or anyone else.
rejected: You want to help save souls and you feel like you have nothing to give. Hear this: the branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine, and neither can you. That is not a reason to sit still, it is the whole secret. Abide in Christ, keep His commandments, and your prayers become powerful. Stop trying to manufacture power and start staying connected to the source of it. Then act. Pray for the people around you, serve them, speak honestly about what God has done in you, and leave the harvest to God. Small, faithful, loving presence is not a consolation prize. It is the work.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
chosen: I'm so sorry. Before anything else, I want to say that what you're carrying is heavy, and you don't owe anyone a tidy lesson from it. But I have to be honest with you about the advice you're likely to hear, the kind that says you should count yourself as already dead since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than to weep over and detest your own faults, because now is the time to lament rather than rejoice. I'd say no to that. Grief over someone you loved is not a summons to spend your one life at war with yourself, and the fact that death is real doesn't mean your days are only for self-accusation. What changes if you drop that framing: you can let this loss make you take your own death seriously without turning it into a verdict on your worth. What stays: death is real, it comes for all of us, and it's worth letting that shape how you live. You can hold that soberly and still be allowed comfort, love, and even joy. Please be gentle with yourself, and let people close to you help carry this.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. The sudden death of someone you love rightly makes you think about your own mortality. Death is real and comes to all of us, and it is wise to let it teach you to number your days and live with seriousness. At the same time, you need not live in fear. For the believer, death is not the end; it is a doorway into the presence of God, where there is no more sorrow or pain. Grieve honestly, lean on God and on others, and let this loss turn your heart toward what matters most. Take comfort that God is near to the brokenhearted and holds your future.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it costs you, and that's worth taking seriously, but it's not something to be ashamed of or shut down. One principle I'd weigh is this: "Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way." Notice what that does and doesn't say. It doesn't say your motive has to be pure before the good counts. It says keep doing good, somewhere, in some way. So the honest answer is that wanting to be seen can thin out your reward and tilt you toward the visible stuff, and you can work on that gently, practicing quiet good that nobody clocks. But the deed itself still lands in someone's life, and that matters. So keep going, and let the motive grow alongside the action rather than waiting to fix it first.
rejected: The question underneath your question is whether a good deed done for an audience still counts. Here's the principle I'd press: every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way. That's a call to keep your hands busy with good, not a demand that your heart be spotless before you start. So don't stall out waiting to feel pure. Do the good, and do it in hidden places too, where no one claps. Let your life show what Truth and Love actually produce, and let the fruits answer the question rather than your self-analysis. The approval you're chasing will never satisfy, but the good you do still reaches people, and the habit of doing it can reshape why you do it.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
chosen: I'd start by saying: expect criticism, and don't let it rattle you. The principle I'd weigh here is that 'we should not boast over an enemy's downfall' — and notice how it pairs that with seeing things as they are, where 'flattery and reproach are alike.' That reframes the whole thing. It means the person praising you and the person tearing you down are both just weather, and your job is to stay steady and keep your humility growing. What that changes: you stop keeping score against your critics, and you don't quietly enjoy it when one of them stumbles. What stays: you still listen, you still sort real feedback from noise, you still answer calmly and correct the record when it's unfair. So yes, this is fine — respond with a level head and a soft heart, and don't gloat.
rejected: Criticism comes with authority, so expect it and don't take it personally. First, listen carefully and separate useful feedback from mere hostility. Respond calmly and avoid defensiveness; ask clarifying questions. If a criticism is valid, acknowledge it and explain what you'll change. If it's unfair, correct the record briefly and move on. Keep your temper, document serious matters, and rely on trusted advisors for perspective. Over time, consistent fairness and humility will build credibility and reduce the sting of criticism.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it matters, and your question is a good one to be asking. Take the first principle on its own terms — "Am I living the life that approaches the supreme good? Am I demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love?" Notice that it doesn't ask whether your life is large or visible. It asks about the quality of the life you're actually living. So the test isn't scale; it's fruit. That changes the frame of your question: a small, hidden life can still be aimed at the supreme good and can still show healing in how you treat the people near you. What stays is the honesty the principle demands — you can't just assume the fruit is there; you have to actually look. And your limits stay too: you've said your life feels small and hidden, and nothing here asks you to inflate it or perform a bigger one. So this is fine, and fine with care — keep serving where you are, and let the fruit, not the visibility, be what you check.
rejected: The question you're really asking is whether hiddenness disqualifies you. It doesn't. Ask yourself the only question that matters: am I living the life that approaches the supreme good, am I demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love? Your fruits will prove what the understanding of God brings to man. That is the measure — not how many see you, not how large your reach is. Faithfulness in the small and unseen place is not a lesser calling; it is the very place where the supreme good gets lived out. So stop weighing your life against visibility and start weighing it against fruit. Serve where you are, aim at the good, and let your life show the healing it's meant to show.

prompt: I feel God is distant and does not hear me. Why are my prayers unanswered?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that feeling like God is far off while you're praying is a heavy thing to carry, and it doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. I'd weigh this principle: God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul, and just as human invention lets people talk across great distances, God understands our innermost thoughts, so we should pray in faith, nothing wavering. What that changes is the assumption that distance equals silence — your prayer isn't lost in the air. What stays is everything you actually said: you feel distant, and you don't experience an answer. That's real, and nothing here erases it or promises you a timeline. So keep praying honestly, doubts and all; that's fine, and it's fine with care — no pressure to manufacture a feeling of closeness.
rejected: Feeling that God is distant and that your prayers are unanswered can be deeply painful. First, remember that God is not distant—He is always near, but our feelings can deceive us. Unanswered prayers may be due to unconfessed sin, wrong motives, or simply God's timing. Sometimes God says no because He has something better. It's also possible that you're not recognizing His answer because it comes differently than expected. Keep praying persistently, and trust that God hears you. He promises to be found by those who seek Him. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Consider fasting, seeking counsel from mature believers, and meditating on Scripture to align your heart with His will.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You're asking whether perfection is possible for you, and the honest answer is that you're right to feel the gap between where you are and where you'd like to be. One principle I'd weigh is that we must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. That sounds demanding, and it is, but notice what it asks: constancy in aspiring, not instant arrival. So what changes is the direction of your desire, not the timeline. What stays is your real limitation, the fact that you can't manufacture holiness on demand. Aspire steadily, and let the striving be patient rather than frantic.
rejected: Perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness, and that call does not come with an escape clause. Be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. Do not settle for a comfortable, partial love. Aim at the whole thing. Growth is lifelong, yes, but the goal is nothing less than perfect love, and a soul that stops short of that has already begun to fall short. Trust in grace, get up when you fall, and keep your aim high.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
chosen: Before anything else, I'd say: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You've already named the real thing — you know God is asking you to give it up — so the question isn't whether to obey but how to do it without crushing yourself. Weigh this one: when you're in doubt about whether you've done your duty or offended God, humble yourself, beg forgiveness, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. That changes the tone of the whole thing. It means a stumble isn't a verdict on you; it's a moment to get up and begin again, gently. What stays is the honest call to let go and the small steps you can actually take. What shifts is the guilt spiral — you don't have to live there. Keep praying, keep trying, and let the starting-over be part of the obedience itself.
rejected: It's common to struggle with attachments, even small ones. If you know God is asking you to give something up, the first step is to acknowledge that and bring it to God in prayer. Ask for the strength and willingness to let go. Don't be discouraged if you fail; keep trying. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God's commands are for your good, and letting go will ultimately bring freedom. Take small steps, and trust that God will help you. If you stumble, don't dwell on guilt; instead, turn back to God and keep moving forward.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
chosen: I'd start by saying this isn't a wrong thing to want. Chasing a promotion and more money for years is a normal human pull, and the question you're asking is a good one, not a confession. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not being in a hurry to get rich: attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up so you can catch the shower when it comes. What that changes is the pace and the posture, not the goal. It says slow down, stay grounded, keep the rest of your life fed while you work at this. What stays is your ambition itself, which is fine. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep the pursuit honest, keep room for the people and practices that hold you together, and don't let the hurry do the deciding for you.
rejected: The question underneath your question is whether the striving itself has become your god. Hear the principle plainly: do not be in a hurry to get rich. Attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up for the shower when it comes. That is the track. The hurry is what corrodes you, not the paycheck. A person who spends years sprinting after the next rung has quietly decided that the shower will never come unless they force it, and that distrust is the real problem. So keep your dish right side up. Do the work, stay faithful in the small practices, and let the increase come the appointed way rather than by your frantic grasping. Ambition is not the enemy; the hurry is.

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you haven't necessarily done anything wrong. I'd weigh this principle: "work with all your might but trust not in your work, pray with all your might for the blessing." That reframes your question from a fault to find into a pair of things to hold together. What it changes is the assumption that an unanswered prayer means a mistake on your part; what stays is the honest effort, the asking, and the patience. So keep praying earnestly and keep doing your part, and let go of the idea that you must have failed somewhere.
rejected: If you pray for something good and don't receive it, several things could be going on. First, check your motives—are you asking for something that would genuinely be good, or for comfort and status? Second, consider timing: sometimes good things come later. Third, make sure you're also doing your part—prayer isn't a substitute for action, so work diligently toward your goal. Fourth, don't be discouraged; keep praying and stay patient. It may also help to talk with a pastor or wise friend about what you're seeking and why, and to stay open to God answering in a different way than you expected.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is not a failure, and it's fine to bring it honestly. The principle I'd weigh first is this one — that the way into loving and adoring God is not by begging God to come down and make you feel something, but by a steady effort to enter into who He is and offer Him love. That reframes your question. You're not waiting on a feeling to arrive; you're learning to give. What changes is the goal: instead of measuring your affection, you practice offering, and affection is free to follow or lag behind without the whole thing collapsing. What stays is your honesty — duty that feels dry is still real, and you don't have to pretend it's warmth. Keep praying, keep reading, keep serving, and ask for affection too; just don't make the feeling the test of whether any of it counts.
rejected: Love grows when you stop waiting to feel something and start giving something. The way into adoration is not begging God to come down and warm you up; it's the steady effort to enter into His estate and offer Him love. That's the entry point. So learn who He is — in Scripture, in prayer — not as a spectator hoping for a spark, but as someone coming to give. And understand what His love actually is: not a mood or a bargain, but a rational, voluntary giving of Himself that seeks your true good, and it's held under holiness, so it wants your good and not merely your comfort. Then let your love be the outgoing of your whole nature in self-sacrificing service — that's the proof of the thing, not the feeling of it. Recall His mercies, thank Him for specifics, serve at cost. Duty done steadily becomes the channel, and affection deepens in time. Keep showing up and offering.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying: wanting to be liked for good work isn't wrong. You're made to value love and approval, and that's not a flaw to fix. The principle I'd weigh is that we must be what we are and be that well, honoring the Master Workman who made us. That means your wish for praise is part of what you are, not a stain on it. What changes is the pressure you put on praise: let it be a gift you receive, not the thing your worth hangs on. What stays is the good work itself, done honestly whether or not anyone claps. So keep wanting to be liked, and keep your gladness resting somewhere steadier than being noticed.
rejected: Wanting to be liked isn't wrong in itself—humans are social, and approval feels good. The danger is when praise becomes your master: when you do good mainly to be seen, or when criticism crushes you. Ask yourself honestly why you do what you do. If the good work is genuinely good, do it whether or not anyone notices. Practise secret generosity and acts of service no one sees, and let that loosen praise's grip. Accept compliments graciously without depending on them. Aim to please God first, and let human approval be a pleasant extra rather than the point. That way your good works stay good, and your worth doesn't rise and fall with other people's opinions.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: this is a good thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care.
