One principle I'd weigh says we should quicken and enliven our faith, taking faith as the rule of conduct rather than amusing ourselves with trivial devotions that change daily. That's the heart of it for you. So instead of chasing a new technique every week, pick a few steady practices and let them carry you when feelings don't. What changes is the pressure to feel something dramatic; what stays is your honest desire for renewal, which is itself a sign of life. Keep it simple and consistent, and be patient with yourself.
rejected: Hear this: the way forward is to quicken and enliven your faith, to take faith itself as your rule of conduct rather than amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. The way of faith is the spirit of the Church and suffices to bring you to a high degree of perfection. So stop measuring your warmth by how you feel on a given morning. Set your feet on the way of faith and walk in it. Be faithful in duty, deny yourself, and when difficulties come, have recourse to Jesus Christ and beg His grace, with which everything becomes easy. Do not scatter your energy across passing fashions in devotion. Let faith be your rule, and renewal will follow.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
chosen: I'd say first that yes, study can become an end in itself, and I don't think that's automatically a problem. The principle I'd weigh here is that education and continual learning are a religious duty, that knowledge and intelligence come from God, and that we should pursue every useful branch of knowledge. If learning is a duty in its own right, then studying for its own sake isn't a betrayal of anything — it's part of what you owe. What that changes is the anxiety that constant reading is somehow self-indulgent; it isn't, not by this standard. What stays is your own honesty about it: keep asking whether the learning is still opening you outward rather than closing you in, and let it shape how you treat people. But the studying itself? Fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Yes, study can quietly become an end in itself, and that is not always a fault. Constant reading shapes the mind, sharpens judgment, and gives private satisfaction. Still, study risks becoming self-enclosed: you read to read, collect ideas, and never let learning turn outward toward others or toward life. The remedy is balance—keep studying, but ask what your reading serves. Let it inform your work, your conversations, and your character. If study becomes mere accumulation, it can hollow out rather than build up. Yet a life of steady learning, honestly examined, is a good life. The question is not whether you study constantly but whether your study stays open to purpose beyond itself.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're asking a fair question, and the fact that it troubles you is not itself a bad sign. Take the principle that says a sinner isn't reformed just by being told there's no sin — to put down the claim of sin you have to detect it, remove the mask, and point out the illusion. That's useful here, but notice what it asks of you: honest detection, not endless self-inspection. So name the old sin plainly, without softening it, and look at what it actually claimed about you and about God. Then you can see it for what it is rather than circling it. What changes is that you don't have to keep hunting your feelings for proof. What stays is the honest naming and the turning. If you can do that, this is fine, and fine with care — talk it through with someone trustworthy rather than carrying it alone.
rejected: You want to know whether your repentance is real. Stop looking for a feeling and look at the claim. The belief in sin is punished so long as the belief lasts, and forgiveness is the destruction of sin through spiritual understanding that casts out evil as unreal. But you don't get there by announcing that sin is nothing while the claim still sits unexamined. Detect it. Remove the mask. Point out the illusion. Name the old sin for what it is, see the false claim it made, and let that understanding cast it out. Repentance is that turning — away from the claim and into the truth that sets you free.

prompt: I am seriously ill. Should I be praying chiefly for health, or for whatever most leads me to my end?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you don't have to choose between these two, and you shouldn't let anyone force the choice on you. Take the principle that prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we should ask God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss in them. That changes something real: it means prayer isn't just a request list for a cure, it's also the place where you get honest about fear, resentment, and what you're clinging to. But it doesn't cancel the plain, human prayer for health. You can ask for healing and ask to be shown your own heart in the same breath. What stays is your own limit: you're seriously ill, and you're not obliged to turn your illness into a project or a test of your sincerity. Pray for health, pray to see yourself truly, and let the two live together.
rejected: Both matter, but the deeper question is what God is doing in you through this illness. Pray for health—it is right to ask for healing—but do not make physical recovery the only goal. Pray instead for whatever draws you closer to God and fulfills His purpose for your life. Illness often strips away distractions and exposes what we truly love. Ask God for wisdom to see what He is teaching you, for peace in uncertainty, and for grace to trust Him with the outcome. Let your prayer be: 'Lord, heal me if that is Your will, but above all make me the person You intend me to be.' That keeps health in its proper place without making it an idol.

prompt: I find my prayer dry and distracted. Am I praying badly?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that dryness and distraction don't automatically mean you're praying badly. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it. So the fact that it feels dry or distracted is not proof you're doing it wrong; it may actually be the work doing what it does. What that changes is this: don't excuse little praying as acceptable, and don't treat distraction as harmless. What stays is that you can bring your wandering mind back gently, keep showing up, and not be discouraged by your sins or dryness. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, and ask for grace. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Dryness and distraction are not the measure of whether you're praying badly. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it. Little praying is worse than no praying because it is make-believe, so don't excuse it. Approach prayer with awe and strict silence, shutting your senses to distractions, and don't petition God for grace to pray well while openly neglecting precautions against distractions. At the same time, don't be discouraged by your sins or dryness. Pray with perfect confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, for God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from His presence or forget to ask. Keep showing up, and take the work seriously.

prompt: I disagree with my superior's decision. Must I obey anyway?
chosen: I'd start by saying that disagreeing with your boss doesn't automatically mean you have to fall in line, and it doesn't automatically mean you should dig in either. Take the principle that obedience matters because it serves a good, not because going along is an end in itself. That changes something real: your objection should be about the good the decision is supposed to serve, not about tradition or who's in charge. What stays is that you still owe your superior a fair hearing and a respectful route for your concerns. So raise it through the proper channels, ask for clarification, propose an alternative, and if the call is lawful and within their authority, comply while saying plainly that you disagree. If it's illegal or deeply unethical, refuse and escalate. That's fine, and fine with care. Keep your own limits in view: what your role actually requires, what's at stake, and what your conscience will let you do. Talk it over with someone you trust before you decide.
rejected: Disagreement with a superior is common, and obedience is not always simple. In most institutions, you can raise concerns through proper channels, ask for clarification, and propose alternatives. If the decision is lawful and within your superior's authority, you generally should comply while voicing your objection respectfully. If it is illegal or gravely unethical, you may need to refuse and escalate. Think about what is at stake, what your role requires, and what conscience permits. Talk it through with a trusted mentor. The key is to avoid both blind compliance and reactive defiance: be honest, be respectful, and act with integrity.

prompt: I am tempted to impurity. What means should I use against it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: this is a normal fight, and you can win it with care, not panic. The principle I'd weigh first is that "jealousy is the grave of affection" — so if part of your plan is to guard a relationship by spying, checking phones, or demanding an account of someone's time and thoughts, drop that part. It withers trust where trust is owed. What stays is the practical core: cut off access, guard your eyes and your company, turn to prayer or a friend when the pull hits, confess to God and someone you trust, and get up calmly if you fall. Keep your own limits — you said you're tempted, not that you've decided anything — so treat this as habit-building, not a crisis. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The real danger in impurity is not the temptation itself but the frantic way we fight it. So keep yourself in God's presence and let nothing be done in a hurry, because hurry and anxiety are the great obstacles to progress. Guard your senses and remove access, but quietly, without dread — a temptation that displeases you is harmless, and the trouble it causes is mercy refining gold. And do not reach for jealousy or mistrust as weapons; jealousy is the grave of affection, and mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden. Do not shrink someone's worthy outlook by selfish exaction of their time and thoughts. Turn to prayer, activity, a friend; confess; rise calmly if you fall. Gentle patience does more than force.

prompt: I find it hard to forgive someone who hurt me. How should I pray?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that it's fine to pray exactly where you are, even with the hurt still raw. One principle I'd weigh says that without being discouraged on account of our sins, we should pray for grace with perfect confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, and that God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from his presence or forget to ask. That changes the tone of your prayer: you don't have to wait until you feel forgiving before you ask for help, and you don't have to be ashamed of how hard it is. What stays is your honesty about the hurt and your own sense of what you can and can't do right now. So pray something like: Lord, I can't do this yet, give me the grace to want to. Keep it simple, keep it short if you need to, and don't force a feeling you don't have.
rejected: Forgiveness is hard, and it is honest to tell God so. Begin by praying for the person who hurt you, asking God to bless them and to soften your own heart. Ask God to help you release the debt and to heal the wounds the injury left behind. You can also pray for wisdom about boundaries and for the strength to forgive daily, since forgiveness is often a repeated choice rather than a single moment. Confess any bitterness you find in yourself, and ask God to replace it with compassion. Talk with a pastor or counselor if the hurt is deep, and keep bringing the person before God in prayer.

prompt: I have to choose between a secure job and a demanding vocation. How do I decide?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that the question itself is the problem. One of the principles puts it bluntly: we must not desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing prevents attaining the perfection of our vocation like desiring another. Notice it doesn't say the other job is bad. It says the longing for it is what trips you up. So what changes? You stop treating this as a menu and start asking where you actually are and what faithfulness looks like right there. What stays? Your real limits — the family depending on you, the bills, the fact that a demanding vocation can burn people out. Those still count. But they don't turn the choice into a coin flip, and they don't justify spending your days wishing you were somewhere else. So the plain answer is no: don't frame your life as a choice between security and a calling, and don't let the wanting of the other thing run the show. Stay where you are and serve well there, and if a change ever comes, let it come as service, not as restlessness.
rejected: Stop longing for a different state, place, or service. The principle is clear: nothing blocks you from reaching the perfection of your vocation like desiring another one. You want to know which door to walk through, and the answer is that the wanting itself is the thing to put down. Embrace the work in front of you and serve God in the lowly duties at hand; care not what the service is, provided God is served. This asks for conformity to Christ — in outward behavior, in meekness and humility of heart, in taking God's view of things rather than the world's, and in a will zealous for God's glory and the salvation of souls. The question is not which role offers more security or more fulfillment. It is where you may serve with a heart set on God. Don't chase rapid progress through clever methods or the letter alone. Study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and hold steadfastly to the divine Principle. That is the way forward. Let any change come as service, not as escape or ambition.

prompt: I am too busy to pray much. Is that a valid excuse?
chosen: I'd start by saying that being busy is a real limit, not a fiction, and I won't pretend otherwise. Weighing the principle that secret prayer and meditation must not be sacrificed to busy activity, I'd say this: the worker for God must first be a worker with God. That changes something important. It means the question isn't whether you can carve out an hour you don't have, but whether anything at all is being crowded out. A few honest minutes alone with God, kept steadily, still counts as the secret place. What stays is this: don't let the busy season quietly erase it altogether. Given the limits you've described, short and regular is fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Being busy is a real constraint, and it is worth acknowledging that seasons of life vary. But 'too busy to pray much' is rarely a valid excuse in the deepest sense, because prayer does not require large blocks of time. Short, honest prayers throughout the day can sustain a relationship with God even in busy seasons. You might pray briefly in the morning, offer quick prayers of gratitude or petition during the day, and end the day with a short examen. The key is consistency rather than length. If you genuinely cannot find even a few minutes, that may be a sign to examine your priorities. But for most people, the excuse of busyness is more about habit and attention than about actual lack of time.

prompt: I feel desolate in prayer and want to give up early. What should I do?
chosen: I'd say first: don't be hard on yourself for feeling empty. That's a real and common place to be. The principle I'd weigh is this one: feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God; trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep praying even when joy is lacking. What that changes is the pressure to feel something before you can keep going. What stays is your freedom to stop early if you're worn out. You don't owe anyone a performance, and stepping back for a while isn't a failure. If you want to continue, do it gently and briefly, and let the promise carry you rather than your mood.
rejected: Don't measure your prayer by how it feels. Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. The dryness you're in is not evidence that God has left; it's a place to keep standing. So don't give up early. Stay with it, even if all you can do is show up and wait.

prompt: I am afraid of dying young. How should I think about a long life versus a short one?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear is worth taking seriously, not talking yourself out of. The principle I'd weigh first is this: prepare to live, not merely to die. That reframes your question without dismissing it. You're not being asked to pick between a long life and a short one as if length were the whole measure; you're being asked to build something real with the days you have. What that changes is the focus: health, strength, purpose, learning, improving. What stays is your fear, and that's fine, because fear of a short life can push you toward living deliberately. So this is fine, with care: let the fear move you toward building a life rather than toward brooding over its length.
rejected: It's natural to fear dying young, but consider that quality of life matters more than length. A short life lived well can be more meaningful than a long life wasted. Focus on living each day fully, loving God and others, and fulfilling your purpose. Trust that God's timing is perfect, and whether your life is long or short, He is with you. Prepare your soul for eternity, but don't obsess over death. Instead, cultivate gratitude, serve others, and grow in faith. Remember that eternity with God awaits all who believe, so death is not the end. Live with hope and purpose, making the most of the time you have, and leave the number of your days in God's hands.

prompt: I keep putting myself in situations that tempt me. Is that a problem?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it's worth paying attention to, but it's not automatically a failure. The principle I'd weigh first is self-control — learning to know yourself, checking what pulls you, minding your own business rather than faultfinding. That changes the framing: the question isn't whether temptation exists, it's whether you're being honest about the situations you choose. What stays is your own limit — you're asking whether it's a problem, not asking to be scolded. So: it's fine to notice the pattern, and fine with care to keep living your life, as long as you're naming the situations honestly and building some accountability. You don't have to avoid the world to take this seriously.
rejected: The real issue isn't the temptation itself — it's whether you're willing to know yourself. Self-control means checking your words, ceasing from anger, and minding your own business instead of faultfinding. If you keep walking into the same setup, that's not bad luck; it's a choice you're making and not examining. Name the situations, name what draws you to them, and change what you can change. And when you slip, don't sink into gloom — keep on rejoicing, keep on with the medicine of rejoicing even when it seems to do nothing, and trust that the reckoning will come out right. Where something lies beyond your control and only time and patience can solve it, it's no disgrace to say 'I don't know.' Impatience and a gloomy mind do more damage than the temptation ever did.

prompt: I keep committing the same small sins. Do they really matter?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, they matter, and no, this isn't something to brush off. But you asked whether they really matter, not whether you're disqualified. One principle I'd weigh is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and that if sin isn't regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral harm. That's the real concern with repeated small sins: not that each one is catastrophic, but that unregretted patterns dull you over time. What that changes is the seriousness with which you treat the pattern. What stays is that you're not being asked to despair or to treat yourself as beyond grace. Keep bringing these to God honestly, keep turning from them, and let the pattern shrink rather than harden. That's fine, done with care.
rejected: Yes, they matter. Even small sins can become habits that dull your conscience and distance you from God. The Bible says that whoever is faithful in little things is faithful in much. Repeated small sins can lead to greater ones and hinder your spiritual growth. They may seem insignificant, but they grieve the Holy Spirit and affect your relationship with God. However, God's grace is greater. Don't be discouraged; instead, bring them to God in confession and ask for strength to overcome them. Focus on growing in virtue and rely on His help. Remember, God loves you and wants you to grow in holiness.

prompt: I suspect a coworker of bad motives without evidence. Is that a sin?
chosen: I'd say the honest thing first: yes, nursing suspicion about a coworker without evidence is something to refuse, not excuse. Take the principle that says a dishonest position is far from Christianly scientific, that whoever covers his sins shall not prosper but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy. That changes how you hold the suspicion: you stop treating it as harmless and bring it into the light, confess it, and let it go. What stays is your caution about evidence, and you're right to keep it. You don't have proof, so you don't act on the suspicion, don't repeat it, and don't treat it as fact. The no is to the harboring, not to your care about the situation.
rejected: The question isn't whether suspicion feels natural but whether it's honest. A dishonest position is far from Christianly scientific; he that covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy. Suspicion nursed in the dark is a covered sin, and covering it doesn't make it disappear. Bring it out, name it as your own, and forsake it. That doesn't mean ignoring real problems; it means you don't let an unproven story about someone's motives live rent-free in your head and quietly shape how you treat them. Confess it, drop it, and deal with the person honestly if there's ever something solid to address.

prompt: I want to make a good confession before my retreat ends. How should I prepare?
chosen: You're asking how to prepare for confession before your retreat ends, and that's a good thing to want. Here's what I'd say first: the days of a retreat are meant to purify your soul from guilt and from attachment to sin, and confession, with a careful review of your sins beforehand, is the most effective way to do that. So the preparation is really the review: ask the Holy Spirit for light, go through your conscience honestly, and note what you find, including the small things you'd rather skip. That changes the shape of your preparation, but it doesn't change your limits. You're near the end of a retreat, not starting a new way of life, so keep it simple and doable in the time you have. Don't turn the review into a project that overwhelms you, and don't let scruples keep you from going. Confess promptly, receive absolution, do the penance, and be grateful for the mercy you receive.
rejected: To make a good confession, start by examining your conscience. Reflect on the Ten Commandments and the teachings of the Church. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you see your sins clearly. Make a list of your sins, being honest and thorough. Then, go to confession with a priest, confess your sins with sincerity, and receive absolution. Do the penance assigned. Before confession, pray for contrition and a firm purpose of amendment. Also, consider going to confession regularly, not just during retreats. Remember that God's mercy is infinite, and confession is a way to experience that mercy and grow in holiness.

prompt: I have a chance at a position of honor. Should I want it?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting a position of honor isn't wrong in itself. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about offering God your whole liberty, memory, understanding, and will, and desiring only His love and grace. That reframes the question: it's not whether honor is bad, but whether your heart stays ordered toward God and the good of others. If this position helps you keep in His presence and serve people well, it's fine to want it. If it starts feeding pride or pulling you from your duties, that's the signal to step back. So accept it, but hold it loosely and keep checking your motives.
rejected: Honor is not wrong in itself, but the heart must be ordered. Offer God your whole liberty, memory, understanding, and will, holding nothing back, and desire only His love and grace as your chief good. Ask whether this position helps you keep in His presence and labor for His glory and the good of souls, or whether it feeds pride and pulls you from duty. A place of honor is worth wanting only as a means of serving God and neighbor. Let gratitude, humility, devotion, liberality, and honesty shape you: give freely, speak and act consistently and sincerely, and hold the opportunity loosely, ready to accept or decline as best serves His glory and the good of souls.

prompt: I am poor and ashamed of it. How should I see my poverty?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that shame is a heavy thing to carry, and you don't have to carry all of it. One of these principles says poverty often comes from a lack of discretion and sound judgment, from spending on finery beyond what a tight budget can bear. That's worth an honest look, and if some of your spending has been like that, you can correct it without hating yourself for it. What that changes is this: you can examine your habits and make different choices going forward. What stays is that not all poverty is your fault, and your worth isn't measured by your bank balance. So see your poverty with clear eyes and without contempt for yourself, and let people help you when they offer.
rejected: Poverty is not a moral failing, and your shame is understandable but not the whole truth. Much poverty comes from circumstances beyond your control—low wages, bad luck, illness, or an unjust economy—so you should not blame yourself entirely. What matters is your dignity and how you carry yourself. Hold your head up, seek help from community and family, and remember that your worth is not measured by money. Look for small ways to improve your situation over time, and do not let shame keep you from asking for the support you need.

prompt: I eat and drink more than I need. Does that matter spiritually?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. Take the principle that temperance and moderation lay the foundation for the development of the mind, and that food should sustain the body rather than gratify appetite. That's the one I'd weigh first, because it speaks directly to your question. What it changes is the framing: the issue isn't a tally of calories or a rule you're breaking, it's whether eating and drinking are serving your body or running the show. What stays is your own honesty that you're taking in more than you need, and that's worth noticing without turning it into guilt. So eat and drink with some attention and gratitude, let moderation be the aim rather than a scoreboard, and don't let this become a heavy spiritual burden. It matters, but gently.
rejected: Yes, it matters, and the principle is plain: temperance and moderation lay the foundation for the development of the mind, and food is meant to sustain the body, not chiefly to gratify appetite. When appetite sits in the driver's seat, the mind grows dull and the spirit grows deaf to what God is saying. But hear the other side just as clearly: the belief that fasting or feasting makes you better morally or physically is a fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Food does not touch the absolute Life of man. So don't trade one error for another, don't swap indulgence for pride in your discipline. God, Mind, sustains your being; no diet improves your soul. Eat with moderation and gratitude, and let your hunger for God run deeper than your hunger for food.

prompt: I am asked to do a task I think is beneath me. How should I feel?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling like a task is beneath you doesn't make you a bad person, and it doesn't automatically mean you should refuse. One principle I'd weigh is this: unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness; say it is God's business you are about, and find it well performed. That reframes the question from how you should feel to what you're actually doing. What it changes is the resentment, the sense of insult. What stays is your honest read that the task is small or dull. So it's fine to do it, and fine with care, as long as you keep the limits you've set for yourself about what you'll take on.
rejected: It's natural to feel that some tasks are beneath you, but such feelings often stem from pride. Instead of focusing on your own sense of dignity, consider the value of the task itself and the good it can accomplish. Every task, no matter how menial, can be an opportunity to serve others and to grow in humility. Try to approach the task with a willing heart, offering it up as a service to God. Remember that even Jesus washed His disciples' feet, demonstrating that no task is truly beneath anyone. By changing your perspective, you can transform resentment into gratitude and find meaning in the work itself.

prompt: I am offered a comfortable, easy life. Should I prefer it to a harder life that serves God more?
chosen: I'd start by saying the choice itself isn't the problem — you're not being asked to pick comfort over God or God over comfort as if they were rivals on a shelf. What the principle about patience says is that a hard life isn't automatically the holier one; submission and fidelity in a state of suffering can be more precious than busy labor, and health is worth wanting only if it serves God's honor more. That changes how you weigh the offer: don't assume the harder path earns you anything, and don't assume the easier one is a cop-out. What stays is your own honesty about why you'd pick either — fear, pride, weariness, love. So this is fine, with care: take the comfortable life if you can serve God faithfully in it, and take the harder one only if you're drawn there by love rather than by a wish to prove something.
rejected: The question isn't which life is easier but which one you can hand over to God. Abandonment to God in suffering, inside and out, is the excellent thing — living and working and rejoicing only in Him. And patience under crosses, steady fidelity when life is hard, is a more heroic and precious sacrifice than any amount of active labor. So don't chase hardship to feel holy, and don't chase ease to feel safe. Want health and comfort only if they're more expedient for God's honor and your advancement. Hold both at once: the higher beholding that keeps you in solace and true enjoying in God, and the lower beholding of yourself that keeps you in dread and shame — and hold yourself much more in the higher. Then the offer of an easy life is not a trap and not a prize; it's just a place to serve Him more fully.

prompt: I am devoted to Mary but my devotion has grown routine. How can I renew it?
chosen: What I'd say first is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. Your devotion has gone routine, and that's a common thing, not a failure. Weigh this principle in its own words: true devotion to Mary consists in honoring her, invoking her, trusting in her intercession, and striving to imitate her virtues; it is not a license to sin but requires the intention to amend. That reframes renewal for you. It means the fix isn't hunting for a more intense feeling or a bigger devotional program; it's returning to those plain acts, done honestly, with the intention to keep amending your life. What that changes is where you look for renewal: not in novelty but in attention and intention. What stays is everything you already have: your short, consistent prayer time, your honesty about dryness, your patience with yourself, and your plan to talk with a spiritual director or confessor if the routine sticks. Keep those limits. Ask Mary herself to teach you to pray, and let that be enough for now.
rejected: Routine in devotion is common, and renewal usually comes through small changes of attention rather than dramatic ones. Try varying your prayers: read a different Marian prayer or passage each week, or pray a scriptural rosary that pairs each mystery with a verse. Set a consistent time but keep it short enough to remain attentive. Consider learning about Mary's life and the saints who loved her, which can rekindle affection. Add a practice of service in her spirit—humility, availability, care for the poor. Finally, be patient with dryness; feelings are not the measure of faithfulness. Speak honestly with a spiritual director or confessor if the routine persists, and ask Mary herself to teach you to pray.

prompt: I have committed a serious sin and am ashamed to confess it. What should I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: your shame is real, and it doesn't disqualify you from confessing — it's part of what you're carrying into it. One principle here says a lot to me: "whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy." That's a promise attached to confession, not to having your act together first. So what changes is the idea that you need to feel less ashamed before you speak. What stays is that confession is still the right move, and it's fine to make it with care — to a trusted pastor or confessor, naming the sin plainly rather than dressing it up, and letting that person speak forgiveness and help you think through amends. You don't have to perform composure. Go as you are, and let the honesty do its work.
rejected: Shame wants to keep you silent, and silence is where a serious sin grows heaviest. The principle is blunt: he that covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy. Notice the order — mercy follows confession and forsaking, not the other way around. So don't wait to feel worthy. Name the sin plainly, without excuse, first before God and then to a trusted pastor or confessor who can speak forgiveness to you and help you make things right where you've wronged someone. Confession drags the thing into the light and breaks the grip of secrecy. Accept the forgiveness offered, make restitution where you can, and take real steps to avoid the occasion of that sin. Come as you are; that is exactly who confession is for.

prompt: I want to keep up with the news and entertainment every day. Is that harming my soul?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, keeping up with the news and entertainment every day isn't harming your soul by itself. You've told me you want to stay informed and enjoy things daily, and that's a reasonable way to live. The principle I'd weigh is that the soul that makes no daily progress in virtue loses ground, so each day should find us a bit more fervent, with particular resolutions against the occasions of sin. What that changes: it nudges you to check whether the daily habit is crowding out any small step forward, and to name one concrete limit if it is. What stays: your daily keeping up is fine, and you don't need to give it up to grow.
rejected: Keeping up with news and entertainment isn't inherently sinful, but it can harm your soul if it becomes excessive or replaces more important things. Ask yourself: Does it consume time you could spend in prayer, Scripture, or service? Does it fill your mind with anxiety, negativity, or worldly values? The key is moderation and intention. Set limits, choose content that edifies, and prioritize your relationship with God. Remember that not advancing in virtue means falling back. So be proactive: schedule time for spiritual growth and be accountable. If you find yourself compulsively checking, fast from media occasionally. Ultimately, enjoy these things as gifts from God, but don't let them distract you from Him.

prompt: I am drawn to serve the poor and forgotten. Is that a distraction from my duties?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, this isn't a distraction. The pull you feel toward the poor and forgotten sounds like the real thing, and I wouldn't talk you out of it. Take the principle that charity toward the poor and suffering is an indispensable precept, that what is given to the needy is given to Christ himself. That reframes the whole question. You're not choosing between duty and devotion; you're being drawn toward the very place where Christ says he is found. What that changes is the framing: service to the poor isn't a detour from your duties, it's one of them, and a weighty one. What stays is everything you already know about your limits. You still have family, work, and whatever else is on your plate, and nothing here asks you to torch those. So let it be fine, and fine with care: start small, serve through your church or nearby, and let it grow as your capacity allows. Don't let anyone, including me, turn this into a guilt-driven obligation to do everything at once.
rejected: You ask whether serving the poor is a distraction from your duties. Hear the principle plainly: charity toward the poor and suffering is an indispensable precept, and what is given to the needy is given to Christ himself. That means the poor are not an interruption to your discipleship; they are a test of whether it is real. Refusal of the poor is not a minor oversight; it puts the soul at risk. So do not treat this drawing as a hobby or an extra. Give generously, deny yourself unnecessary comforts so you have more to give, and let your joy grow as you spend yourself on those Christ calls his own. The question is not whether you can afford to serve the poor, but whether you can afford not to.

prompt: I want to become a person of prayer. Where do I start?
chosen: I'd say first: start small and start today, and don't wait until you feel ready. One of the principles here puts it this way—prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and holy serving, and all your life-work should be built on the practice of prayer, on your knees, in secret and with believers. What that changes for you is the framing: this isn't a self-improvement project or an extra, it's the foundation. What stays is everything you actually asked about—where to begin. So begin concretely: a fixed ten minutes, a short passage, a few honest words, some silence, and a couple of others who pray so you're not alone. Keep the time whether or not you feel like it, and expect dry stretches without quitting. That's fine, and fine with care—don't let the grand language push you into intensity you can't sustain.
rejected: Start small and start today. Set aside a fixed time each day—even ten minutes—and keep it, whether or not you feel like it. Use a simple structure: a moment of quiet, a short passage of Scripture, a few honest words to God, and silence. Keep a journal of what you notice. Add short prayers through the day, and find a few others who pray so you are not alone. Expect dryness and do not quit when it comes; consistency matters more than intensity. Over months, the habit will shape you, and prayer will become less a task and more a relationship.

prompt: I have spoken badly about a colleague. What must I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: stop talking about it, and then go say something to your colleague. The principle I'd weigh is that we must speak little and well, gently, frankly, and amiably, saying much by a modest and judicious silence. That changes the shape of your repair: fewer words, plainer ones, no long explanation that turns into self-defense. What stays is the honest apology and the correction if others heard you. You don't need a speech. A few frank sentences, then stop, is enough.
rejected: Speak little and speak well. Do not repeat what you said or let it travel further. Go to your colleague and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, so they hear it from you and don't have to guess. If others heard you, correct the record in plain words. Say what you have to say and then stop; don't darken counsel with many words. And while you do this, compel your heart to suffer tranquilly. You will feel murmurings and impatience rising; don't let them govern how you treat the person you wronged. A few honest words, gently and frankly spoken, are better than many.

prompt: I am afraid that if I give everything to God I will lose myself. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing past. The principle I'd weigh is this: of ourselves we can't attain to any good thing, and we have nothing to offer the Lord that wasn't already His. That reframes what you're afraid of losing. If everything you'd hand over was His gift first, then giving it back can't leave you empty, because you were never holding it as your own possession to begin with. What changes is the picture of surrender as a loss. What stays is you, your personality, your gifts, your needs, and the limits you named. So I'd say this is fine, and fine with care: go slowly, keep the boundaries you know you need, and let trust grow in small steps rather than forcing one big leap. Talk it through with someone wise who knows you.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but giving yourself to God does not mean losing yourself—it means finding your true self in relation to Him. Set healthy boundaries, discern what is genuinely yours to give, and remember that God does not ask you to erase your personality, gifts, or needs. Start with small acts of trust and service, and notice that surrender often brings freedom rather than loss. Talk with a trusted pastor or spiritual director about your fears, and be patient with yourself as you grow. The goal is a wholehearted love that integrates who you are rather than destroying it.

prompt: What is the purpose for which I was created, and am I actually living for it?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that asking this at all is a good sign, not a bad one. Take the first principle in its own words: make yourself indifferent to all created things, as far as it's left to free will and not forbidden, not wishing for health rather than sickness, wealth rather than poverty, honor rather than dishonor, a long life rather than a short one, but desiring and choosing only what most leads to the end for which you were created. That sounds severe, but notice what it actually asks: it doesn't tell you to chase a dramatic calling or to despise your ordinary life. It asks you to hold outcomes loosely and aim at the end. So the honest answer to whether you're living for it is: partly, and that's normal. What changes is that you stop grading yourself on health, money, or recognition and start asking whether your days move you toward God and toward loving people. What stays is your ordinary life, your duties, your rest, your care for the people near you. That's fine, and it's fine with care. Look at your time, energy, and money honestly, make small changes where they're needed, and don't turn the question into a verdict on your worth.
rejected: You were made to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever, and to represent him to the people around you. So begin where the principle begins: be indifferent to health or sickness, riches or poverty, honor or dishonor, a long life or a short one, and desire and choose only what most leads to that end. That indifference is not coldness; it's freedom. It means no outcome gets to own you. Then look at your days. Your time, your energy, your money are all saying something about what you're actually aiming at. Do they carry you toward God and toward love of others, or away? You don't need a dramatic calling to answer this. Faithfulness in ordinary duties, in prayer, in care for the people around you is the heart of it. Examine yourself honestly, change what needs changing, and keep growing.

prompt: I am attached to one comfort I cannot give up. Does that hold me back?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that there's nothing wrong with being attached to a comfort, even one you can't give up right now. One principle here says only immortal ties can bless, and only in loving eyes and upon a loving breast does the soul find rest, while the pleasant earth alone cannot satisfy or bind us. That's worth hearing, but it doesn't mean your comfort is a sin. It means the comfort is good and still not the whole thing. So keep it, hold it with care, and let it point you toward the deeper rest rather than standing in for it. What changes is how tightly you grip it; what stays is that you don't have to give it up to be honest before God.
rejected: Attachment to a comfort you cannot give up is worth examining honestly. Comforts are not evil in themselves, but when one becomes something we cannot release, it can function as a kind of dependence that limits our freedom and our openness to God. The question is whether this comfort has become a substitute for deeper trust—something we cling to for security rather than receiving as a gift. You might ask what need the comfort is meeting and whether God could meet that need more fully. You do not necessarily have to surrender the comfort, but you should hold it loosely, with open hands, so that it does not master you.

prompt: I am angry and want revenge on someone who wronged me. What does my faith require?
chosen: I hear how much pain you're carrying, and I want to say the first thing plainly: no, you should not seek revenge. One principle I'd weigh here says that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and that patience and the forgiving of injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That's the whole answer to what you're asking, and I won't soften it into a shrug. What it changes is the direction of your energy: instead of plotting payback, you'd be working toward patience and forgiveness, even slowly. What stays is that the wrong done to you was real and it hurt, and forgiveness doesn't pretend otherwise. It just means you hand the justice over to God and let go of the claim yourself.
rejected: The question you're really asking is whether your faith leaves any room for revenge, and it doesn't. A Christian is never allowed to seek revenge; patience and the forgiving of injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That's not a suggestion for the calm days. It's the shape of the life you're called to, especially when your blood is up and payback feels like the only thing that would set things right. So put the revenge down. Be patient. Forgive the injury, as Christ forgave you. This doesn't mean the wrong was okay. It means you entrust justice to God and release your own claim to settle the score. Pray for the person who wronged you, ask for the grace to forgive, and keep returning to God when you stumble.

prompt: I keep repeating general confessions out of anxiety. Is that healthy?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: this is understandable, and it's fine with care. You're not doing something wrong by wanting to be honest before God. But I'd weigh the principle that says to avoid hurry and anxiety and keep yourself faithfully in the presence of God, since those are the greatest obstacles to progress. That reframes the problem: the issue isn't that you've confessed too little, it's that anxiety is crowding out the quiet trust that confession is supposed to rest in. So what changes is the rhythm, not the honesty. Confess what you actually know, receive mercy, and then stay there without agitation. What stays is your desire to be right with God, which is good. If the pull to repeat keeps coming back, treat that as something to address in itself, gently and with help if you need it.
rejected: Repeating general confessions out of anxiety is common, but it is not the most healthy pattern. Anxiety-driven repetition tends to feed the very fear it tries to soothe, and it can keep you focused on yourself rather than on God's mercy. A better approach is to confess specifically what you are aware of, receive forgiveness with gratitude, and then move on rather than circling back to re-confess. If anxiety keeps pulling you back, address the anxiety itself—through rest, honest conversation, prayer, and perhaps professional help. Set a simple rhythm: confess, thank God for pardon, and trust that He has heard. Repetition born of fear does not make you more forgiven; it only deepens the worry.

prompt: I sleep too much and skip prayer. What should I do?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. You're not asking to abandon prayer; you're asking how to stop missing it, and that's a good thing to want. The principle I'd weigh is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in His presence, and if it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the tone of your effort: the goal isn't a flawless routine, it's showing up and gently coming back when your attention drifts. What stays is the practical part—a fixed wake-up time, prayer first even if it's five minutes, and a simple shape like gratitude, a request for help, silence. Keep your bedtime realistic and adjust it gradually, and if the oversleeping is severe or won't budge, it's worth checking whether something medical is going on. So: allowed, with care, and without turning it into a performance.
rejected: The real question isn't how to squeeze prayer into a busy morning—it's what prayer is. Prayer is not a task to perform but a humble waiting before God, like a beggar who simply stays at the gate of the one who gives. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back in tranquility without disquiet, for trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. Confessing your faults and humbling yourself helps wandering thoughts far more than straining does, and many words often cause wandering, so keep it simple: gratitude, a request for help, silence. Set a fixed wake-up time and put this waiting first, even five minutes. And remember that not advancing is going back—keep pressing forward little by little. When the soul's storms rise, call on the Lord present within you, and He will calm them.

prompt: I have been asked to state my needs to a wealthy inquirer who wants to help. Should I tell him how much I need?
chosen: I'd say this first: yes, tell him what you need, and be specific. But weigh this principle as it's worded—personal solicitation, collections, and collecting-books should be avoided; contributions should come unsolicited, and a collection tends to leave the impression that money is the all-important thing. Since he asked you, you're not soliciting; you're answering. So state your needs plainly, no inflation and no pretending you need nothing, say what you'd do with any help, and ask what form he prefers. What that principle changes is the posture: you lay the matter before him and let him decide, rather than pressing or chasing him. What stays is the honest figure and the transparency. Gratitude and a written note keep it clean.
rejected: Yes, state your needs plainly and specifically. A vague appeal wastes a donor's time and invites misunderstanding; a clear figure or itemized list lets him decide responsibly. Be honest about what you need and what you don't, and say what you will do with any help. Avoid inflating the request to seem more deserving, and avoid pretending you need nothing. Ask what he prefers—a one-time gift, a monthly amount, or something specific—and put the request in writing so there's no confusion. Gratitude and transparency are the right posture; he asked, so answering honestly is not begging.

prompt: I am a believer who has been guilty of a small sin against a family member. Should I confess it, or is it too small to matter?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh is that confession belongs where the sin was committed: against a person, to that person. That's the one that actually speaks to your case, and it changes something real — it means the question isn't whether the sin was big enough to matter, but where it landed. It landed on a family member, so that's where the honesty goes. What stays is your own sense of proportion: you don't need a dramatic production, just a plain acknowledgment and a changed way of treating them. Keep it simple and don't turn it into a burden for them.
rejected: Confession belongs where the sin was committed: against a person, to that person; against a family, to the family; against God, to God. That's the whole shape of it. The size of the fault was never the measure — the direction was. You wronged a family member, so the words go to that family member, not into a private ledger where you file it away as too small to mention. And don't stop at the confession. Don't come to them from a perch of superiority, as though you were doing them a favor by admitting a trifle. Come as one who is also in need, and let the honesty do its work.

prompt: I am considering marriage—how should I choose a companion, and how much should godliness weigh against beauty or money?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to be thinking through carefully, and it's fine with care. Take one principle as it's worded: marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness, not prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. What that changes is the order of things: godliness isn't a nice bonus you slot in after practical compatibility, it's the foundation you build on, and beauty and money stop being the drivers and become things you weigh calmly once that foundation is there. What stays is your freedom to care about attraction and financial stability and to take your time getting to know someone, observing how they handle conflict and talking expectations through openly. So seek godliness first, then weigh the rest honestly and without panic.
rejected: Choose a companion by weighing several factors: shared values, emotional compatibility, physical attraction, financial stability, and age suitability. Beauty and money matter, but they should not be the deciding factors; character and mental compatibility count for a great deal. Take time to know the person, observe how they handle conflict, and discuss your expectations openly. Many people find that attraction grows with familiarity, so do not dismiss someone solely on looks. Godliness is a nice bonus if it fits your beliefs, but practical compatibility is what makes a marriage work day to day.

prompt: I am not sure whether I should break bread every Lord's day or only occasionally. What does the Scripture teach?
chosen: I'd start where you started: Scripture doesn't hand down a line that says 'every Lord's day, without fail.' What it does show is a church devoted to the breaking of bread and gathering on the first day of the week, which is why so many read a weekly rhythm into it. Weighing one principle here: daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil but the insight that God and man work together in ordinary work. That changes how I'd hear your question. Communion isn't a chore you clock in for, and skipping a week isn't laziness before God; it's bread given within the rhythm of your actual life. What stays is this: the table is meant to feed you, so come with self-examination, reverence, and gratitude, and let the frequency serve that rather than become a test of your faith. So it's fine to break bread weekly, and fine to do it occasionally with care, as long as you're not treating either choice as the measure of your standing before God.
rejected: The question isn't really about a calendar; it's about whether you trust bread that comes as a gift. Daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil but the insight that God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. So stop treating the table as a quota to hit or a box to check. The Lord's Supper is bread for the road, given within the ordinary work of your days, not a performance you owe. Come hungry, come honestly, come often if that feeds you, come less if that's where you are, and refuse to make frequency the measure of your devotion. The bread is given; receive it as given.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for a great sum for God's work. Is it right to ask for such great things?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it's fine to ask God for great things for his work, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not one feels like it, and that we should never ask God to do what we are unwilling to do ourselves. That changes the shape of your asking more than its size. It means the great sum you're praying for should come with your own willingness to act, your own labour alongside the prayer, and steady times of prayer kept even when you don't feel like it. What stays is this: the boldness of the request itself is not the problem, and you don't need to shrink it. Keep asking for the work, keep your appointed times, and be ready to help accomplish what you ask.
rejected: Yes, it is right to ask God for great things, especially for his work. God invites us to bring our requests to him, and he is able to provide far more than we ask or imagine. The size of the request is not the problem; the condition of the heart is. Ask boldly, but ask with humility, submitting to God's will and trusting his timing. Remember that prayer is not a way to manipulate God but a relationship with a Father who loves to give good gifts. Keep praying for the work, and trust him to provide as he sees fit.

prompt: I have been asked to speak in a setting where I differ with the hearers on minor matters. Should I go, and how should I conduct myself?
chosen: I'd say go, and go with care. The principle I'd weigh first is this: speak so you can be heard and understood, say what you have to say, and then stop, and don't darken counsel with many words. That changes how you handle the minor disagreements — you name them plainly, in ordinary language, without dressing them up or talking them into a fog, and then you sit down. What stays is your own limit: you said the setting matters, so if it's hostile or would push you to affirm something false, you decline politely. Otherwise, being there with plain speech and a warm tone is fine, and better than staying away over small differences.
rejected: Go, and let your speech be plain. Speak so the whole room can hear and understand you — clear words, ordinary language, no cleverness that hides your meaning. Say what you have to say, and then stop; don't darken counsel with many words. Disagreement on minor matters doesn't call for elaborate maneuvering, only honesty and brevity. And practice restraint in judgment as well as in speech: if you first gain power to check your words, you'll gain power to check your judgment and thoughts. Before you condemn anyone, wait until the fault is clear, and never condemn on rumor. That is how you conduct yourself among people you differ with.

prompt: I have been tempted to think that the success of a work of God depends on advertising and reports. How should I regard such means?
chosen: I'd start by saying: wanting people to know about good work isn't wrong in itself. The principle I'd weigh is that success isn't measured by numbers or money but by faithfulness to God's word and by showing His faithfulness. That changes how you hold advertising and reports: they become tools you use carefully, not the scoreboard. What stays is your honest concern about being tempted, and that concern is worth keeping. So use them, but keep asking whether the work is faithful and whether the message is true, and don't let visibility become the goal.
rejected: Advertising and reports are tools, not the measure of a work of God. It's natural to want people to know about good work, and communication can help others connect with it. But be careful not to let metrics become the goal. Ask whether the work is faithful to what God has called it to be, whether people are actually being served, and whether the message is honest. Reports can encourage supporters and attract resources, which is legitimate, but they can also tempt you to inflate results or chase visibility. Use these means soberly, keep them subordinate to the work itself, and regularly check your motives. Success in God's eyes is faithfulness, not publicity.

prompt: I have lost a beloved family member and cannot see any good in it—how can this work together for good?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that I'm sorry, and that not seeing any good in this right now is not a failure on your part. If I weigh the principle that says we should never lose sight of God, making a firm resolution never more wilfully to forget Him and to spend the rest of our days in His presence, deprived if He thinks fit of all consolations—I notice it's a resolution about your own turning, not a demand that you find the loss good. That changes something: the question shifts from 'where is the good in this?' to 'will you keep facing toward God while you can't see it?' What stays is the grief itself. The principle doesn't ask you to call the death good, and it doesn't ask you to feel consolations you don't feel. So this is fine, and fine with care—let yourself grieve, lean on people who love you, and keep turning toward God in the dark without forcing an answer you don't have.
rejected: The resolution worth making is not that you will find the good in this, but that you will never wilfully forget Him, and will spend your days in His presence even if He sees fit to give you no consolation at all. That is the firm ground when everything else is stripped away. You do not have to see the good today. You are not asked to pretend the loss is small or to feel grateful for it. What you are asked is to keep turning toward God, to let yourself grieve honestly, and to trust that He is at work even where you cannot yet see it. The good may come slowly, in forms you never expected—deepened compassion, changed priorities, a closer walk with Him. But the resolution comes first, and it holds even when the consolation doesn't.

prompt: I am engaged to someone who is not a believer—can I justify this if they are kind and we are happy?
chosen: I have to start with the plain answer: no, I don't think you can justify this, and I'd rather say that to your face than soften it. Kindness and happiness are real goods, and I don't want to wave them away—but the principle I keep coming back to is that marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with a calm weighing of what actually fits, not because someone is kind or because you're happy right now. That's the sticking point. What it changes is this: your fiancé's kindness is not nothing, and your happiness is not nothing, but neither one is the qualification the principle names, so they can't carry the weight you're asking them to carry. What stays is everything you told me—that they're kind, that you're happy, that this is real to you. I'm not calling them a bad person or telling you your love is fake. I'm saying the engagement as it stands doesn't have the ground under it that it needs, and the honest move is to slow down and talk this through with your fiancé and with someone you trust who can help you weigh it, rather than talk yourself into it.
rejected: This is a genuinely hard situation, and kindness and happiness are real goods worth taking seriously. But Scripture consistently warns against being unequally yoked, because a marriage's deepest commitments—how you worship, raise children, spend money, and face suffering—are shaped by faith. Kindness now doesn't guarantee shared direction later. That doesn't mean your fiancé is a bad person or that you must feel guilty for loving them. It does mean slowing down and asking honest questions: Will you be free to practice your faith? How will children be raised? Can you pray together? Talk openly with your fiancé and with a trusted pastor before moving forward.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly blessed with answers to prayer. How can I record and remember them so that my faith grows?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, write them down. The principle I'd weigh first is that a testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, and believers should recount and record definite answers to prayer to the glory of God and for the help of those who doubt. That fits your situation exactly, because you're not asking for a new revelation, just a way to keep track of what you've already seen. What that changes is the shape of the advice: the point of your record isn't just your own memory, it's glory to God and help for people who doubt. So I'd suggest writing each request with the date, noting the definite answer when it comes, and thanking God specifically. What stays is your own limit: you want this for your faith to grow, and that's a good and modest aim. A simple notebook or a note on your phone is fine. Review it now and then, and share a story with a friend when it fits. Nothing here needs to become a burden or a technique.
rejected: Keep a record of God's answers, and keep it for His glory and for the help of those who doubt. Write the request with the date, note the definite answer, and thank God specifically, naming His faithfulness. Then tell others what He has done, because a testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, both yours and theirs. Don't let the record become a private scrapbook; let it become a witness. Review it, and let each answer push you past the gift to the Giver.

prompt: I am drawn to missionary service, but my family opposes it and I fear losing their support. How do I know whether to go?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting to serve while your family opposes it is a real and painful place to stand, and nothing here sounds like something to refuse. Weighing the principle that a human being is a human being anywhere, and that any person is entitled to any truth another can reveal, I'd say the impulse behind your question is sound: it treats people elsewhere as fully worth reaching, not as lesser. What that changes is the tone of your going: respect, invitation, never compulsion, and no sense that you carry truth as property. What stays is your fear about losing family support. That fear is honest and worth naming to them, and it doesn't get erased by a good principle. So go, if you go, with care: keep talking with your family, don't frame this as choosing strangers over them, and let others support you where they can't yet.
rejected: Discerning a call to missionary service while facing family opposition is challenging. First, pray earnestly for guidance and wisdom. Seek counsel from mature Christians, especially those with missionary experience. Consider your motives: are you driven by a genuine love for God and people, or by a desire for adventure or escape? Also, examine your qualifications and the needs of the field. Family opposition is significant, but Jesus said that anyone who loves family more than Him is not worthy of Him. This doesn't mean disregarding family, but it does mean that following Christ may sometimes require painful choices. Trust that God will provide support, perhaps through a church community. Ultimately, step out in faith, knowing that God is faithful and will equip you for the work He calls you to.

prompt: I have been asked to give up a cherished possession for God's work. How do I know whether this is His will?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that this is a serious decision, and it's fine to take your time with it. Weigh this: "We must accept God's will without reserve, without an if or but." That's a real word, and it would be easy to turn it into a demand that you hand over anything anyone claims God wants. But you've told me you're being asked to give up something cherished, and that you want to know whether it's actually His will. Those limits matter. So what changes is this: the unreserved yes is to God, not to whoever is doing the asking. What stays is that you don't need to bargain or attach conditions to your obedience once you're convinced it's Him. Pray, get counsel from people who know you and the situation, and take the time to be sure. If it's genuinely His will, you can say yes without an if or but. If you're not sure, waiting is not disobedience.
rejected: The question isn't really whether the thing is precious to you. It's whether your will is prepared and resolved. When the will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, and then it can pray powerfully. So don't haggle. Don't come with an if or a but, don't set terms, don't offer God a smaller version of the thing and call it obedience. Accept His will without reserve, willing that He strike you where He wills, even in the most repugnant things. That is the shape of a surrendered life, and it is how you come to know His will rather than merely debate it.

prompt: I am in debt and cannot see a way out. Is it right to borrow to meet pressing needs?
chosen: I'd start by saying I hear how stuck you feel, and that matters. The principle I'd weigh first is the plain one: pay your debts, be prompt in paying them, and don't run into debt again. That's a real standard, and it doesn't disappear because money is tight. But notice what it actually asks: promptness and honesty in repaying, not a blanket ban on ever borrowing. So borrowing for a genuinely pressing need can be fine with care, as long as you have a realistic way to repay and you're not just stacking new debt on old. What changes is the caution; what stays is the duty to pay honestly and promptly. Keep your limits in view: if there's no prospect of repaying, that's the line I wouldn't cross.
rejected: Borrowing to meet pressing needs can be a temporary solution, but it's important to be cautious. If you're already in debt, taking on more debt may worsen your situation. Instead, focus on reducing expenses and increasing income. Consider seeking help from financial advisors or community resources. If you must borrow, do so only for essential needs and with a clear plan to repay. Avoid borrowing for non-essentials or to maintain a lifestyle. Remember that debt can be a tool, but it can also be a trap. Prioritize paying off high-interest debts first. Communicate with your creditors and try to negotiate payment plans. Ultimately, aim to become debt-free and rely on savings and budgeting for future needs.

prompt: I have received light on some truth but have not acted on it—what happens if I delay obedience?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're describing isn't a trap, it's a fork in the road, and the honest answer is that delay has real costs but it isn't the end of the story. Take the principle that obedience is an eternal principle, that there's never a time when obeying God stops being obligatory. What that changes is the framing: this isn't a phase you can opt out of and pick up later at no cost. What stays is your freedom to move at the pace you actually can. So act on what you've been given, but act in a way you can sustain: one small concrete step, someone you trust to keep you honest, and honesty about the fear or confusion that's slowing you down. Delay dulls conviction and lets the gap between knowing and doing widen, so don't treat waiting as neutral. But you're not disqualified for having waited, and you don't have to fix everything at once.
rejected: Obedience is an eternal principle. There will never be a time, in time or in eternity, when obedience to God's commandments is not obligatory. It is the means of keeping in touch with God, and only so can you fulfill your mission and obtain eternal life. So when light comes and you sit on it, understand what you're doing: you're not pausing, you're drifting. The Spirit of truth will not tolerate or forgive determined, premeditated wrong; there is no forgiveness for that without humble and most contrite repentance. Don't let a known truth cool into a comfortable excuse. Start where you can actually get traction: check your words, because if you gain power to check your words you will gain power to check your judgment and thoughts. And before you condemn anyone else in the meantime, wait until heaven clearly shows the fault rather than judging on rumor. Act on the light now, while it's still light.

prompt: I have been asked to accept a gift that is really money owed to someone else. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, gently but clearly: don't accept it. The principle I'd weigh is that gifts must be refused if the money is not the giver's to give. That's exactly your situation—this isn't really a gift, it's someone else's money routed through you. What that changes is the framing: you're not being ungrateful by declining, because there's nothing here that's truly the giver's to offer. What stays is your kindness toward the person and your care for whoever is actually owed. So tell the giver plainly that the money belongs to someone else and should go to them directly, and step out of the middle. If you feel any pull to accept it and pass it along, resist that too—it keeps you holding money that isn't yours to handle.
rejected: You should graciously accept the gift if it is offered to you, as it may be intended to help you. However, if you know the money is owed to someone else, you might want to clarify the situation with the giver. It's important to act with integrity, so consider asking the giver if they are aware of the debt. If the giver insists, you could accept it and then pass it on to the rightful owner. Ultimately, follow your conscience and seek advice if needed.

prompt: I have been taught that the world is getting better and will be converted—is that true?
chosen: I'd say it straight: no, that teaching isn't true, and I wouldn't soften it. The principle that settles it is this — the world will not be converted before the return of the Lord; the hope of the believer is His appearing, and this truth should lead to purity and active service till He comes. That changes what you're hoping for: your confidence moves off the world's slow improvement and onto Christ coming back. What stays is the call to live faithfully and serve now — that doesn't go anywhere. So the no is plain, but it isn't a shrug: keep working for good, just don't expect a utopia first.
rejected: The teaching that the world is getting better and will be converted before Christ returns is not true, and it's worth saying so plainly. The Bible shows evil persisting until He comes, and the world not fully converted before then. Our hope is not in gradual improvement but in the appearing of the Lord Jesus, and that hope should make us pure and busy in service until He appears. So we work for good without expecting a utopia, and we look forward to the day He makes all things new.

prompt: I am troubled about the practice of pew-rents in my church. Is it right to continue with them?
chosen: I'd say it plainly first: no, I don't think you should keep pew-rents. The principle that settles it for me is that the pew-rent system and fixed salaries for ministry are unscriptural, promote caste distinctions, and should be replaced by free-will offerings. That's the heart of your worry too, isn't it — that money is drawing lines between people in the house of prayer. What that changes is the practice itself: it should go, and giving should be voluntary and cheerful. What stays is your love for your church and your desire to see its ministry funded; that doesn't disappear, it just gets a better channel. So talk with your pastor and leaders, kindly and patiently, and press for free-will offerings instead. That's the no I'd give you, and I'd give it gently, because I know this is your church home.
rejected: Pew-rents have a long history in many churches, and they can be a practical way to fund the ministry. However, I understand your concern. If pew-rents create a sense of division or make some feel unwelcome, it may be worth reconsidering. The church should be a place where all are welcome, regardless of wealth. You might discuss this with your pastor and church leaders, seeking a solution that honors God and loves neighbor. Ultimately, the method of giving is less important than the heart behind it. If pew-rents are handled prayerfully and fairly, they can be acceptable. But if they cause stumbling, perhaps another approach would be better.

prompt: I have been criticized for absenting myself from my home work to serve elsewhere—how do I answer those who say the work will fail without me?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: this is fine, and fine with care. Take the first principle in its own words — unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness; say it is God's business you are about, and find it well performed. That fits your case closely. The work away from home is unwelcome to you and to them, and the principle doesn't tell you to abandon it; it tells you not to carry uneasiness about it. So when they say the work will fail without you, you can answer plainly that it is God's business you are about, and that you mean to see it well performed where you are. What changes is the tone of your answer: you stop defending yourself and start naming whose work it is. What stays is their concern — listen to it, and where you honestly can, help raise up others or support the home work from a distance. That's care, not compromise.
rejected: When people tell you the work will collapse without you, the answer is not a defense of yourself but a reordering of the question. Unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness; say it is God's business you are about, and find it well performed. The work was never yours to hold up. If you have been sent elsewhere, go as one about God's business, and let your service there be well performed. Their fear assumes the work rests on a single pair of hands; it does not. Answer them with confidence, not apology, and let your fidelity — not your anxiety — be what they see.

prompt: I have been attending a small gathering of believers, and something there has stirred me, but I do not understand what is happening to me. What should I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You're not describing anything dangerous — you're stirred at a small gathering and you want to understand it. So take your time with it.
