Practically, examine why you do what you do, and ask God to shape your affections so that obedience springs from delight in him rather than from obligation.

prompt: How do I commit everything—my past, present, and future—to God's Providence?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and you can do it. Take the first principle as it stands: commit yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace, accepting what comes as from a fatherly hand rather than wearing yourself out with anxious, wandering thoughts. That fits what you described—past, present, future—because it's about entrusting rather than controlling. What changes is the tone: less striving, more quiet trust. What stays is your own part—you still pray, still make plans, still act; you're not asked to stop thinking or caring. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep your feet on the ground while you hand the outcome over.
rejected: Commit your past, present, and future to God's Providence by entrusting yourself and everything that concerns you to it in silence and peace. Accept whatever comes, whatever its cause, as from a fatherly hand, and set aside the vain, wandering thoughts that only weary your soul and body. Learn to trace His leadings—even a chance meeting, even a gathering of the serious and the careless at a grave, may hold a real link in His purpose of grace; adore rather than scoff. And remember that all evil, of whatever kind, happens only by God's permission and always for some good end: it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will turn all to good. So commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that I might not be among the elect?
chosen: I'd start by saying this fear is worth taking seriously, not brushing aside. But I'd weigh the principle that fear is born of Satan and is the great enemy of faith, that every fear is a falsehood, and that trust is the remedy. That reframes your question: the fear itself isn't a reliable report on your standing. What it changes is that you stop treating the anxiety as evidence and start answering it with trust. What stays is your honest self-examination and the desire for holiness, which are good and worth keeping. So this is fine with care: pray, use the ordinary means of grace, talk with a pastor, and don't let endless introspection run the show.
rejected: The fear that you may not be among the elect is a common and serious anxiety, and it deserves careful attention rather than dismissal. Begin by examining your life honestly: do you love God, grieve over sin, and desire holiness? These desires are themselves evidence of grace at work. Remember that assurance is not something you manufacture by anxious self-scrutiny; it grows from trusting the promises of God, who calls sinners to himself and will not cast out those who come to him. Pray for assurance, use the means of grace, and speak with a pastor. Avoid endless introspection, which feeds doubt. Rest in the character of God rather than in the intensity of your feelings.

prompt: How do I love God with my whole heart when I still feel attached to creatures?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your attachment to creatures isn't the problem you fear it is. Take the principle that love is rational and voluntary, not mere emotion, and that it's subject to holiness. That means loving God with your whole heart is a choice you make and keep making, not a feeling you have to manufacture by first draining every other affection. So the question becomes whether any of your attachments pull you from holiness, and that's worth looking at honestly. What changes is that you stop treating feeling attached as a failure. What stays is the real work: ordering those loves under God's will and letting go of whatever draws you from Him. You can love Him today, from exactly where you are.
rejected: Stop waiting until you feel detached enough to love God. Love is a rational, voluntary self-giving: you choose Him as your true good, and every affection is regulated by holiness. Your smallness doesn't make you unnoticed either—God's knowledge is undivided, His attention rests wholly on each soul, so the ocean-tides of His love pour into even the smallest heart. So quit moaning over your unworthiness as though you had to become better before you may love Him. Rise up now and bless God with all the love you have, keeping none back, and order your creaturely loves under His will.

prompt: What is the role of good will if I desire good but can't accomplish it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your good will counts, even when your hands can't finish the job. Take the first principle on its own terms — good will is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues, and if you desire what is good and can't accomplish it, God will reward it as though it had been performed, for merit lies in the will. That changes something real: it means you're not empty-handed just because circumstances block the outcome. What stays is your honesty about the limits — you still can't do what you can't do, and this doesn't magically remove the frustration or the practical obstacles. So hold the desire without despising yourself for the gap, and keep looking for the small opening where it might still act. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Good will still matters even when you cannot accomplish the good you desire. Your intention reflects your character and your values, and it can be a source of moral integrity. While outcomes are important, they are not always within your control. You should not be discouraged if circumstances prevent you from achieving what you want; the effort and desire themselves have worth. At the same time, you should continue to look for ways to bring about the good you desire, and accept your limitations. Ultimately, good will is the foundation of moral life, and it is what makes you a good person even when you fall short.

prompt: What should I do when I feel God has abandoned me in trial?
chosen: What I'd say first is that feeling abandoned in a trial is heavy and common, and it doesn't mean you've done something wrong. Of the principles here, the one I'd weigh is this: trials are well and wisely chosen and make the Word and presence of God more precious. That reframes the season without pretending it's easy, and it keeps you from reading your pain as proof God has left. What changes is how you interpret the silence; what stays is the honest lament, the trusted friends, the small rhythms of prayer and Scripture even when they feel dry. So this is fine, and fine with care: name the feeling plainly, lean on others, and be patient with yourself.
rejected: When you feel God has abandoned you in trial, don't let the thought that everything is against you take root; that suggestion is false. Trials are well and wisely chosen, and they make the Word and presence of God more precious to you. So bring the feeling into the open honestly, recall his past faithfulness, and keep praying and reading even when it feels dry. The feeling of absence is not the fact of absence. Return to him gently and trust him fully.

prompt: What is the value of silence and solitude for someone living in the world?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're describing is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself, and that the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That reframes your question in a useful way: the value of silence and solitude for someone living in the world isn't measured by how many hours they get alone, but by whether the quiet reaches inward. So a walk, a closed room, an early morning can be genuinely valuable, but the walls alone don't do the work. What changes is that you stop treating solitude as a technique for recharging and start asking whether your inner life is actually quiet. What stays is your ordinary life in the world, with its work and relationships, as the place where this gets lived out. Keep it realistic: you don't need a monastery, just real interior attention.
rejected: Silence and solitude are valuable mainly as a retreat from the noise and demands of daily life. Stepping away from crowds, screens, and conversation lets a person rest, think clearly, and return to work and relationships with renewed energy. Quiet places—a walk alone, a closed room, an early morning—offer perspective and calm. In this view, solitude is chiefly a practical tool: it protects mental health, sharpens judgment, and helps someone engage the world more effectively. The world is where life happens, so silence serves the active life rather than replacing it.

prompt: How can I pray without ceasing in the middle of a busy daily life?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that secret prayer and meditation on the word of God must not be sacrificed to busy activity — the worker for God must first be a worker with God. What that changes is the order of things: the short whispered prayers through your day are good, but they rest on some unhurried time alone with God and his word, so protect a real slot for that even if it's short. What stays is everything you actually asked about — a busy life doesn't disqualify you from ceaseless prayer, and brief prayers, reminders, and turning your heart toward God between tasks are exactly how it works. Keep your limits; don't turn this into a rigid schedule or a guilt trip. Just don't let the busyness crowd out the quiet root.
rejected: Prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and holy serving, the corner-stone on which all your life-work is built. So build on it: take time alone with God and his word, and let meditation on Scripture fill your heart, because no amount of activity, public service, or fellowship makes up for losing that. Keep your appointed times of prayer whether or not you feel like it, pray with your family, and ask God to help you do what is asked of you rather than expecting him to do it all. Make prayer your first resort in every crisis, great or small, not your last. Then the short prayers through the day rest on that foundation. Guard the secret place jealously, let nothing crowd it out, and ceaseless prayer will follow.

prompt: How do I handle it when someone praises me or thinks highly of me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: take the compliment, say thank you, and don't overthink the moment. One principle worth weighing here is that flattery and reproach become alike to someone who sees things as they are and is growing in humility. That changes how much weight you give the praise—it becomes information, not a verdict on your worth. What stays is the simple, human response: be gracious to the person in front of you, and keep your feet on the ground. Nothing here needs refusing.
rejected: Receiving praise well is a skill. First, accept it graciously—a simple thank-you is usually enough; deflecting can make others uncomfortable. Then, privately redirect the credit where it belongs, recognizing your gifts and opportunities as gifts. Keep a realistic view of yourself: neither inflate nor dismiss what others say. Use praise as information, not identity. If it tempts you toward pride, let it prompt gratitude and humility instead. And remember that the people praising you are valuable; respond in a way that honors them and points beyond yourself.

prompt: How do I pray the way Christ taught, entering into my inner chamber and shutting the door?
chosen: I'd start where you started: Christ's own instruction to go into your inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. That's the heart of it, and nothing here needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh is the one about adoring God in spirit and in truth, with a knowledge and love, an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. What that changes is the picture of the room: the chamber isn't only a physical quiet spot, it's the inmost place of your heart, and the door you shut is also the door on the noise and pull of everything that would crowd God out. What stays is exactly what you asked about: a real, quiet, private place, honesty before a Father who sees in secret. So find your quiet corner, close the door, put the phone away, and speak plainly. Let the silence be more than silence, though. Let it be a turning of your whole self toward God, and let what you pray show up in how you live.
rejected: Christ's teaching on prayer is not finally about architecture. He says go into your inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret, and the deeper reading of that is that the room is the inmost chamber of the heart and the door is the door of the senses. To pray as He taught is to adore God in spirit and in truth, with a knowledge and love, an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. That means closing out the clamor, denying sin, and affirming God's allness, and it means praying that God would help you search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Prayer like that becomes your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and sincerity gets proven in practice, as purified desire turns into pure living.

prompt: How do I deal with discouragement and confusion of mind?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about holding yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in the Lord's presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the tone of how you handle confusion: you don't have to wrestle your scattered mind into submission or panic when it drifts. You bring it back gently. What stays is your discouragement and confusion themselves; they're real, and this practice is meant to sit alongside them, not erase them. If forcing yourself through it only makes things worse, you're free to set it aside and learn from your own experience.
rejected: When you feel discouraged and confused, it can help to take a step back and breathe. Try to identify the source of your confusion—perhaps write down your thoughts to gain clarity. Remember that everyone faces such moments; it's part of being human. Reach out to a trusted friend or mentor who can offer perspective. Engage in activities that bring you peace, like walking in nature or listening to music. Avoid making major decisions while you're feeling this way. Give yourself time; confusion often clears with patience. If the feelings persist, consider speaking with a counselor. You are not alone, and these feelings will pass.

prompt: How do I keep my conscience at peace when others think badly of me?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself but bringing it back in tranquility. That changes the target: the work isn't managing what others think of you, it's returning your attention to God, gently, each time it drifts. What stays is that other people's low opinions still sting, and you still have real duties and real limits. So keep it small and honest — a few quiet minutes, few words, no scolding yourself when your mind slides back to the criticism. Confess your own faults plainly; that steadies you more than defending your reputation. And commit the whole matter, reputation included, to God's providence in silence and peace. That's enough for today.
rejected: Turn from their opinions to God and wait before him like a beggar at a rich man's gate. Your business is to keep your mind in the presence of the Lord. When it wanders into replaying what people think of you, do not disquiet yourself — trouble and disquiet scatter the mind rather than gather it. Bring it back in tranquility. Keep your words few, because many words and long discourses often cause wandering. Humble yourself and confess your faults honestly before God; that steadies the mind far more than defending yourself. Then commit yourself and everything that concerns you, your reputation included, to the unfailing and most sure providence of God, in silence and peace, accepting whatever comes as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and refusing the vain thoughts that weary soul and body. Peace is received in humble waiting, not manufactured by reasoning about criticism.

prompt: How do I bear injuries without resentment and truly forgive those who hurt me?
chosen: I'd start by saying what you're asking for is good, and it's fine to pursue it with care. Take the principle that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and that patience and forgiving injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That doesn't ask you to pretend the hurt didn't happen or to stay in harm's way. It asks you to let go of payback. So keep your honest grief, keep safe boundaries, keep telling the truth about what was done. What changes is the aim: you stop trying to settle the score yourself. What stays is your dignity and your right to protect yourself.
rejected: Bearing injuries without resentment and forgiving others is a central Christian challenge. Start by acknowledging your pain honestly—resentment often grows when we deny our hurt. Pray for the person who wronged you, asking God to bless them; this softens the heart. Remember that forgiveness is not excusing the wrong but releasing the debt to God. Reflect on your own need for mercy, as Jesus taught in the Lord's Prayer. Set boundaries if necessary, but let go of vengeance. Community support and spiritual direction can help. Over time, through grace, you can forgive and find peace, free from the bitterness that resentment breeds.

prompt: How do I love my neighbour while keeping my heart fixed on God alone?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and nothing in it needs to be refused. Take the principle that says we must bear with one another in our imperfections, since it's a great part of perfection and the way to practice love of neighbor. That reframes the whole question: loving your neighbor isn't a distraction from a heart fixed on God, it's one of the main ways that heart gets trained. What changes is that you stop treating attention to people as competition with attention to God. What stays is your limit: God alone stays first, and the neighbor is loved from that center, not instead of it. So keep your prayer and silence, and let patience with irritating people be part of the same devotion.
rejected: The heart fixed on God alone is not a heart closed to the person in front of it. Bear with one another in your imperfections, because that forbearance is a great part of perfection and the very way love of neighbor is practiced. When irritation rises, don't let it steer your words; compel your heart to suffer tranquilly and offer the disturbance to God instead of dumping it on the person near you. Pray for the ones who annoy you, listen before you speak, serve without looking for anything back. Your love for God and your love for neighbor are not rivals; the second is how the first becomes visible.

prompt: What is the difference between Christian contemplation and just studying philosophy or theology?
chosen: I'd start by saying these aren't rivals, and the difference is mostly about where each one is headed. Take the principle as it's worded: the contemplation of the Saints seeks as its end the love of the God contemplated and penetrates to the will to enkindle love, desiring above all the increase of charity. That's the hinge. Studying philosophy or theology can sharpen your mind and fill your head with true things, and that's genuinely good. But it can stop at the intellect, and contemplation is meant to go past that into love. What changes is how you hold your study: it's a servant, not the destination. What stays is that study still matters, and so do the ordinary means, since faith is grounded in the historical resurrection of Christ and you begin with history and go on to experience. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep studying, and let it feed your prayer rather than replace it.
rejected: Studying philosophy or theology is an intellectual activity: you read texts, analyze arguments, and try to understand concepts. Christian contemplation is different in that it involves prayer and a relationship with God. Philosophy and theology aim at knowledge and understanding, while contemplation aims at communion with God through prayer and reflection. In practice, the two can overlap—theology can feed contemplation, and contemplation can deepen theology. But the basic difference is that study is about knowing, while contemplation is about praying and being present to God. So if you want to understand doctrines, study theology; if you want to grow in prayer, practice contemplation.

prompt: What does it mean that the kingdom of God is within me?
chosen: I'd start by saying that reading 'within you' as God's reign taking root in your heart is a fine way to hear it, and it's fine with care. Weigh one principle as it's worded: 'The kingdom of God will be a literal, tangible kingdom on the earth, not a mere spiritual or inward reign, with laws, officers, and resurrected saints.' That keeps the inward sense from shrinking the kingdom down to just a private feeling. What changes is that 'within you' becomes the starting point, not the whole story—the reign in your heart points toward something public and real. What stays is your own question: yes, God's rule genuinely begins inside you, shaping your desires and choices. Just don't let the inward reading crowd out the outward hope, and don't turn it into a private project that never looks beyond yourself.
rejected: The kingdom of God is a literal, tangible kingdom on the earth—with laws, officers, and resurrected saints—not a mere spiritual or inward reign. So when Jesus says the kingdom is within you, he is not shrinking it to a mood or a private devotion. The reign takes root in your heart, yes, but it is not confined there. It develops gradually through individual labor; it is the business of the Saints, and it is the Kingdom of God or nothing. And it cannot be realized without the world passing through fearful struggles and judgments, after which He that sits on the throne makes all things new. So let the reign inside you grow outward, and labor faithfully, trusting that He will finish the work.

prompt: What does it mean to be transformed in God, and how do I begin?
chosen: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is: this is a good question, and you're not asking for anything dangerous. What you're describing—being changed by God—is fine, and fine with care. Take one of these ideas and hold it up: 'He takes our vanities and strews them among the winds, breaks our prides, reduces our self-gratifications to dust, and transfigures the natural lusts to Holy Love, and we submit; the Divine Anaesthetic He gives in this pain of transition is His Grace.' That's a vivid way of saying transformation will feel like loss before it feels like freedom, and that grace is what carries you through the pain rather than around it. What that changes: don't expect your beginning to be all sweetness—some of it is letting go, and that's normal, not a sign you're doing it wrong. What stays: your own honest starting point. You begin by turning toward God, admitting where you fall short, and asking for grace, with simple habits of prayer, Scripture, and fellowship. Keep it small and steady. The 'submit and stay at peace' language is fine as a description of trust, but don't let anyone use it to tell you to sit still in harm or to stop asking questions. You're allowed to move slowly and to have limits.
rejected: Being transformed in God means a gradual change of heart and life, moving from self-centeredness toward love of God and neighbor. It is not a single event but a lifelong process of growth in virtue, prayer, and obedience. You begin by turning honestly toward God, admitting where you fall short, and asking for grace. Establish simple habits: daily prayer, reading Scripture, and fellowship with other believers. Examine your attachments and ask God to reshape them. Expect slow progress and setbacks; transformation is God's work in you, and your part is to cooperate. Start small, stay faithful, and trust that God completes what He begins.

prompt: I'm afraid of being despised and mocked by others—how should I respond when people insult me?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: you don't owe anyone a performance of shame when they mock you. The principle I'd weigh here is that we should be sweet and affable to all, condescending to the humor of others and bearing with rude and tiresome manners, since such victories are more fruitful than we can imagine. That changes something real: it means the first move isn't to win the exchange or to prove them wrong, but to stay soft and not let their rudeness set your temperature. What stays is your boundary—being affable doesn't mean staying around people who keep tearing at you. So it's fine, with care: answer calmly or not at all, keep your dignity, and step away from repeat cruelty.
rejected: The principle stands on its own: be sweet and affable to all, condescend to the humor of others, and bear with rude and tiresome manners, because such victories are more fruitful than we can imagine. So when someone insults you, don't trade contempt for contempt. Let the words land, take whatever truth is in them quietly, and let the rest go. The mockery says more about the mocker than about you. Answer gently or say nothing, and keep your peace—that is the victory worth having.

prompt: How do I resist the devil's attempts to distract me through cares and anxieties?
chosen: I'd start by saying: this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about coming before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate — your business is simply to keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and if it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. That changes how you fight: the goal isn't a locked-down mind, it's a quiet return, again and again, without scolding yourself for every lapse. What stays is the real work — showing up, bringing your attention back in tranquility, and treating the cares as things that pass through rather than enemies you must crush by force. So keep your fixed times of prayer, keep returning gently, and don't turn the battle itself into one more anxiety.
rejected: Distraction through cares and anxieties is one of the devil's favorite tactics, because it scatters the mind and keeps it from resting in God. The first step is to name what is happening: when you notice your thoughts churning over responsibilities, finances, or worries, recognize it as an invitation to return to God rather than a verdict on your spiritual state. Practically, set aside fixed times of prayer and keep them even when your mind wanders. When it does wander, do not panic or scold yourself endlessly; gently bring your attention back. You might also write down your anxieties as a way of handing them over, and limit the mental clutter you invite in. Over time, these habits train the mind to stay steadier in God's presence.

prompt: I keep getting plagued by blasphemous thoughts—am I sinning by having them?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that having a thought cross your mind is not the same as agreeing with it. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says useless thoughts spoil all, and that we should reject them as soon as we perceive their impertinence and return to communion with God. Notice what that principle actually asks of you: it asks you to turn away from the thought when you notice it, not to have never had it. That distinction matters for you, because you've told me these thoughts plague you, which means they're intruding rather than being welcomed. So what changes is this: your job is the turning, not the preventing. What stays is that you're not sinning just by being bothered by a thought you didn't invite. If they're wearing you down, it's worth talking to someone you trust about the strain they're putting on you.
rejected: Useless thoughts spoil all, and the mischief begins there. So the counsel is plain: the instant you perceive a thought that is impertinent to your salvation, reject it and return at once to communion with God. Do not sit with it, do not argue with it, do not treat its arrival as a verdict on your soul. The mind is to be kept, and kept by turning, again and again, back to God. That is the work, and it is enough.

prompt: How do I reconcile my desire for comfort and honour with the call to seek God in silence and peace?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting comfort and honour isn't the problem — the question is what you do with that wanting. The principle I'd weigh first says to commit yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace, accepting all things as coming from a fatherly hand rather than giving yourself up to vain and wandering thoughts that wear out soul and body and waste time and strength. That reframes your question: silence isn't a technique for getting comfort, it's a place to hand over the worry that keeps you churning. What changes is the goal — you stop trying to talk yourself out of wanting honour and start letting God hold the outcome. What stays is your honesty about wanting comfort and honour; that doesn't get erased, it gets carried. So yes, seek God in silence and peace — that's fine, and fine with care: keep it gentle and regular, don't turn it into a performance or a test of whether you feel peaceful, and don't let it become an excuse to ignore real needs or real people.
rejected: Your desire for comfort and honour is natural, but the spiritual life calls you to something deeper. Begin by setting aside time each day for silent prayer, where you can listen for God's voice. In that silence, you will discover that true comfort is found not in external honors but in the peace of God's presence. Offer your desires to God, asking for the grace to seek Him above all else. Remember that honor in the world is fleeting, but the honor that comes from God is eternal. As you practice silence, you will gradually find that your longing for comfort is transformed into a longing for God, and your desire for honor is purified into a desire to serve Him.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear of losing my reputation if I pursue holiness?
chosen: I'd start by saying the fear you're naming is real and worth taking seriously, not something to be ashamed of. The principle I'd weigh is that the great hindrance to holiness is unbelief and holding back some known thing, and that every light received and not obeyed leaves the soul darker. That's a strong word, but notice it's about holding back what you already know to be true, not about being reckless with your livelihood or your relationships. So what changes: don't treat the fear as a reason to stall indefinitely on the small, clear obedience in front of you. What stays: your caution about your reputation is legitimate, and you can move at a pace that respects your actual situation, your family, your work. This is fine, and fine with care. Take the next honest step, keep your footing, and don't let fear become the thing that quietly decides for you.
rejected: The fear of losing your reputation will talk to you in reasonable tones, and it will ask you to wait. But hear this: the great hindrance to holiness is unbelief and holding back some known thing. Every light received and not obeyed leaves the soul darker, and the nearer one comes and then draws back, the less likely one is ever to enter in. So do not draw near to the blessing and then shrink away. Obey the light you have now. Venture on Christ without delay, because delay grieves the Spirit. And do not mistake this for a gloomy withdrawal into yourself. True holiness is fellowship with Christ in the inner life that then gets you out of yourself to help others and prepare the world for His appearing. Serve your neighbor, do good quietly, and let your reputation rest in better hands than the crowd's.

prompt: How do I accept adversity as coming from God's hand rather than resenting it?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about considering your ways in the day of adversity, asking whether you failed to acknowledge God's hand in prosperity or spent too much on yourself. That's worth sitting with, but gently. It's a question to hold, not a verdict to pronounce on yourself, and it doesn't mean every hard thing you face is a correction for something you did. What changes is that you stop treating resentment as the only honest response and start looking honestly at your own grip on comfort. What stays is the grief itself. You don't have to explain away the pain or force a tidy reason for it, and you don't owe anyone a quick peace.
rejected: Accepting adversity as from God's hand begins with trust in His sovereignty and goodness. When hardship comes, remember that God allows trials for our refinement, not to harm us. Instead of resenting, ask Him for grace to see His purpose. Practice gratitude for His past faithfulness, and recall that even Jesus suffered. Resist the urge to demand explanations; instead, surrender your desire for control. Fellowship with other believers helps, as they can remind you of God's promises. Over time, this perspective shift will help you receive adversity with peace, knowing He works all things for good.

prompt: How do I deal with vain curiosity and the urge to read every new book and hear every rumour?
chosen: I'd start by saying this isn't a vice you need to crush—it's a habit you can learn to hold loosely. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about keeping your mind in the Lord's presence like a beggar at a rich man's gate: when your attention wanders off toward the next new book or the latest rumour, don't disquiet yourself, just bring it back in tranquility. That changes the tone of the whole thing. You're not fighting an enemy; you're gently returning. What stays is your own limit—you've told me you want to stop chasing every book and every rumour, and that limit holds. So keep it: pick the few books worth your time, let the rumours pass, and when the itch rises, notice it and come back without scolding yourself. This is fine, done with that kind of care.
rejected: The urge to read every new book and catch every rumour is not a small thing to manage—it is a door left open, and you are meant to stand porter at it. Admit only the thoughts you would actually want to see take shape in your life; shut the unhealthy ones out before they cross the threshold, because a fear or a craving let in becomes the body's suffering soon enough. And do not imagine this costs nothing. To have your mind kept in the presence of the Lord asks a real lowliness and a loneliness of spirit, and the ordinary pleasures of curiosity dry up along the way, because God means to have the whole of you. Do not turn back at that price. Let prayer be your waiting, and let books and news come later, in their place.

prompt: Should I desire to be honoured and respected by others, or is that dangerous?
chosen: I'd start by saying: wanting to be honoured and respected isn't wrong in itself. But you're right to sniff out a danger, and I'd weigh this principle: "We must be what we are and be that well, honoring the Master Workman who made us, since nothing avails if we are not pleasing to God's will." That changes things — it means the real question isn't whether people respect you but whether you're being what you were made to be. If you're living well before God, respect may come or not; either way you're not chasing it as the point. What stays is your caution: let respect be a byproduct of integrity, not the thing you're serving. So go ahead and want to be respected, with care — just keep it anchored to pleasing God rather than to applause.
rejected: Desiring honour and respect is natural and can be good, as it motivates us to live virtuously and contribute to society. However, it becomes dangerous when it turns into vanity or people-pleasing, leading us away from God. The key is to seek honour for God's glory, not our own. We should aim to be respected for our integrity and love, but always remember that ultimate approval comes from God. So, desire respect in a balanced way, ensuring it serves God's purposes rather than inflating our ego.

prompt: I want to be perfect as my heavenly Father is perfect—what does Christian perfection actually consist in?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting what you want is not a problem—it's the right aim. The principle I'd weigh first is this one: we must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. That's the heart of it. Aspiring to perfect love isn't the same as expecting to arrive at it by your own effort, and it doesn't mean measuring yourself against an impossible bar. What it changes is the direction of your striving: you aim at wholehearted love of God and neighbor rather than settling for a comfortable partial version. What stays is everything you already know about your limits—that you'll fall short, that grace does the shaping, that progress is slow. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep aiming high, and keep your hope in God's mercy rather than in your own performance.
rejected: Christian perfection consists in holy love—love of God and love of neighbor—and that love must aspire to nothing less than perfection. A love content to remain imperfect, that treats shortfall as the normal state of things, cannot fail to be imperfect. So do not settle. Aim at the whole heart given to God and to the people in front of you. And do not imagine this depends on your striving alone, or that your circumstances are obstacles to it; God's way is perfect, He makes no mistakes, and He who counts the hairs of your head knows the way to your truest good. Nor is perfection confined to a cloister—every lawful profession and state of life can be sanctified, and you need not leave your station to pursue it. Examine yourself, receive the sacraments, pray, serve, and let all of it serve this one aim: a love pressing on toward perfection in whatever state you are called to.

prompt: How do I find God when He seems utterly beyond my senses and imagination?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your question is honest, and it's a good one. The principle I'd weigh first says that as long as a person lingers trifling with the objects of the imagination and senses, they haven't passed beyond the limits and instincts of an animal nature shared with brute beasts—but by intelligence, affections, and will, made in God's image, we ought purely and directly to commune with God and cleave to Him. That actually meets your situation well. You've already noticed that senses and imagination aren't getting you there. So the counsel isn't to strain harder with pictures or feelings; it's to turn your mind, your love, and your will toward Him in plain faith, without demanding that He show up as an image or a sensation first. What that changes: you can stop treating the blankness as failure. What stays: the seeking itself, and the honesty about your limits. So this is fine, and fine with care—don't force experiences, and don't conclude He's absent just because He's beyond your senses.
rejected: When God seems beyond your senses and imagination, remember that He is not far from you. You can find Him in silence, in Scripture, in the beauty of creation, and in the love of others. Start by acknowledging your desire for Him—that desire itself is a sign of His presence. Practice stillness and let go of the need to grasp Him with your mind. God often reveals Himself in the ordinary moments of life: a kind word, a sunset, a moment of peace. Trust that He is near even when you cannot feel Him. Prayer, especially the prayer of simple attention, can help you become aware of His quiet presence. Don't be discouraged by dryness; keep seeking, and you will find Him in ways you never expected.

prompt: Should I withdraw from society and seek solitude to grow spiritually?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting space to grow spiritually is a good impulse, and nothing here needs to be shut down. But one principle should shape how you do it: solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself, because the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That changes the question from 'should I leave?' to 'can I be still inside?' What stays is your freedom to step back and seek quiet. Keep the limits you named: don't cut yourself off entirely, stay accountable to someone wise, and test whether the quiet is drawing you toward God or just away from people. Done that way, this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Solitude is not a spa for the soul. If you withdraw, the end must be penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation, and without great fervor and constancy in those, close solitude is the road to perdition. Walls and silence are a weak fence if the interior faculties are still noisy with self. True solitude is the soul dwelling with God and with itself. And remember why you go at all: your own salvation and spiritual progress come first, for what would it profit to gain the whole world and lose your own soul? So do not drift into isolation for comfort. Enter it as labor, under direction, watching and praying.

prompt: I'm anxious about my future and can't stop worrying—how do I cast all my care upon God?
chosen: I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about committing yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence in silence and peace, accepting all things as coming from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence. That's the heart of what you're asking, and it's a good thing to want. What it changes is the tone of your effort: the point isn't to white-knuckle your way out of worry, it's to hand things over and let peace be the posture. What stays is your part—you still bring your mind back when it wanders, gently, without scolding yourself for it. So pray, commit, and return your attention in tranquility; that's enough.
rejected: Start by recognizing that worry is a habit you can break. Set aside time each day to write down your concerns and then consciously hand them to God in prayer. Use deep breathing and meditation to calm your mind. Create a plan for the practical steps you can take, and trust that God helps those who help themselves. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God wants you to be proactive and responsible, so do your part and leave the rest to Him. Over time, you'll find that your anxiety decreases as you take action and see progress.

prompt: How do I handle memories of past sins and past events that keep coming back?
chosen: What I'd say first is that remembering past sins isn't itself a failure—what matters is what you do with the memory. One principle puts it this way: a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral harm. That reframes the memory as a signal rather than a verdict. So let it push you toward honest regret and a change of direction, and let it soften as that change takes hold. What stays is this: you don't have to erase the past to be okay now, and you don't have to punish yourself with it either. Handle it with care—talk to someone you trust if it gets heavy—but this is fine to work through.
rejected: Memories of past sins are not noise to be dismissed. A guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right; if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens to moral ruin. So do not sit with the memory passively—name the wrong, regret it, and turn from it. Confess your faults and humble yourself; pride scatters the mind, while humility gathers it. And in prayer, avoid a multiplicity of words, since many words often occasion wandering—speak simply and briefly from a humble heart. Remember too that every blessing rests on obedience to law, and late repentance cannot restore what sin has already cost you. Let the memory drive you to change, and let it teach you the price of delay.

prompt: I love fine clothes and dressing above my station; is this a spiritual danger, and how do I put it off?
chosen: I'd start by saying that loving beautiful clothes isn't automatically a spiritual problem. The principle that matters here is that the love of outward adorning can become a ruling passion of pride, and the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is of great price in God's sight. So the question is whether your love of fine clothes is ruling you or you're ruling it. You said you love dressing above your station. That's the part to watch. If it's about feeling superior or needing attention, that's pride creeping in. But you also asked how to put it off, which tells me you're not clinging to it. So here's what changes: you don't have to throw out every nice thing you own. What stays is the call to humility and modesty, but you can enjoy clothing with care, checking your motives and simplifying where needed. It's fine with care.
rejected: Loving fine clothes and dressing above your station can be a spiritual danger if it stems from pride and a desire for attention. The Bible warns against vanity and encourages modesty and humility. However, enjoying beautiful clothing is not inherently sinful; it depends on your heart. To put off this habit, examine your motives. Are you dressing to impress others or to feel superior? If so, repent and ask God to help you find your worth in Him. Cultivate humility by focusing on inner beauty and character. Also, consider simplifying your wardrobe and choosing clothes that are modest and appropriate for your station. Ultimately, the goal is to glorify God in all things, including your appearance.

prompt: I am a minister and want to know how to strengthen a dying believer's weak faith—what means are most effectual?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a good and tender thing to want, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that says faith is kept in lively exercise by trial and straits. That principle would tell you that God sometimes lets needs press hard and answers come slowly, and that this is not a sign the person has been abandoned—it's a place where trust gets exercised and where God's help becomes visible. What that changes: you can stop treating every doubt or delay as a failure to fix, and instead sit with them in it, naming it as a hard season rather than a verdict on their faith. What stays: the person is dying, weak, and frightened, so your job is comfort, Scripture, prayer, and your steady presence—not pressure to perform or prove anything. Keep it gentle, keep it short, and let the Spirit do the strengthening.
rejected: Strengthening a weak faith at the end of life is not mainly about talking someone out of their doubts. It's about keeping faith in lively exercise. God permits needs to be pressing and answers to be delayed—not to crush, but to test faith, to encourage importunity, to make His interposition the more manifest. So read Scripture with them, pray with them and for them, and don't be afraid of the straits they're in. Name them honestly: this is hard, and God is not absent in it. Encourage them to hold their confidence firm to the end, to keep asking, to keep trusting even when the answer tarries. Point them always to Christ, the author and finisher of faith, and let your calm presence and the community of faith be a means of grace.

prompt: I am dying of a consumption and my mind is sometimes clouded with doubts—how do I know my hope is not a delusion?
chosen: What I'd say first is that your question is not itself a sign of unbelief—it's the honest question of someone whose body is failing and whose mind sometimes slips. So let me weigh one principle in its own words: "Hold yourself in prayer before God like a dumb or paralytic beggar at a rich man's gate; let it be your business to keep your mind in the presence of the Lord, and if it wanders do not disquiet yourself, for trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect." That fits you exactly. A beggar doesn't have to produce a convincing argument to be at the gate; he just has to be there. So don't measure your hope by the clarity of your thoughts on a bad day. What changes is this: you can stop treating every clouded doubt as evidence against your hope. What stays is that hope still rests on God's faithfulness, not on your grip—so keep turning back gently when your mind wanders, and let the prayers of others carry you when you can't carry yourself. That is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Your fear is natural when the body weakens, but do not measure hope by how you feel. Hope rests not on your clear thoughts but on God's faithfulness, which does not waver when your mind clouds. When doubts come, do not fight them by sheer will; turn gently to what you know of God's mercy, and let the truths you have received steady you. Use the quiet means available—rest, Scripture read slowly, the prayers of others—and let them carry you when you cannot carry yourself. A delusion would be trusting your own strength; true hope trusts Another. Even a faint cry, even a wordless turning toward God, is enough. He holds you more surely than you hold Him, and He will not let you go.

prompt: I have been a Christian for some years and find my feelings less ecstatic than at first—is my religion declining?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: no, this doesn't mean your religion is declining. Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God—they rise and fall with health, stress, and routine, and they were never meant to be the measure. What I'd weigh is that first principle: trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, and keep on in prayer even when joy is lacking. That changes how you read this quiet season—it's not evidence of decline. What stays is your honest concern, which is worth taking to a pastor if the flatness lingers and weighs on you.
rejected: Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God. The believer is to trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and to continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. So do not read the fading of early ecstasy as decline. Count it all joy by faith even when you do not feel joyful, reckoning the trial a blessing until rejoicing becomes a habit. And remember that love is not mere sentiment or desire—it is the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof of the reality of your Christian profession. Let that love, not fading feeling, answer the question.

prompt: My sister is dying and I want to speak to her about her soul but I fear I am too ignorant—what can I say?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that you don't need to be an expert to talk with your sister about her soul. You're not being asked to teach her anything; you're being asked to sit with her. When you say you fear you're too ignorant, I hear how much you love her, and that love is already the beginning of the conversation. One of the principles puts it this way: when a soul has shaken off the dust of earth and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she receives, undertakes, and does becomes a pure and true prayer. What that changes is this: you don't have to manufacture the right words or the right mood, because her turning toward God is already happening, and your presence can simply join it. What stays is your honesty—if she asks something you don't know, say so gently. So ask her what she's hoping for, tell her you love her, and let silence and a held hand do their work. That's not ignorance; that's care.
rejected: You do not need theological expertise to speak with your sister about her soul; presence and love matter more than perfect words. Ask her gently what she is feeling and what she hopes for, and listen without rushing to fix anything. You might say simply that you love her, that God loves her, and that you are praying for her. If she wants to talk about God, follow her lead and admit honestly when you do not know something. Silence, a held hand, and a kind word can carry more grace than a sermon. Trust that God is nearer to her than you are, and let your visits be gentle and unhurried.

prompt: I am a poor laborer and want to know how to see God in the fields where I work—can nature teach me anything of grace?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, the fields can teach you, and you don't need money or schooling to notice it. Take the principle that God is the one living Worker and we are only His instruments—that one sits well with what you're asking. It means the growth you see isn't yours to force, and the worry you carry about whether you're doing enough isn't the same as trust. What that changes is the pressure; what stays is your part, which is to show up, pay attention, and do the work with care. Your limits stay as they are: you're a laborer with little to spare, so keep it simple—short prayers while you work, thanks for what you see, and let the seasons do the teaching. That's fine, and fine with care: don't turn it into a burden you have to perform.
rejected: Yes—nature can teach you much about grace if you look with attention. The seed that dies and rises, the rain that falls on good and bad ground, the slow growth that can't be rushed: all of it pictures how God works quietly and generously. And here is the heart of it: God is the one living Worker, and all human workers are only His instruments. So cast your care on Him, because anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Do your work for the love of God, praying as you go for grace to do it well, and love makes the burden bearable. Read His word on your knees, turning its promises and precepts into prayer, and expect that such use of Scripture will give you insight and self-searching and the very language of prayer. Let the fields remind you that He is patient and abundant, and let your work itself become prayer.

prompt: I am a Christian and I have lost a dear friend in the Lord—may I hope to meet her again, and how should that hope affect my life now?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: yes, you may hope to meet her again, and that hope is fine. It's fine with care, because grief is heavy and hope can quietly turn into pressure on yourself. The principle I'd weigh is the first one: knowing our need of God's grace and assistance, we should never lose sight of Him for a moment, making a firm resolution never more wilfully to forget Him and to spend the rest of our days in His presence, deprived if He thinks fit of all consolations. What that changes is this: your hope of seeing her shouldn't become the thing you cling to instead of God. What stays is the hope itself, and the comfort it gives. You asked how it should affect your life now, and the honest answer is that it should keep you walking with God day by day, in sorrow as much as in joy, without making reunion the whole point. Your grief is real, and you don't have to perform strength for anyone.
rejected: Yes, as a Christian, you can have hope that you will meet your dear friend again in the presence of the Lord. The Bible teaches that for believers, to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, and that we will be reunited with those who have died in Christ. This hope should comfort you and give you strength to continue your journey of faith. It should also motivate you to live in a way that honors God, knowing that your friend is now with Him. While you grieve, you do not grieve as those who have no hope. Let this hope fill you with peace and joy, and let it draw you closer to God, who is the God of the living and not of the dead. Your friend is alive in Christ, and you will see her again.

prompt: I delayed speaking to a friend about his soul and he died suddenly; can I be forgiven for that neglect?
chosen: I'd start by saying I'm sorry, and then I'd say this: you're not being asked to carry a sentence here. The principle I'd weigh is that you should never let your soul live in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear, since the One who loved it and died for it is good, sweet, and amiable. What that changes is the way you hold this: you can grieve the missed chance without turning it into a verdict on yourself, and you can bring it honestly and ask for forgiveness. What stays is the simple fact that the opportunity passed and it hurts. You said he died suddenly, so nothing here is about a long, calculated refusal, and I'm not going to treat it as one. This is fine, and fine to bring to God with care.
rejected: Think about where you're standing: a friend is gone, and you're wondering whether you can be forgiven for silence. Hear this plainly. The One who loved your soul and died for it is good, sweet, and amiable, and He does not want you living in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear. Confess the neglect, ask for forgiveness, and then stop treating yourself as though mercy were something you have to earn. Guilt that keeps you bowed down is not humility; it's a fog that keeps you from the One you're trying to reach. Let the sorrow be real, let the confession be honest, and let the goodness of God be bigger than the thing you're ashamed of.

prompt: I am a young woman and my sister mocks my new religion, saying my head is turned—how should I answer her?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your sister's mockery says more about her worry than about your head being turned. One principle I'd weigh is that in the third stage we become unable to pray or approach God except with a raised head and uncovered face, forced by a sweet necessity, and this change isn't to be revealed to others except in special instances. That changes how I'd answer her: you don't owe her a full account of what's happening inside you, and you can keep the deepest part quiet without lying. What stays is your own honesty and your care for her. So answer gently and briefly, something like, 'I hear that you're worried about me. This has brought me peace, and I'm not trying to push you away.' You don't have to win the argument or explain everything. Keep your limits: don't mock back, don't pretend you haven't changed, and don't hand over what isn't hers to inspect.
rejected: When your sister mocks your new religion, it can be hurtful, but try to respond with grace. You might say something like, 'I understand you're concerned, but this faith has brought me peace and purpose. I'm not trying to offend you; I just want to live out what I believe.' Avoid arguing or defending yourself too much. Instead, focus on showing love and respect. Over time, your actions may speak louder than words. Pray for your sister and ask God to soften her heart. Remember that Jesus faced mockery too, and He responded with love. Keep your head up and stay true to your convictions.

prompt: I am old and my believing child is dying before me—how can I be reconciled to parting with her?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that you're not being asked to stop loving her or to pretend this doesn't hurt. You asked how to be reconciled to parting with her, and I'd start there: grief and faith can share the same room. One of the principles here speaks of a soul that has shaken off the dust of earth and cleaves to the one Sovereign Good, and says that then everything becomes prayer. I'd hold that gently rather than as a demand on you. What it changes is this: her dying is not a door slammed shut but a turning toward the One she already trusts. What stays is your sorrow, and that's allowed. So take it slowly, keep praying as you're able, lean on your pastor and the people around you, and let your grief itself become a kind of prayer. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: When a soul has shaken off the dust of earth and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all it does becomes pure and true prayer, and contemplating God becomes as simple as breathing. That is what your child's faith is reaching toward, and it is why her death is not unmixed loss. Do not grudge what Christ takes into His arms. The childlike and the baptized are dear to Him, and their passing is a joy rather than a grief to be resented. So let your mourning be turned into prayer, cleave to the Sovereign Good yourself, and see her end as happier far than this life. Grieve, yes, but grieve as one who knows where she is going.

prompt: I am a minister and a parishioner asks me to bury her sister though I am not her parish minister—should I comply?
chosen: I'd start by saying this sounds like a genuine pastoral request, not a power grab, and nothing in the principles you're weighing actually forbids you from burying her. The one that comes closest is the rule that clergy must not live under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters, since that's called an occasion of evil and a scandal to the weak. That principle is about shared housing and appearances, not about who presides at a funeral, so it doesn't settle this. What it does change is that you should keep the arrangements clean and above board: be clear with the parish minister, don't create confusion about whose role it is, and avoid anything that looks like you're setting up a parallel ministry. What stays is the family's grief and their right to ask for someone they trust. So yes, you can comply, and with care: check in with the parish minister, keep it simple and transparent, and focus on the family.
rejected: As a minister, you should consider the pastoral needs of the parishioner and the circumstances. While you are not her parish minister, you can still offer comfort and support. However, it is important to respect the role of the parish minister and coordinate with them. If the parish minister is unavailable or if the family specifically requests you, it may be appropriate to comply, provided it does not cause confusion or conflict. Ultimately, seek to act with compassion and wisdom, and pray for guidance. The priority is to minister to the grieving family and honor the deceased.

prompt: I am a Christian and wonder whether funeral singing and solemn music are proper in religion—may they be used?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that the service of song belongs to the whole church under the Spirit's guidance and is mutual, so what matters most is that the singing comes from the gathered body of believers rather than from hired voices or a performance. That changes how you'd plan it: let the congregation sing, choose texts that carry faith and resurrection hope, and keep the music serving worship rather than show. What stays is your original instinct that solemn music and funeral singing are proper in Christian worship, and nothing you've described puts them out of bounds.
rejected: The service of song belongs to the whole church under the Spirit's guidance and is mutual; unconverted or hired performers are disqualified from this ministry. So the question isn't whether music is allowed but who is singing and in what spirit. Funeral singing and solemn music are proper when the regenerate body lifts them to God together, and they are hollow when they become a performance. Let the congregation sing, let the texts speak of faith and resurrection hope, and let the music serve worship rather than display.

prompt: I am a minister and I wonder whether the piety of the poor is as valuable as that of the rich and learned—how should I regard it?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: yes, the piety of the poor is as valuable as that of the rich and learned. God looks at the heart, and trust that grows in hardship is precious to him. One principle worth weighing here is that poverty often comes from want of discretion, calculation, and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. That changes something real: alongside honoring their faith, you can teach prudent management and frugality without treating poverty as a spiritual failing. What stays is your main point—wealth and learning don't make faith more acceptable to God, and you must not show partiality to the rich. So honor the poor, learn from their trust, and add practical wisdom gently, never as a condition of their worth.
rejected: As a minister, you should regard the piety of the poor as equally valuable in God's eyes. Wealth and learning do not make one's faith more acceptable to God; He looks at the heart. The poor often demonstrate profound trust and dependence on God, which are precious in His sight. However, poverty can also bring challenges that affect spiritual life, such as anxiety about daily needs. Your role is to encourage and support the poor in their faith, helping them see their worth in Christ. Avoid showing partiality to the rich; instead, create a community where all are valued. Remember that Jesus Himself identified with the poor and marginalized. So honor the piety of the poor and learn from their example of faith.

prompt: I am a Christian and I find that the things of earth draw my mind from God—how do I set my affections above?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is a real and old struggle, and the direction you want to go is good. Take the first principle as it's worded—'keep the heart occupied with God, the object of our love, rather than turning back to gaze upon ourselves to discover what we are doing.' That changes the method more than the goal. Instead of monitoring your drift and grading your attention, you'd turn toward God when you notice the pull, and let your affection rest on him rather than on your own performance. What stays is your daily prayer and Scripture, your honest noticing, and your care about distractions—none of that gets thrown out. What shifts is the self-scrutiny: you don't have to keep checking whether you're doing it right. So this is fine, and fine with care—keep the habits, drop the scorekeeping.
rejected: The heart was made to be occupied, and it will be occupied with something. So don't sit and study your own drift; that only turns you back on yourself. Keep God as the object of your love, and when the things of earth pull, turn to him rather than inspecting the pull. Live as one who believes he is loved and who seeks his approval, not as one grinding through duty or chasing sensation. Give yourself to deep recollection, letting 'God and I' be the whole of your thought, and cut away the unnecessary traffic—the chatter, the screens, the noise—that scatters your attention. Do that, and the pull of lesser things loosens because a greater and loving object has your heart.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has died in the faith—how do I think of her body in the grave and her soul with Christ?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your question is a faithful one to ask, and you can hold both of those truths at once: her body in the grave, resting and awaiting the resurrection, and her soul with Christ, safe in His presence. I'd weigh the second principle here, that little children who die before accountability are redeemed through Christ and that parents will have the joy of rearing them to the full stature of their spirits in the resurrection. What that changes is the frame of your grief: this is not a loss without hope, and the bond you had with her is not simply severed. What stays is everything you said — she died in the faith, so her soul is with Christ, and her body lies in the grave until the resurrection. Your sorrow is still real and doesn't need to be explained away. So think of her as whole and safe in Him, and let yourself mourn her absence while you wait.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. It is a profound grief to bury a child, even one who died in the faith. You may think of her body in the grave as resting in hope, awaiting the resurrection, while her soul is with Christ, safe in His presence. Scripture speaks of the dead in Christ as asleep and awaiting the resurrection, and of the soul being with the Lord. Your grief is real and should be honored; there is no need to pretend it away. Take comfort in the hope of reunion, in the prayers of the church, and in the promises of God. Let yourself mourn, and let others mourn with you.

prompt: I am a servant and my fellow servants think me proud and hypocritical because I will not join their vanities—how should I bear it?
chosen: I'd say first: you're not doing anything wrong by staying out of their vanities. This is fine, and fine with care. One principle worth weighing is that the Lord's servants should be ready to be made all things to all men in matters of indifference, but never at the cost of truth or conscience. That changes how you handle the small stuff—the shared jokes, the little rituals that don't touch conscience, the way you talk with them over a meal. Be flexible there, so your stand reads as conviction rather than contempt. What stays is your limit: you won't join what your conscience calls vanity, and you don't have to. Keep your manner warm and your words plain, and let them see that the difference is about what you owe God, not about thinking you're better than them.
rejected: The principle is this: be made all things to all men in matters of indifference, but never at the cost of truth or conscience. So sort your days honestly. Where nothing is at stake but preference and pride of appearance, bend. Sit with them, laugh with them, share what they share, and let love set the pace. But where conscience is pricked, stand, and stand without apology, because a servant's first loyalty is to the Master, not to the crowd in the kitchen. That's the shape of a faithful life: soft where you can be, firm where you must be, and never confusing the two.

prompt: I am a poor man and the rich pass by my cottage without notice—does God regard the lowly dwelling?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, God regards the lowly dwelling. The principle I'd weigh is that Christian worth may dwell unseen like a diamond in the mine, and the poor and desolate best bring prayers to the Lord's ear. That changes how you read the rich passing by—their notice was never the measure. What stays is your cottage as a real place of prayer, and you as someone whose prayers are heard. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep the devotion of that humble room, and don't let others' neglect convince you God has.
rejected: Yes, God regards the lowly dwelling. Throughout Scripture, God shows special concern for the poor and marginalized. Your worth is not measured by your wealth or by the notice of the rich, but by your faithfulness and character. God sees your heart and knows your struggles. The rich may pass by without notice, but God never overlooks you. He promises to be a father to the fatherless and a defender of the widow. Your cottage, though humble, can be a place of prayer and devotion, and God hears the prayers offered there. So take heart: God values you not for what you have but for who you are, and He will never forsake those who trust in Him.

prompt: I am a young woman and my brother is careless about his soul—what can I do to win him?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: wanting to win your brother isn't wrong. You're not trying to control him, you're trying to love him. So take the principle that says the real love-charm for a brother is to seek the Saviour first, then go and win the erring brother. What that changes is the order of things—your own drawing near to Christ comes before any move toward him, so your effort isn't you white-knuckling his soul. What stays is your care for him and your freedom to act on it. You're a young woman, not his parent and not his judge, so keep it gentle and keep your own life as the main thing he sees. It's fine to pray, to love him, and to speak when the moment is right.
rejected: Seek the Saviour first, and then go and win your brother. That's the whole shape of it. Don't start with arguments or pressure; start on your knees, and let your own walk with Christ be the thing that speaks loudest. Give him hope, not a lecture—wreaths of hope, not fading memorials of your own effort. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own; find God's will in prayer and in the Word before you open your mouth. Then speak, when you sense the leading, and wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation. You are your brother's keeper, and love that refuses to move toward him is a wound to your own soul. Trust Christ to save him, and be the sister who never stops hoping.

prompt: I am a minister and a careless profligate man came to a funeral out of curiosity and was affected—should I follow up with him?
chosen: I'd have said first: yes, follow up with him—gently, and soon. A careless man who wanders into a funeral out of curiosity and leaves stirred is not nothing. Ask him what struck him, listen more than you talk, offer to pray. But weigh this too, in its own words: a pastor owes his own soul's care first, and charity cannot be kindled in others if it is extinguished in oneself. That changes how you go about it—keep your own reading, self-examination, and private devotion steady while you reach out, so the follow-up comes from a full heart rather than a frayed one. What stays is the plain answer: yes, go to him. Curiosity and emotion aren't conversion yet, so be patient and let the Spirit do the deeper work.
rejected: Yes, follow up—but wisely. A curious visitor who was moved at a funeral is a seed worth tending. Reach out gently within a few days, without pressure, and invite him to talk. Ask what struck him, listen more than you speak, and offer to pray with him. Invite him to church or a small group where he can meet believers. Be patient: curiosity and emotion are not yet conversion, so pray for him and let the Spirit do the deeper work. Also, remember that your own ministry's effectiveness depends on your walk with God, so keep tending your own soul as you reach out to him.

prompt: I am a poor old man and my daughter has been the instrument of my awakening—how do I show gratitude to God for her?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: let the gratitude start small and concrete. You asked how to thank God for your daughter, and that question is itself a good prayer. Where I'd weigh a principle is this one—that gratitude is shown by living the truth in deeds, not words only. What that changes is the shape of your thanks: it moves from a feeling you carry privately to something your daughter can actually see in you—patience, honesty, tenderness, the kind of man she helped wake up. What stays is your situation exactly as you described it: you are poor, you are old, and she is the instrument. Nothing here asks you to buy her anything or perform some grand public gesture you can't afford. Say thank you to God in your own words, thank her plainly while you still can, and let your days quietly show it. That is enough, and it is fine.
rejected: Gratitude to God is not a sentiment you store up and admire; it is a life turned toward Him in obedience, in deeds and not in words only. Your daughter was the instrument, but the waking is yours to answer. When the soul shakes off the dust of earth and clings to God, dreading even the least separation from Him, then whatever it receives, undertakes, and does becomes pure prayer—and rejoicing in God becomes as natural as breathing. So do not merely feel thankful; become the thanks. Let your conduct be the hymn. And where you meet others carrying different gifts and different measures of light, do not weigh their fruits against yours; all who belong to God form one Spirit, and you are to acknowledge them as brothers and sisters. Let your gratitude run out past your own door.

prompt: I was awakened under a sermon but the people around me laughed and called me a hypocrite—should I keep going?
chosen: I'd say this first: keep going. What happened to you—being laughed at right after something real stirred in you—is painful, and it doesn't by itself mean the awakening was fake. Weigh this one principle as it's worded: beware of imitating hypocrites who try to appear outwardly more holy than they know themselves to be, and don't seek or desire human praise. That changes something: it means the question isn't whether the people around you are impressed, and it isn't whether you can prove them wrong. It stays true that you can go back to the sermon, pray, read, and be honest about what you actually know of yourself. If their word 'hypocrite' has any truth in it, face that quietly and turn from it. But their laughter doesn't get to decide whether you keep going. So yes—keep going, with care to be honest rather than impressive.
rejected: Yes, keep going—but go for God, not for them. Being laughed at for taking faith seriously is painful, and their mockery may sting, but it does not decide whether the awakening was real. What matters is whether God is at work in you. Still, their accusation deserves honest reflection: ask yourself whether there is any truth to it, and if so, repent. Do not perform for the crowd or try to prove them wrong. Go back to the sermon, to prayer, and to Scripture quietly. Find a few sincere believers who will encourage you rather than mock you. Over time, a changed life will answer their laughter better than any argument. Keep going, but keep your eyes on God rather than on your reputation.

prompt: I am a Christian and I have neglected secret prayer and reading—how do I return to the ways of God?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you haven't lost God's welcome, so don't come back to him as though you have to earn your way in. One principle I'd weigh is this — hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and when your mind wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect; bring your attention back in tranquility. What that changes is the tone of your return: short, honest, unhurried prayer beats an ambitious plan you'll abandon by Thursday. What stays is your own sense of what you've neglected — secret prayer and reading — so keep those as the aim, just start small and gently. If a wandering mind is your main worry, that principle is your permission slip to begin again without scolding yourself.
rejected: Come back to God like a beggar at a rich man's gate — that is the whole posture. You have nothing to bring and everything to receive, so stop treating prayer as a debt you fell behind on. Keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and when it drifts, do not disquiet yourself; trouble and disquiet scatter the heart rather than gather it, so bring your attention back in tranquility, again and again, without drama. And give prayer the best of your time, not the scraps — let the closet come first and study and work second, refreshed by what happens there.
