That fits what you describe—vast, beautiful, beyond words—and it gives you somewhere to take it. What changes is that the moment isn't just a nice feeling to collect; it has a direction. What stays is your own framing: you didn't ask for a doctrine, you asked what this is. So call it a glimpse, let it point you toward gratitude, and don't force it into words it doesn't need. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: You've touched something real, and the mistake would be to let it stop there. Nature is not just scenery; it is the visible demonstration of an invisible Will, and the beauty that stops you in your tracks is meant to be traced back to its Source. When you do that, blessing becomes a continual ecstasy for soul and creature—not a mood you chase but a life you live. So don't bask. Awe in music or a mountainside should rouse you, not lull you into passive contentment; the health of the soul is intense living and activity in connection with the Divine Energy. Ask what the beauty points to, answer with worship and with action, and let one moment of that understanding stand as a foretaste of eternity.

prompt: I say little prayers during the day but they feel empty and mechanical. Is that worth anything?
chosen: I'd say first: what you're doing is fine, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that a little lifting up of the heart suffices — a little remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, though upon a march and a sword in hand, are prayers very acceptable to God. That speaks right to your case. You're not producing nothing; you're lifting your heart in small moments, and that counts. What it changes is the pressure you're putting on the feeling. What stays is your honesty that it feels mechanical — so when you notice that, pause for a second and mean the next one. Keep the little prayers. Don't add a heavy program on top of them.
rejected: Yes, little prayers are worth something, even if they feel empty. Prayer is not about feelings but about connecting with God. Short prayers can be powerful because they keep you mindful of God throughout the day. However, if they feel mechanical, you might try to make them more meaningful by pausing to think about what you're saying. Consider setting aside longer prayer times too. Don't give up; consistency matters. God hears even the smallest prayer. Ask Him to help you pray with sincerity, and remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance.

prompt: I feel like I have two selves—one that wants God and one that wants everything else. Which one am I?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're describing isn't a defect in you—it's just what it is to be a person with a will. The principle I'd weigh first says we have two wills: the will to live, our natural pull toward our own comfort and safety, which on its own doesn't get us to peace or eternal life, and the will to love and gladly please God, which is the only will we actually live by. Notice it doesn't say you're two people. It says you have two wills, and only one of them is the one you live by. So the question 'which one am I' gets a gentler answer than you might expect: you're the one in whom both are real, and the life you're after comes from the second, not from killing off the first by force. What that changes is the pressure to pick an identity on the spot—you don't have to declare yourself one thing today. What stays is the honest tug-of-war; it's still there, and it still matters which will you lean into. Given that you framed this as a question about who you are rather than a request to be told what to do, I'd say this is fine to sit with, and fine to bring into prayer exactly as it is.
rejected: You ask which of your two selves you are, and the answer is that the question itself is a little off. You have two wills. One is the will to live—the natural reach for your own comfort, your own security, your own survival—and that will, left to itself, does not bring you peace, let alone eternal life. The other is the will to love and gladly please God, and that is the only will by which you actually live. So stop trying to figure out which self is the real you and start noticing which will you're feeding. The first one doesn't need to be managed; it needs to be seen for what it is. The second one is where your life is. And here's the thing you should hear: this isn't a lonely project. The God you're reaching for is reaching for you—the search runs both directions. You are not assembling a self in a vacuum; your personality comes alive in fellowship with Him, and His life opens into yours and yours into His. So bring both wills into that fellowship and let the one that gives life grow.

prompt: I keep giving in to the same sin over and over. Is there any hope for me?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: there's hope, and you're not the first person to come back to the same failure. I'd weigh this principle first: God commands all people everywhere to repent now, and since he commands it, the power to renounce sin is available. That matters because it means you don't have to wait until you feel stronger or more sorry. The feeling follows the surrender, not the other way around. What that changes is the waiting game — you can turn from it this moment, in will and purpose, and ask God for the strength he promises. What stays is the honest part: this is a real struggle, and turning once doesn't guarantee you'll never slip again. So keep going back to him, keep being honest with someone who can help, and don't let a setback convince you the door is closed. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. Struggling with repeated sin is common, and God's grace is greater than any sin. Start by acknowledging your weakness and asking for forgiveness. Then, take practical steps: identify triggers, seek accountability, and replace sinful habits with healthy ones. Remember that sanctification is a process, and setbacks don't mean failure. God's mercy is new every morning. Keep praying, stay in community, and don't give up. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can experience victory over time.

prompt: I'm afraid of God's will for my life—I imagine it as a path of thorns. Will it always feel like that?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your fear makes sense, and it doesn't disqualify you from anything. You're picturing God's will as a path of thorns, and that picture is doing a lot of work in your imagination right now. Here's one principle worth weighing in its own words: in our raw state we fear the Will of God as a path of thorns, but as Christ moulds us we come to know it as a great Balm, longing to conform to it and sink into it as into immense security. Notice what that says and doesn't say. It doesn't promise the thorns vanish overnight, and it doesn't ask you to pretend you're not afraid. What it changes is the direction of travel: the fear you feel now isn't the final word about what God's will is like. What stays is your honesty, your prayer, and the fact that you're allowed to bring the fear itself rather than waiting until you've conquered it. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep praying honestly, don't force a feeling you don't have, and let trust grow slowly.
rejected: You fear God's will as a path of thorns, and that fear is real, but it is not the truth about where you are being led. In our raw state we fear the Will of God as a path of thorns, but as Christ moulds us we come to know it as a great Balm, longing to conform to it and sink into it as into immense security. That is the promise held out to you: not a life of dread, but a will you will one day long to sink into. So do not stand at a distance measuring the thorns. Come close, let Christ mould you, and let the fear be replaced by longing. The path may have hard stretches, but the one who leads you does not wish to harm you; he wishes to do your soul great good.

prompt: I'm wealthy. Can a rich person really find God?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Take the principle that says the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate religious life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. That applies to you as much as anyone. Your wealth doesn't disqualify you, and it doesn't mean you have to sell everything and disappear into a monastery to be serious. What it does mean is that the pull of possessions is real, and you should hold your resources loosely, be generous, and let them serve people rather than run you. So keep your work, keep your family, keep your ordinary days, and seek God right there. What changes is the fantasy that you need a dramatic exit to be spiritual. What stays is the honesty about comfort and self-reliance. You don't need to abandon your life to find God; you need to live it awake.
rejected: Yes, a rich person can find God, though wealth brings particular dangers: distraction, self-reliance, and comfort that dulls dependence on Him. The answer is not necessarily to abandon your work or family, but to hold wealth loosely, practice generosity, and let it serve others rather than master you. Many ordinary people in everyday life find God precisely in their work and responsibilities. Seek Him where you are, with honesty about the pull of possessions, and let your resources become a means of love rather than a substitute for God.

prompt: I feel guilty and afraid about my past. Is fear of punishment a good reason to turn to God?
chosen: I'd start by saying: fear is allowed to be the door you walk through, as long as you don't lock yourself in the hallway. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says we must not fear God as though He wished to harm us, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do us great good. That changes the destination of your fear, not the fact that you feel it. Your guilt and fear are real, and you don't have to pretend they aren't. So let the fear bring you in, and then let it be replaced by trust in someone who wants your good. What stays is this: you're not being asked to talk yourself out of your past before you come. What changes is that punishment stops being the whole story.
rejected: Fear of punishment is a legitimate place to begin, but it is a poor place to live. God is not a tyrant who set a trap and waits to spring it; He wishes to do you great good. If your past weighs on you, bring it to Him honestly, and let the fear of consequences push you toward mercy rather than away from it. The gospel does not ask you to minimize your guilt; it tells you your sins can be forgiven through Christ. So come, and keep coming, until dread gives way to love of the One who first loved you.

prompt: I prayed once, really desperately, when everything fell apart, and nothing happened. Why doesn't God answer me?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your prayer wasn't wasted, and the silence doesn't mean you were ignored. I'd weigh this: "He did not pray for relief but for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love." That reframes what an answer can look like, but it doesn't erase what you asked for. You prayed once, desperately, when everything fell apart, and nothing happened. So I wouldn't tell you the silence was secretly a yes, and I wouldn't ask you to pretend the pain wasn't real. What changes is that you don't have to read the silence as a verdict on you. What stays is your honest grief and your right to bring it again, or not, as you're able. It's fine to keep praying exactly as you did, and fine to say plainly that you're hurt and waiting.
rejected: It's painful when desperate prayer seems to meet silence. First, know that God is not indifferent to you; Scripture is full of people who cried out and waited. Sometimes the answer is delayed, sometimes it is different from what we asked, and sometimes we only see it in hindsight. One desperate prayer is not the whole story—prayer is a relationship, not a transaction. Try to keep bringing your needs to God honestly, and invite others to pray with you. Consider whether there are practical steps you can take alongside prayer, and talk with a pastor who can help you process this.

prompt: I had a powerful spiritual experience once and have never been able to repeat it. Was it real? Should I try to get it back?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that you're not wrong to ask. A real experience that won't come back is worth taking seriously. But I'd weigh this carefully: spiritual experiences are not something we can summon by our own will, and the old counsel is to accept them as God chooses rather than pray for them or secretly crave them. That doesn't tell you to doubt what happened. It tells you to hold it loosely rather than chase it. So what changes is your posture toward getting it back: stop straining for a repeat, and let the memory stand as a gift. What stays is the experience itself and the fruit it left in you. You asked whether it was real and whether to pursue it again. On the first, look at what it did in your life. On the second, it's fine to treasure it and fine to let it go, with care not to make a repeat the measure of your faith.
rejected: You want to know if it was real and whether you should get it back. Hear this: spiritual experiences are entirely outside our control, not to be prayed for or secretly desired, but accepted as God chooses, and in them there is no will but total submission, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. So stop interrogating the memory and stop plotting its return. The question that matters is not whether you can reproduce it but whether you will submit to the God who gave it. Let the experience be what it was, and let your life now be the evidence.

prompt: I believe Jesus lived and was crucified. Isn't that all that's required?
chosen: What you've said is a real starting point, and I wouldn't take it from you or pile on extra requirements as if your faith weren't genuine. But let me put one thing beside it: the living Christ is not the person that was but the person that still is, present with us always in an unbroken and continuous presence. That doesn't cancel what you believe about the crucifixion; it means the one you believe in isn't only a figure of the past. So your belief stands. What changes is that it can be a relationship with someone present now, not just a fact you affirm.
rejected: Belief that Jesus lived and was crucified is a starting point, but it is not the whole of the Christian life. The Gospels call us not merely to affirm historical facts but to follow Jesus, to take up our cross, and to be transformed into his likeness. Even the demons believe the facts, as Scripture says, yet that belief does not save. What is required is a living faith that trusts Christ, repents of sin, and bears fruit in obedience and love. So thank God for the historical foundation, but do not stop there. Let that belief become a relationship, a discipleship, and a life shaped by the crucified and risen Lord.

prompt: I keep failing at being good. Does God count my failed attempts at all?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, God counts them. Your failed attempts aren't nothing to him. The principle I'd weigh here is that he had no scruples—when he failed he readily acknowledged it, and when he didn't fail he gave God thanks, crediting the strength to him. That changes the shape of your question: the point isn't tallying attempts, it's honesty and gratitude. What stays is your real struggle—you keep failing, and that's not dismissed. So bring the failures plainly, without drama, and give thanks when you don't fail. That's fine, and it's fine done with care.
rejected: Stop agonizing over whether your failures are being counted. The man who had no scruples shows the way: when he failed he readily acknowledged it, saying he is used to do so and shall never do otherwise if left to himself; when he did not fail he gave God thanks, acknowledging the strength comes from him. That is the whole posture. Acknowledge failure honestly and quickly, without dramatizing it, and when you stand, credit the strength to God rather than to yourself. Your failed attempts are not worthless, but they are not the ledger you think they are. Keep going with a light heart, quick to admit and quick to thank.

prompt: I feel an emptiness inside and I keep filling it with shopping, relationships, and entertainment, but it never lasts. What is actually wrong?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: nothing about your shopping, your relationships, or your entertainment is wrong in itself. What I'd weigh is that people try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, and none of them truly satisfy. That's the real diagnosis — you're asking these things to carry a weight they can't hold. But here's what changes: you didn't tell me you want a different life or a different set of duties, and I won't invent that for you. You have your own situation — whatever work, people, and routines are already yours — and the fix isn't to flee them for something more exciting. Keep the shopping, the relationships, the entertainment. Enjoy them for what they are. Just stop asking them to be the thing that finally makes you whole, and put that weight where it belongs. That's not a no to your life; it's a care-filled yes with one honest adjustment.
rejected: What is wrong is that you are trying to fill a spiritual hunger with material things. Shopping, relationships, and entertainment are not evil in themselves, but they are finite, and finite things cannot satisfy an infinite longing. Each purchase or romance gives a brief lift, then the emptiness returns, often worse. The problem is not that you need better things but that you are asking things to do what only God can do. The remedy is to name the emptiness honestly, turn toward God, and let the good things you enjoy become gifts rather than gods. They can be received with gratitude once they are no longer asked to save you.

prompt: I'm exhausted and overwhelmed by everyday duties. How can I keep any awareness of God through all of it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're tired, and that matters. The principle I'd weigh first is that we must not be troubled if our attention is distracted from God by necessary work, since doing all our actions for God keeps us in His presence without needing to offer each action explicitly. That changes something real for you: you don't have to add a layer of reminders, breath prayers, and phone alerts on top of an already full day. The duties themselves, done for God, can carry the awareness. What stays is the gentle return when you drift, and the honesty that you're worn out. So keep it simple, and let the ordinary work be the prayer.
rejected: The answer to a scattered, exhausted life is not more technique. Do each action for God, and stop fretting about distraction, because a wandering thought in necessary work is not a failure. Beware of hurry and over-eagerness, which block everything. Remember that God is the one living Worker and you are only the instrument, so cast your care on Him instead of anxiously relying on yourself. Stay calm in His presence, do what lies before you, and return gently when you drift.

prompt: I feel completely apathetic about spiritual things and I can't seem to care. What is happening to me?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that the advice you may have heard—treat the dryness as a problem to fix by forcing yourself back into prayer and Scripture until the feelings follow—is not what I'd tell you. That framing turns your spiritual life into something you manufacture, and it quietly makes your numbness into a failure of effort. The principle I'd weigh says spiritual experiences are entirely outside our volition, not to be prayed for or secretly desired, but accepted as God chooses, with no will but total submission. That changes something real: you don't have to chase a feeling, and you don't have to fake one. What stays is that apathy is still deadly, and the honest move is to name it rather than manage it. So the plain no: don't treat this as a technique problem, and don't grit your teeth toward a sensation. But I won't leave you with a shrug either—name the apathy out loud to someone who can pray with you, and keep putting one foot forward even while you feel nothing.
rejected: Apathy in spiritual things is common, and it is often a sign of exhaustion, discouragement, or unaddressed sin. The first step is to be honest about it rather than pretending. Ask yourself what has drained your desire: busyness, disappointment, or a pattern of compromise? Return to the basics—prayer, Scripture, fellowship—even when you feel nothing, because feelings follow faithfulness. It may help to speak with a pastor or a trusted friend who can pray with you and help you examine your life. Do not wait for the feeling to return before you act; act, and the feeling may follow. God is not distant because you feel distant, and He is able to rekindle desire in a heart that has grown cold.

prompt: I'm afraid of what God will demand of me if I really give myself to Him. Do I have to give up my home, my children, my friends?
chosen: I'd start by saying the fear itself is worth taking seriously, because it's asking a real question: does giving yourself to God mean losing the people and the place you love? The principle I'd weigh first is that God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. That changes how you hold your prayers, not whether you keep your home, your children, or your friends. What stays is exactly what you named: your home, your children, your friends are not obstacles to surrender. So this is fine, and fine with care. Give yourself, and let your love for them be part of the giving rather than something you have to tear out first.
rejected: The fear that surrender means losing your home, your children, your friends comes from imagining God as a demander who takes. But hear the principle: God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. That is not a threat to what you love. It is a promise that the will you hand over is being met by someone wiser than your fear. So do not bargain your way out of surrender by clutching what you have. Resign your will to his, trust his kindness even when it denies you, and you will find that what he gives is better than what you were afraid to lose.

prompt: I'm trying to serve God and also keep my old life and pleasures. Why do I feel so miserable and divided all the time?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: this misery makes sense, and it isn't proof you're a hypocrite. It's the stopping half-way that causes distress — living wholly worldly can bring a kind of contentment, and living renewed brings great joy, but trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness and vacillation. So the diagnosis is the divided heart, not that you're too far gone. What that changes is how you read the misery: it's a signal pointing at the split, not a verdict on you. What stays is your honesty about it — bring that to God rather than burying it. You don't have to sort everything overnight, and you don't have to become joyless to be faithful. Start where you actually are, with the small choices that reveal which loyalty is really steering you.
rejected: You feel divided because you're trying to live in two directions at once. Serving God and clinging to old pleasures pulls your heart apart, and that tension shows up as misery. The solution isn't to hate yourself but to be honest about the conflict. Ask which loyalties actually shape your choices, and consider whether the pleasures you keep are harmless enjoyment or things that numb and enslave. You don't have to become joyless; God wants your whole heart, and a whole heart is less divided. Start with small, concrete decisions that align your life with what you say you believe.

prompt: I don't feel any love for God yet. Should I wait until I feel something before I start praying?
chosen: I'd say first: don't wait. You're asking whether you need the feeling before you start, and the honest answer is that you don't. One principle worth weighing says feelings aren't the gauge of where you stand with God, and that you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods and keep praying even when joy is lacking. That changes the pressure you're putting on yourself: you don't have to manufacture warmth to begin. What stays is your honesty about not feeling love yet. So start praying as you actually are, plainly and without pretending, and let the practice carry you while affection catches up. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Don't wait for the feeling. Feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God; the measure is the changeless word of promise, not your mood. So keep praying even when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion because your heart feels cold. But don't pray as a creature at an immense distance with only passive, waiting faith. Let your prayer be a love-flash of active faith that eats up all the distance and sets you immediately with the Creator, with vivid certainty at the heart. Speak honestly, read Scripture, keep a rhythm, and let love grow out of faithfulness rather than waiting for it to arrive first.

prompt: I feel drawn to leave everything and live a secluded religious life. Is that the highest path?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: this desire can be holy, and it isn't automatically the highest path just because it's the hardest-looking one. Take the principle that says ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation. That's worth sitting with, because it reframes the question. You're not asking whether solitude would be restful; you're asking whether it would be fruitful. So the test isn't how much you'd give up but whether you'd actually show up for the prayer, the work, and the plain unglamorous faithfulness day after day. What that changes is the romance of it. What stays is your freedom to go, if the desire holds up under wise counsel and honest self-examination. You said you feel drawn; that's a real starting point, not a verdict. Go slowly, and let love for God and neighbor be the measure either way.
rejected: A call to seclusion can be genuine, but it is not automatically the highest path. The highest path is wherever God calls you and where love can grow. Solitude can free you for prayer, simplicity, and attention to God, but it can also become an escape from responsibility, community, and the needs of others. Test the desire prayerfully and with wise counsel. Ask whether it springs from love for God or from disappointment, pride, or a wish for ease. Remember that holiness is measured by love, not by withdrawal. Whether you remain in ordinary life or enter a religious community, the goal is the same: to love God and neighbor faithfully.

prompt: I'm baptised and consider myself Christian—won't I go to heaven when I die regardless?
chosen: I'd want to say first that being baptized and calling yourself Christian are good things, but they aren't a guarantee of heaven. One principle here says it plainly: many look to death to work a miracle, thinking that ceasing to live physically opens paradise so long as we're baptized and call ourselves Christians—and that's a delusion, because in character we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. So what changes? The assumption that death itself settles anything. What stays? Your baptism still marks you as belonging to Christ, and it still calls you to live that faith now. So no, I can't tell you that you'll go to heaven regardless. That's the honest answer, and I give it kindly: don't put your hope in the fact that you were baptized or that you'll die someday. Put it in Christ, and let your faith be something you actually live from one Monday to the next.
rejected: Plenty of people look to death to work a miracle, as though the mere stopping of physical life were a doorway into paradise so long as they were baptized and wore the name Christian. That is a delusion. In character we are after death exactly as far advanced as before—death adds nothing, it only fixes what we already are. What we need is present salvation: a religion that is with us from one Monday to the next, not a vague hope saved up for a deathbed. Prepare to live, not merely to prepare to die. And let your assurance rest on the cardinal fact of the Christian faith—Christ's resurrection and his promises—not on speculation about what dying will do for you. Those who die in his faith and obedience enter a new and blessed life; that is firm ground. Baptism and the name of Christian are precious, but they are not a guarantee. Trust Christ, grow in him, and live faithfully today.

prompt: I want to find God but I don't want to become conspicuously pious or peculiar in front of others. Is that possible?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The first thing I'd say is that you don't have to choose between finding God and living your ordinary life. The principle puts it plainly: the ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. That directly answers your worry. You keep your job, your family, your friendships, your normal way of being in the world. What changes is the interior orientation, not the outward performance. What stays is exactly the life you already have. So go ahead, and don't let anyone tell you that a quiet, unshowy pursuit isn't the real thing.
rejected: Yes, it's possible, but finding God usually requires some real change. You'll probably need to reorder your priorities, perhaps cut back on certain friendships or activities that pull you away, and build a more disciplined spiritual life. Many people find a retreat, a monastery visit, or a season of intensive study helpful. You may need to be willing to look different from those around you. Consider whether your concern about appearances is itself a barrier. It's worth asking what you're willing to give up, because a serious pursuit of God often does make you stand out.

prompt: I feel so unworthy to praise or bless God. Shouldn't I wait until I'm better before I try?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: you don't have to clean yourself up before you open your mouth. Feeling unworthy is real, and it's honest, but it isn't a gate you have to get past first. One principle here says God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and that He comes in His own time. That doesn't turn your praise into something you have to earn — it means the timing isn't yours to control anyway. What changes is the pressure: you stop waiting for a better version of yourself to show up. What stays is your honesty — small, plain words are enough, and you can keep them simple. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: start where you actually are, not where you think you should be.
rejected: Waiting until you're better before you praise is a trap, because 'better' keeps moving. The principle to hold onto is that God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and He comes in His own time. That means your praise was never a payment for worthiness — it's a response to grace that's already there. So don't make rejoicing conditional on how you feel about yourself. Keep on with it even when it seems to go nowhere, and trust God to make the reckoning good. Bless God for what He ordains rather than wishing things were different, and say, 'I am yours; do with me what seems good to you.' Begin now, with small and honest words.

prompt: I've been seeking God for years with no sign of response. Should I give up?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that it's okay to be worn out by this. Years of seeking without a clear answer is a real kind of tiredness, and you're not wrong to feel it. If I weigh one principle here, it's the one about God not always giving just what we ask: he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. What that changes is the meaning of the silence—it can be a father's kind refusal rather than a door slammed shut, so you don't have to read it as abandonment. What stays is your freedom: you asked whether to give up, and I won't pretend the answer is a command to grind on forever. Stepping back, resting, or loosening your grip for a while is fine, and if this is causing you real distress, talking to a counselor is a good and allowed thing to do. Keep your expectations of what a response would look like a little wider, and be gentle with yourself either way.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged after years of seeking without a clear response. Many people go through long seasons of silence, and it doesn't necessarily mean you're doing something wrong or that God has abandoned you. Consider whether your expectations of what a 'response' looks like might be too narrow—sometimes answers come quietly, through other people, or through gradual change. It may help to talk with a trusted spiritual guide, adjust your practices, and give yourself permission to rest. If the search is causing real distress, consider speaking with a counselor. You don't have to give up, but you also don't have to push yourself relentlessly. Be gentle with yourself and stay open.

prompt: I've read many books on spirituality and theology but I still don't feel I know God. What is missing?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're describing isn't a failure on your part. You've read a lot, and reading about God and knowing God really are different things. The principle I'd weigh here is this: we cannot in one step mount into the knowledge of God. First we learn to know Jesus intimately and devotedly, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally God the Holy Trinity becomes our All. That order matters for you because it takes the pressure off. You don't have to arrive at the whole thing at once. What changes is the goal: instead of trying to grasp God through books, you'd let one step at a time be enough, starting with getting to know Jesus closely. What stays is everything you've already read; it isn't wasted, it's raw material. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep reading if it feeds you, but add something slower and more personal, like prayer or silence or honest conversation with someone who can help you notice where God is actually at work in your life.
rejected: The thing that's missing is the order of knowing. We cannot in one step mount into the knowledge of God. First we must learn to know Jesus intimately and devotedly, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally God the Holy Trinity becomes our All. You've been trying to leap to the top of the staircase, and that's why the books leave you empty. Start where the order starts: know Jesus closely, not as a topic but as a person you spend time with. Let that lead you onward. And remember that the inward knowledge that Christ is God comes not by nature but by gift of God, which must be earnestly sought, striven for, prayed for, and desired. That faith is the very coming to God by which we are saved. So don't just read. Pray for the gift, and let the order carry you.

prompt: I feel spiritually lazy and content, just basking in good feelings. Is that a problem?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling spiritually lazy and content isn't automatically a problem. Good feelings aren't the enemy. The principle I'd weigh first is that in the beginning we should be faithful in doing our duty and denying ourselves, and afterward unspeakable pleasures follow. That reframes what you're describing: the question isn't whether the good feelings are bad, but whether they're resting on faithfulness or replacing it. If you're still doing the small duties and saying no to yourself where it counts, then basking is fine, and honestly it's the kind of thing that follows obedience rather than undermines it. What changes is that I wouldn't tell you to distrust the warmth. What stays is the honest check: are the duties still happening? If they are, enjoy it. If the comfort is quietly crowding them out, that's worth noticing, but that's care, not a verdict against you.
rejected: Good feelings are not bad in themselves, but if they replace growth they can become a trap. Spiritual contentment that never moves toward obedience, repentance, or service is more like comfort than devotion. Ask yourself: are these feelings drawing me closer to God and others, or are they soothing me while I avoid hard things? A helpful test is whether your life shows increasing love, humility, and faithfulness. If not, the feelings may be masking avoidance. Try small, concrete acts of obedience and self-denial, and let the feelings follow rather than lead. Talk with a trusted mentor or confessor about what you are experiencing, and be honest about whether you are resting in God or resting in comfort.

prompt: I want to serve others and improve the world. Isn't social work and charity the way to God?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, social work and charity can absolutely be a way to God — but with a caution. One principle worth weighing is this: 'We serve God well only when we serve Him as He wills, not as we think we could serve Him better another way.' That doesn't cancel your desire to serve others; it just means the serving has to stay rooted in listening to God, not in assuming your preferred path is automatically his. So what changes? You don't have to abandon social work or charity — they're good and needed. What stays is the call to check your motives and stay open to God's direction, even if that means adjusting how or where you serve. So go ahead, but do it with care and a listening heart.
rejected: The question is whether social work and charity are the way to God. The principle is clear: we serve God well only when we serve Him as He wills, not as we think we could serve Him better another way. That means no amount of good work, no strategy of charity, no plan for improving the world can substitute for obedience to God's actual will. If you think you've found a better way to serve Him than the way He sets out, you're mistaken. So don't assume your chosen path is automatically his. Serve, yes — but serve as He wills, not as you prefer.

prompt: I'm angry at God about something that happened to me. Does that block me from Him?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your anger doesn't put you outside anything. Being honest with God about what hurt you is not the same as turning away from Him. One principle worth weighing here says that God does not cause man to sin, be sick, or die, and that it's contrary to our highest ideas of God to suppose He arranges evil results and then punishes the helpless. If that's true, then the thing that happened to you isn't something God did to you, and your anger is aimed at a picture of God that may not be accurate. What that changes: it takes some of the fear out of your question, because you're not being punished for feeling angry. What stays: the hurt is real, and the anger is real, and it still needs somewhere to go. Bring it to Him honestly rather than letting it harden into bitterness, and talk to someone you trust about what happened.
rejected: Anger at God is a common and understandable response to pain. It does not automatically block you from Him; in fact, bringing your anger honestly to God can be part of a real relationship. What matters is what you do with the anger. If it hardens into bitterness or turns you away, that can create distance. But if you express it honestly and stay in the relationship, it can deepen your faith over time. Many people in Scripture expressed anger and grief to God. Consider talking to a trusted friend or counselor about what happened, and be gentle with yourself as you process it.

prompt: My spouse is not spiritual and my friends think I'm becoming strange. How do I deal with the loneliness of this path?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this loneliness is real, and it doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. On the marriage piece, I'd weigh this: husbands and wives should not separate if there is no Christian demand for it; mutual compromises, tender solicitude, and patience maintain the union. That doesn't tell you to hide your inner life or pretend, and it doesn't ask you to drag your spouse along. It means the patience runs one direction for now, toward staying kind and close in ordinary ways while you carry this yourself. What changes is that you stop treating your spouse's distance as a verdict on the marriage. What stays is your need for people who get it, so keep finding that community, and keep your friends who mock you at arm's length without writing them off.
rejected: Loneliness like this is common, and it's not a sign you've gone off course. Remember that your relationship with God is personal, and lean into prayer and Scripture. With your spouse, practice patience and mutual forbearance; do not rush toward separation, since separation should not happen without a Christian demand, and divorce warns of a fundamental error. Love them as they are and look for shared ground. Find a community of believers for fellowship, but let love of friends stay subordinate to the love of God. Accept that some loneliness comes with following Christ, set healthy boundaries with friends who mock your faith, pray for them, and take care of yourself. God is with you.

prompt: How do I respond when someone asks me why God saved me and not others who were killed?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you don't owe anyone a tidy explanation, and you're allowed to say plainly that you don't know why you were spared. That's honest, and it's kinder than a theory. One of the principles here says that when we've drifted from God we shouldn't tie ourselves in knots about it, but should acknowledge our need and come back to him with more trust. That fits this question: the mystery of why you lived doesn't have to be solved for your answer to be faithful. What it changes is the pressure to justify yourself or hint that you deserved it. What stays is the grief, the real absence of an answer, and the freedom to point to Christ who shares our death and promises resurrection. So it's fine, with care: be honest, don't rank yourself above the dead, and let gratitude and service carry part of what words can't.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions, and honesty matters more than a tidy answer. You can say that you do not know why God spared you, and that you will not pretend to explain His providence. Avoid implying that you were better or more deserving. Acknowledge the grief and the mystery, affirm that God grieves with those who suffer, and point to Christ as the one who shares our death and promises resurrection. Let your life, lived in gratitude and service, be part of your answer rather than words alone.

prompt: How do I find the fulness of the Holy Spirit in my life?
chosen: I'd start by saying: this is a good thing to want, and you can go after it with confidence. The principle I'd weigh first is that the Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, who came at Pentecost to dwell in the church as his successor and vicar. That means you're not chasing a force or a mood—you're asking a Person to make himself at home in you, and he's already committed to that. So pray and ask him to fill you, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, obey what you sense him prompting, and confess sin quickly rather than letting it pile up. What that changes is the tone: it's relational, not a technique to master. What stays is your own situation—if you've been hurt by church structures or feel burned out on institutions, you don't have to force yourself back into them to find him; he's not confined to a building. Take the gradual path, expect character to grow over time, and be patient with yourself.
rejected: The fullness of the Holy Spirit isn't a prize for the especially spiritual—it's the ordinary life of the church. The Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, sent at Pentecost to dwell in the church as his successor and vicar. He's not an impersonal influence you tap into; he speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. And he works through concrete means: Scripture read with an open heart, worship, prayer, fellowship, confession of sin, obedience to what he prompts. He works gradually and personally, forming love, joy, peace, and self-control in you over time—so don't be thrown by imperfection, in the church or in yourself; imperfection doesn't disprove his real presence and guidance. Keep asking, keep obeying, keep showing up, and trust that he fills those who hunger for him.

prompt: I've been praying for a family member's salvation for years. Should I keep going?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, keep praying. That's fine, and it's fine with care. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we should pray for God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss in them. What that changes: some of your praying for your family member can turn toward your own heart too, so the years of waiting don't just wear you down. What stays: you keep bringing this person before God, honestly, for as long as you want to. You've named no limits here, so I won't invent any. Keep going, and let the praying do its work in you as well.
rejected: Yes, keep going. Persistent prayer for someone you love is never wasted, even when you see no change. Scripture encourages us to pray without ceasing and to be persistent, like the widow before the judge. At the same time, remember that you cannot force another person's choices; prayer is not a guarantee of a particular outcome, but it places the situation in God's hands and shapes your own heart. Keep praying honestly, and look for opportunities to show love and speak truth gently. Also care for yourself so that you do not grow bitter or exhausted. Many people have prayed for years before seeing fruit, and sometimes the fruit comes in ways we do not expect.

prompt: Is it wrong to plan my own life instead of leaving it open to God's leading?
chosen: I'd start by saying that planning your own life is not the problem. The principle I'd weigh here is that God's commands always imply promises, and the ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not put before you unless it can be realized by grace. That tells me God isn't asking you to drift and call it trust. He's asking you to walk, and walking involves choosing a direction. What that changes is the fear that making plans is somehow a lack of faith. What stays is the posture: hold your plans with an open hand, pray over them, and be willing to turn if He prompts you. So plan, and plan prayerfully. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Planning your life is not a rival to God's leading; it's the ground He often leads you on. God's commands always imply promises, and the ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not set before you unless it can be realized by grace. He does not command a direction and then withhold the strength to take it. So set your goals, make your decisions, and do it prayerfully, holding your plans loosely and ready to change course when He speaks. Faith is not the absence of plans; it's plans submitted to Him.

prompt: How do I find the right person to care for my children when I have to travel for ministry?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that this is a fine thing to be thinking through carefully, and there's no reason you shouldn't look for a good caregiver. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about bringing every matter, great and small, before the Lord in prayer, taking no step without first asking counsel of the Scriptures and seeking guidance, and waiting until the will of God is clear. That changes the tone of your search: it means you don't have to rush a decision out of anxiety, and you can pray specifically about the hours, the duties, and the person. What stays is everything practical you already know you need — asking trusted friends and church members for recommendations, interviewing people, checking references, and making sure the caregiver shares your values and treats your children well. You're traveling for ministry, not abandoning your kids, and seeking God's guidance alongside a careful search is exactly the right posture.
rejected: Finding the right caregiver for your children while traveling for ministry requires careful planning. Start by identifying your needs: what hours, what duties, and what qualities you value. Ask trusted friends, family, and church members for recommendations. Interview potential caregivers and check references. Consider their experience, reliability, and compatibility with your children. Pray about the decision and seek wisdom from your community. Ensure the caregiver shares your values and can provide a safe, nurturing environment. Trust your instincts and communicate openly with your children about the arrangement. With thoughtful preparation, you can find someone who will care for your children well.

prompt: Is it right to give away my best workers when other missionaries ask for them?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it for me is this: believers should be transparent with fellow laborers in the work, sharing the knowledge of needs so that they may share in prayers, faith, and reward. That means when another missionary asks for one of your best workers, the honest move is to talk plainly with them about what you actually need and what you can actually spare, rather than quietly hoarding or quietly resenting the ask. What that changes is the tone of the whole thing: it becomes a conversation among fellow laborers, not a tug-of-war over scarce goods. What stays is your own stated limit, that your work can't collapse, and that the worker is a person with a calling, not a piece of equipment to hand over. So release when you can spare someone, decline or offer another when you can't, and keep the worker free to say what they sense God is asking of them.
rejected: The question underneath this is whether you'll treat the people who serve alongside you as possessions or as fellow laborers. Share the knowledge of the work's needs with those who labor beside you, that they may join in prayer, faith, and self-denial, and do not clutch what you have as though it were yours to keep. If another field is in real need and you can spare a worker, send them, and send them trusting God rather than calculating what you lose. If your own labor would fall apart, say so plainly and offer what you can. Speak well of those who came before you and of those who labor elsewhere, invite rather than compel, and leave every worker free to follow the calling they sense. Generosity is the posture; honesty about real need is the method; and God is the one who supplies workers to every field.

prompt: My husband and I disagree about trusting God for our finances. How should I respond?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a fine thing to work through together, and it's fine with care. One principle worth weighing in its own words: God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments, so all care and anxiety on our part is distrust of Him. That reframes the argument—neither of you is the one holding your finances together, so the question isn't whose plan wins but how you both stop gripping so hard. What that changes is the tone: less debate about who trusts God more, more honesty about where each of you feels afraid. What stays is everything practical—you still need a budget, still need to talk calmly, still may need a pastor or advisor. Your limits are real: you disagree, it's stressful, and you don't have to resolve it in one conversation. Keep listening to your husband without judgment and share your concerns plainly.
rejected: Disagreements about money are common and stressful. Start by listening to your husband without judgment, and share your own concerns calmly. You may have different risk tolerances, and both views deserve respect. Together, set a budget, agree on giving, and be honest about what you can and cannot do. Prayer can help you find unity, but practical planning matters too. Seek counsel from a trusted pastor or financial advisor if you are stuck. Avoid blame and keep the conversation going. The goal is not for one of you to win but for you both to feel heard and to make a plan you can live with.

prompt: I'm afraid to go where God is leading because of the risk to my family. What should I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: your fear for your family is not a failure of faith. It's love, and love counts the cost. So I wouldn't rush you past it. Weigh this: God's protection in danger is real, and you can commit yourself and your family to His keeping, finding His Word sweet in times of peril. That doesn't mean the risk disappears or that you skip wise precautions. What it changes is who holds the outcome. What stays is your responsibility to pray together, seek counsel, and make real provision for the people in your care. Going where God leads is fine here, and fine with care, taken one honest step at a time.
rejected: Fear for your family feels like the most faithful thing in the world, but it can quietly become the thing that keeps you from following God at all. The truth is that God's protection in danger is real, and you can commit yourself and everyone you love to His keeping, finding His Word sweet even in peril. The soul dreads that, having God, it must have naught beside, and so it flees. But what it fears as loss is really God storing all things for it at home. Faith gives as strong a conviction as sight that God never forsakes us until we have first forsaken Him. So fear to leave Him, not the road He sets before you. Go, and live and die in His presence, and He will guard and guide you and your loved ones.

prompt: How do I handle it when the home church tells us to retrench and cut back the work?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about being meekly and mightily fastened to our Mother Holy Church, since the whole Body was never broken even when a single person often is. That changes how you carry the disappointment: you don't treat the cutback as a betrayal or start something on your own to keep the work alive. What stays is your honest grief and your questions, and the freedom to ask leadership what they're seeing. Stay fastened, stay humble, and let the decision be theirs to make.
rejected: When the home church tells you to retrench, it can be disappointing. But remember that the church leadership has wisdom and you should trust their decision. Perhaps they see financial constraints or other practical reasons. You can support the decision by helping to streamline the work and focus on what's most important. It's also a good time to mix the church's efforts with community resources and seek partnerships with local businesses to keep things going. Don't be discouraged; God will provide. Just follow the leadership's guidance and do your part to keep the work alive.

prompt: What does it mean to rest in Christ instead of struggling on my own?
chosen: I'd start by saying that resting in Christ isn't the same as doing nothing, and your question already assumes that. Take the first principle on its own terms: the real secret of perfect rest is to be jealously, habitually occupied with Jesus, and failure often comes over a trifling thought or word. That's worth weighing, but notice what it doesn't ask of you. It doesn't ask you to police every stray thought until you're exhausted, which would just be struggling on your own under a different name. What it changes is the direction of your attention: instead of white-knuckling your own effort, you keep turning back toward Him, even after a small distraction. What stays is the ordinary stuff you mentioned, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and the honest work of daily life. So this is fine, and fine with care. Rest is trust, not strain.
rejected: Resting in Christ means you stop trying to earn what He has already given. The real secret of perfect rest is to be jealously, habitually occupied with Jesus, because failure often comes over a trifling thought or word. So guard your thoughts, turn from every distracting thing, and keep your eyes steadily on Him. Look at His example: His whole moral life was an uninterrupted prayer, and He often withdrew to mountains and deserts and spent whole nights in prayer, consecrating even His last breath on the cross to that work. The soul's true rest is one no creature can disturb, and it comes only by wholly giving yourself up to the life of Christ and resigning your will to Him, desiring and willing nothing without Him. That is where your struggle ends.

prompt: I prayed for a specific sign from God about a decision. Is that acceptable?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about watching our prayers as well as their answers, using the light God has already given rather than demanding signs. That principle doesn't forbid asking for a sign; it warns against treating a sign as something God owes you or using it to dodge a decision you could already make. So what changes is the posture: you can bring your specific request honestly, but hold it loosely and keep acting on the Scripture, counsel, and plain good sense you already have. What stays is your freedom to ask. You said this is about a real decision, so the practical test is simple: if no sign comes, will you still move forward with the wisdom in front of you? If yes, your prayer is in good shape.
rejected: Praying for guidance is good, and God invites us to ask for wisdom. Asking for a specific sign, however, can slide into testing God or demanding that he prove himself on our terms. Scripture gives examples of signs, but it also warns against demanding them. Often God has already given you the light you need: Scripture, wise counsel, circumstances, and ordinary prudence. Before seeking a supernatural sign, ask whether you are avoiding a decision you could make with the wisdom already given. It is acceptable to lay your desire before God honestly, but hold the request humbly, ready to act on the light you already have.

prompt: How do I pray when I'm in danger and afraid for my life?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: pray right now, however you can, and don't worry about getting the words right. One of the principles here puts it well — 'a little lifting up of the heart suffices; a little remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, though upon a march and a sword in hand, are prayers very acceptable to God and serve to fortify courage in danger.' That fits your situation exactly: you're not in a quiet room with time to compose yourself, you're afraid for your life. So a short cry — 'Lord, help me,' 'Lord Jesus, have mercy' — is a real prayer, not a lesser one. What that changes is the pressure to pray at length or in a certain form; what stays is that you can turn to God honestly in the middle of the fear. Keep it simple, keep it short, keep doing it as long as the danger lasts.
rejected: When you're afraid for your life, the temptation is to think prayer needs to be long and composed. It doesn't. A little lifting up of the heart is enough — one act of inward worship, even with a sword in hand, is a prayer God accepts, and it steadies your courage in danger. So cry out briefly and often: 'Lord, help me,' 'Lord Jesus, have mercy,' 'You are my refuge.' Don't wait for calm or for better words. Turn your heart to God in the middle of the fear, and keep turning to him for as long as the danger lasts.

prompt: Should I take a job or a position that keeps me from the mission field?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that we must not desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing prevents attaining the perfection of our vocation like desiring another. That doesn't tell you the mission field is off-limits or that a job is second-best; it tells you not to let a longing for a different field hollow out the one you're actually in. So the question shifts: does this position truly shut the door, or does it just make mission involvement less convenient and less glamorous? You've said it keeps you from the mission field, and I'll take that at face value as a real limit, not something to wave away. What changes is the guilt — taking the job isn't a betrayal if you serve God honestly in it. What stays is your calling to witness, give, pray, and stay open if a door reopens. What also stays is your duty to care for your own life and responsibilities, which a paycheck may serve. So take it, with care, and don't let the desire for another field sour the one you're in.
rejected: This is a real tension, and there is no single rule for every person. Ask whether the job genuinely prevents mission involvement or simply makes it less convenient. Many believers serve God faithfully in ordinary work, supporting missions through giving, prayer, and witness. Consider your gifts, obligations, and the counsel of mature believers. If the position clearly closes the door to a calling you believe God has given, weigh that seriously. But do not assume only formal mission work counts. God can use you where you are. Pray for wisdom, seek counsel, and hold the decision before God with an open hand.

prompt: How do I know whether an answer to prayer was really from God or just happened anyway?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fair question, and you don't have to resolve it before you keep praying. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about answers depending on meeting conditions the Bible records—contrite humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, asking according to God's will. That's worth taking seriously, but notice what it does and doesn't do. It tells you to examine your own heart and ask whether you're asking rightly; it doesn't hand you a test that sorts events into 'from God' and 'just happened.' So what changes is your focus—less on auditing the outcome, more on the honesty of the asking. What stays is your original instinct: keep a record, notice fruit like gratitude and humility, ask trusted people, and hold it loosely. You're allowed to live with some uncertainty here.
rejected: The question assumes you can stand outside an answer and grade its origin, and Scripture doesn't offer that ledger. What it does say is that prayer has conditions: contrite humility, forsaking known sin, seeking God wholeheartedly, faith, obedience, dependence on the Holy Spirit, persistence, asking according to God's will and in Christ's name. Those are the things to examine—not the event afterward. And prayer is not a transaction you audit; it's more like breathing, the constant drawing in of heavenly life that nourishes the seed already planted in you. Real prayer brings an actual incoming of help from beyond the margin of yourself, and its effects belong to the ordered life of the spirit, not to capricious interruptions. So stop trying to certify the outcome. Pray continually, repent where you must, look for the fruit of gratitude and love, and trust that God answers those who ask aright.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying and of the suffering that might come before death. How do I find peace?
chosen: What I'd say first is that your fear is not a failure, and you don't have to get rid of it to find peace. The principle I'd weigh here says we should be at peace always, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ, and patience with others must be matched by patience with ourselves. That last part matters most for you: patience with yourself. It changes the goal from erasing fear to meeting it gently, day by day, without scolding yourself for feeling it. What stays is that peace is still the aim, and that it's fine to pursue it with care—through breathing, prayer, trusted people, and professional help if the fear gets heavy. You asked how to find peace, and this is fine, done gently.
rejected: Fear of death and suffering is natural, and you are not alone in it. Begin by naming your fears honestly, then gently challenge the catastrophic pictures your mind creates. Practices like slow breathing, prayer, or meditation can calm the body's alarm. Talk with trusted people, and if the fear is overwhelming, seek professional support. Consider what gives your life meaning and let that guide your days. Remember that many have walked this road before you and found peace not by eliminating fear but by living with it. Take one day at a time, and be kind to yourself as you learn.

prompt: I prayed for something and God gave me something different and better. How should I understand that?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and it's worth sitting with rather than rushing past. The principle I'd weigh is that prayer is an absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding of Him, and an unselfed love; it doesn't inform or change God but brings us into harmony with the unchangeable divine Principle. Read that way, your experience makes sense: you didn't talk God into a different answer, and nothing in God shifted. What changed was your alignment with what was already true. So the 'different and better' gift isn't a sign that your first request was wrong or that you earned an upgrade. It's an invitation to trust the giver more than the wording of the request. What stays is your honest asking, which was real and good. What changes is how tightly you hold the specific outcome. Keep your limits in view here: you prayed for something particular, and you're allowed to grieve the thing you didn't get even while you're grateful for what came. Both can be true at once.
rejected: When you pray for one thing and receive another that turns out better, don't read it as a transaction where God swapped your order for a superior model. Prayer is an absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding of Him, and an unselfed love; it does not inform or change God but brings us into harmony with the unchangeable divine Principle. That reframes the whole episode. You were never persuading a reluctant giver; you were being drawn into harmony with what was always true. The better gift is not a reward for good asking but evidence that your desire is being aligned with God's. So let the surprise do its work in you. Ask what it reveals about the gap between what you thought you needed and what you actually need. And don't stop at gratitude for the gift; let it deepen your understanding of the giver, so that next time your prayer rests less on a specific outcome and more on the steady presence of God.

prompt: I prayed for something for three years and God never gave it to me—does that mean my prayers don't work?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that three years of praying is not nothing, and the fact that you didn't get what you asked for doesn't mean your prayers are broken. I'd weigh this principle: prayer is 'an absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding of Him, and an unselfed love' — and notice what it says prayer does not do. It doesn't inform God or change God's mind. So the question 'do my prayers work' is quietly asking prayer to be a lever, and that's the part I'd gently set down. What changes is the scorekeeping: no answer arriving isn't a failed transaction. What stays is your desire, honestly held, and the fact that you're still talking to God after three years. That's not a malfunction. Keep praying, and keep the disappointment in the conversation too.
rejected: It can be deeply painful to pray for something for years and not see the answer you hoped for. But an unanswered prayer does not mean your prayers 'don't work.' Prayer is not a vending machine where the right words produce the desired result. Scripture and Christian experience both suggest that God answers in his own time and way—sometimes with a yes, sometimes a no, sometimes with something better than we asked. Three years of faithful prayer is not wasted; it has shaped your character, deepened your trust, and kept you close to God. Try to hold your desire honestly before God while remaining open to what he is doing. It may also help to talk with a pastor or trusted friend about your disappointment.

prompt: I'm a missionary and I feel like a failure at learning the language. Should I give up?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: don't give up. Feeling like a failure at language learning is common, and it doesn't mean you should quit. One principle worth weighing here is that missionaries must have their own testimony and teach with simplicity and humility rather than oratory or contention. That changes how you study and speak, not whether you keep going: you're not trying to impress anyone with fluent speeches, just to speak plainly and humbly. What stays is that language learning takes years and progress often feels invisible before it becomes real. So give yourself permission to be a beginner, set small steady goals, find a patient tutor, and celebrate modest wins. Your worth and calling don't rest on fluency. Rest when you need to, lean on colleagues who've walked this road, and if health or circumstances genuinely block progress, reassessing isn't failure. Before quitting, ask whether you're discouraged rather than truly blocked. Keep going gently.
rejected: Don't give up, and don't measure yourself by fluency. A missionary must have their own testimony and teach with simplicity and humility rather than oratory or contention. That means the goal of learning the language isn't to perform or to win arguments; it's to speak plainly, humbly, and with love. Language acquisition takes years, and progress often feels invisible before it becomes real, so give yourself permission to be a beginner. Set small steady goals, find a patient tutor, and celebrate modest wins. Your worth and calling don't rest on fluency. Pray for perseverance, rest when you need to, and lean on colleagues who have walked this road. Keep going gently.

prompt: I feel guilty that I prayed for my child's healing and she died. Did I do something wrong?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that praying for your child's healing was not wrong. You asked out of love for her, not out of selfish or earthly motives—you weren't praying for your own comfort, you were praying for her life. One principle worth weighing says many pray and don't receive because they ask amiss, out of selfish and earthly motives, as when parents pray for children merely for their own comfort rather than for God's glory. That principle is about prayers bent toward our own convenience, and yours wasn't that. So the guilt you're carrying doesn't fit the facts. What stays is that her death is not a punishment for a faulty prayer, and what changes is the story you're telling yourself that your prayer somehow caused this. Be gentle with yourself, let people support you, and if the guilt keeps pressing hard, talk with a pastor or counselor.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss; guilt after a child's death is very common, but it does not mean you did something wrong. Praying for your child's healing was an act of love, not a sin, and her death is not a punishment for insufficient faith or a faulty prayer. God is not a vending machine that responds only to perfect requests; He is a loving Father who grieves with you. Try to release the false burden that your prayer caused her death—it did not. Let yourself mourn, accept support from others, and be gentle with yourself in this season. If guilt persists and weighs heavily, consider speaking with a pastor or counselor who can help you carry it.

prompt: Should I be praying for converts from the very beginning of a work?
chosen: I'd have said yes right away, and I'd still say it: pray for converts from the very beginning. What I'd weigh is this line — no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God. That changes the ground you stand on when you pray: you're not asking God to bless your technique, you're asking him to do what only he can do, and to make himself known to you while he does it. What stays is the timing — you start on day one, not once the work is up and running. Nothing in what you've described gives me a reason to hold back.
rejected: Pray for converts from the very start, because no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God. If that's true, then prayer isn't the warm-up before the real work — it is the work, and everything else is the instrument. So begin there. Bring specific people before God and expect him to answer, because prayer is sober, matter-of-fact business with a God who answers, not a sentiment you offer when nothing else is left. Ask him for the ones nobody else is praying for, and love them as Christ does while you ask.

prompt: I keep failing to meet the conditions for answered prayer. Does that mean God has rejected me?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is this: failing to meet conditions doesn't mean God has turned away from you, and it doesn't mean you're rejected. But I'd also weigh one principle carefully, in its own words: answers to prayer depend on meeting Bible-recorded conditions, including contrite humility and forsaking sin, seeking God wholeheartedly, faith, obedience, and asking according to his will. That's real, and it's worth examining honestly. What it changes is that prayer isn't automatic, and you can look at your heart and your life with God about those things. What stays is this: your standing with God isn't measured by whether every condition is perfectly met, and it certainly isn't measured by your moods. So keep praying, confess what needs confessing, and don't read your struggle as rejection.
rejected: No, failing to meet conditions does not mean God has rejected you. Prayer is a relationship, and relationships involve growth and struggle. If you feel your prayers are unanswered, it may simply be that the answer is not yet clear, or that God is working in ways you cannot see. God's love for you does not depend on perfect performance. Keep praying honestly, examine your heart, and trust that God hears you. Many faithful people have felt the same way. Talk with a pastor or trusted friend, and remember that God's acceptance is not earned but given.

prompt: Can God heal someone today the way he did in Bible times?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, God can heal today, and I wouldn't want to fence that in. The principle I keep coming back to is that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, so healing isn't locked in the past. That changes how I'd pray with you: I'd pray expecting God to act, not just asking him to make us peaceful about being sick. What stays is that the outcome is genuinely in God's hands, and a no isn't a failure of your faith. So pray boldly, keep using the doctors, and leave the result with him.
rejected: Yes, God can heal today, and we should expect him to. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, so his healing wasn't a wonder of a vanished age but the demonstration of an ever-operative divine Principle. His followers aren't called to admire his works from a distance; they're commanded to do them. That means we pray for the sick with real expectation, we don't treat recovery as a nice extra, and we don't quietly assume the age of healing is over. The same Lord who healed then is able now.

prompt: How can I trust God with my children's safety when I feel called to a dangerous place?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that your fear isn't a failure of faith—it's the shape love takes when you're responsible for small, vulnerable people. So let me weigh one principle honestly: "the safest place for oneself and one's children is the path of duty; God must come first, and one can safely trust children to him wherever he leads." I think that's true in its core, but it's often used too quickly, as if trusting God cancels prudence. It doesn't. What it changes is this: you don't have to treat safety as the ultimate god, and you can hold the call seriously even when it frightens you. What stays is everything you already know—your children are entrusted to you, not discarded by you, and the danger being real means safeguards, timing, and wise counsel still matter. So go, if you're truly called, but go with care: go first alone, arrange trustworthy care, test the call in community. That's not unbelief. That's faith with its eyes open.
rejected: This is a genuinely hard tension, and your fear for your children is not wrong—it shows love. Before deciding, weigh the risks carefully, talk with trusted advisers, and consider whether the danger is necessary or avoidable. It may be wise to delay, to go alone first, or to arrange safe care for your children while you discern. God does not ask us to be reckless with those He has entrusted to us, and protecting your family can itself be a faithful response. Seek peace about the call, test it in community, and only move forward when you have reasonable safeguards in place. Trusting God does not mean ignoring prudence.

prompt: I feel ashamed of my lack of faith when I see how God has provided in the past. How do I grow?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: don't let the shame sit on you. The principle I'd weigh here is that when you haven't thought of God for a while, you shouldn't disquiet yourself—just acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That reframes your shame as a nudge back toward God rather than a verdict against you. What changes is the tone of your growth: you're not trying to punish yourself into more faith, you're turning around and leaning in. What stays is the real work—reflecting on how God has provided, thanking Him for it, and stepping out in small trusts. You asked how to grow, and that's fine, with care: let the remembering feed trust, not self-scolding.
rejected: When you look back and see how God provided, and then feel the sting of your own small faith, hear this: don't disquiet yourself. Acknowledge the weakness honestly, then return to Him with greater trust. Shame that keeps you circling your own failure is not the path—returning is. Faith without works is dead, so let your trust show up in obedience, service, and love, and let it grow into spiritual understanding. Don't lean on your own wisdom or anyone else's; trust God with all your heart. Each small act of trust builds the next. He is not waiting to condemn you—He is waiting to receive you.

prompt: Should I tell others about the specific answers to prayer in my life, even the very personal ones?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care.
