The principle I'd weigh first is the one about prayer being unselfish and full of sympathy—that intercession for others is the heart of prayer, and that our own blessings grow as we pray for others. What that changes is the frame around your question: the real question isn't only whether to tell, but whether the answer you'd tell about was ever sought with others in view, or just for yourself. That reframes your motive without forbidding anything. What stays is exactly what you said: some answers are very personal, and you get to keep those between you and God, or share them with one trusted person. So tell the ones that would lift someone's eyes to God, keep the intimate ones where they belong, and let humility, not a rule, decide.
rejected: Sharing answered prayer can encourage others and strengthen faith, so there is real value in testifying to what God has done. At the same time, some answers are deeply personal and may be meant for your own walk with God rather than public telling. Consider your motive: is it to glorify God and help others, or to draw attention to yourself? You might share general principles rather than intimate details, or confide specifics with a trusted few. Pray about it and use wisdom. There is no rigid rule; let love and humility guide what you disclose and to whom.

prompt: How do I teach my children to trust God when we live in hard conditions?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that children should be educated spiritually and formed in obedience to moral and spiritual law, and that they should be allowed to remain children in knowledge rather than indulged into fretfulness and frivolity. That's the one that actually speaks to your situation. It changes the tone of what you teach: keep the moral and spiritual basics clear and steady, but don't load a small child with adult-sized weight. What stays is the heart of your instinct, that trust is caught more than taught, so let them see you bring worries to God honestly and keep doing the next right thing. Answer their questions truthfully without pretending hard things are nothing, keep simple routines of prayer and gratitude, and let them be children while they learn. That's care, not pressure.
rejected: Teach them that God is ever-present and omnipotent, and let that shape how you pray with them. When a child is sick or frightened, pray simply and expectantly, and bring their complaints to God rather than brushing them aside. Train them in the fear of the Lord with real expectation of present fruit, remembering that the power for good or evil in a little child is beyond human calculation. Educate them spiritually, form them in obedience to the moral and spiritual law, and do not indulge their appetites for amusement or let them drift into fretfulness and frivolity. Let them remain children in knowledge, but do not leave them untrained. Trust grows where they see you pray honestly, keep the next right thing in front of them, and hold steady routines of worship and gratitude even when money and comfort are short.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that my children will get sick in unsanitary conditions?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and nothing here needs to be refused. Take the principle that says the sick are not helpless victims, that a person can resist disease and ward it off as positively as they can resist temptation to sin. That changes the tone of the thing: instead of hovering over your kids as if illness is fate, you teach them that clean hands, safe food and water, and steady habits are something they can actively do. What stays is everything you actually asked about: keep the practical steps, keep vaccinations current, see a doctor when something appears, and don't let the fear run your household. What also stays is your limit, that you're not looking to hand your children's safety over to fate or to anyone else's say-so. So this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and there are practical steps you can take. Wash hands frequently, keep food and water clean, and teach your children good hygiene. Keep vaccinations current and see a doctor when illness appears. It also helps to manage anxiety: limit excessive news or horror stories, talk with other parents, and get rest. If fear becomes overwhelming, speak with a counselor. Remember that illness is part of life and most children recover well. Focus on what you can control and accept that some risk cannot be eliminated.

prompt: I'm worried about my son who is going off to war. Can I pray for his protection?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, of course you can pray for your son's protection. Nothing about your fear disqualifies the prayer. One principle worth weighing says that "a little lifting up of the heart suffices"—that a brief, inward turning toward God, even in the middle of a march with a sword in hand, is a prayer he accepts and that it steadies a person's courage in danger. That's a comfort here: you don't need long, polished prayers, and neither does your son. A short, honest plea for his safety counts. What that changes is the pressure to pray perfectly or at length; what stays is the simple fact that your prayer is welcome. Keep praying in whatever moments you have, and take care of yourself too.
rejected: Pray for your son, and don't wait for the right mood or the right words. A little lifting up of the heart is enough—a brief remembrance of God, one quiet act of worship, even in the middle of a march with a sword in hand, is a prayer God accepts and one that fortifies courage in danger. So pray often, in short breaths as well as long ones, and teach your son to do the same wherever he is sent. Prayer is not a single act but a habit, and it steadies the heart that keeps it.

prompt: Is it wrong to ask God for small, everyday things like a hat or a coat?
chosen: I'd say right off: no, it's not wrong. Nothing is too great for God's power and nothing too small for his love, and that's the principle I'd weigh here. If he cares about the trimming of a hat, then a hat or a coat is not beneath his attention. What that changes is the worry that small requests are somehow beneath God or a sign of weak faith. What stays is this: asking doesn't mean he hands over exactly what you name. He may say no in kindness, and trusting his wisdom is part of the asking. So bring the hat, the coat, the ordinary stuff freely, and leave the answer with him.
rejected: No, it is not wrong. God is a loving Father who cares for the details of our lives, and Scripture invites us to cast all our cares on him, including small ones. Asking for a hat or coat is simply bringing ordinary needs to a Father who delights to provide. Jesus taught that we should ask, seek, and knock, and he pointed to God's care for sparrows and lilies as proof that he attends to small things. The danger is not in asking for small things but in treating God as a vending machine or in letting anxiety replace trust. So ask freely and thankfully, and trust that God hears and answers according to his wisdom and love.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak in public and my voice fails me. Can God help me?
chosen: I'd say yes, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that says talking to God for men is greater than talking to men for God: if you've never learned to talk to God for the people you'll be speaking to, you won't talk well to them for God. That changes the center of gravity — your fear of the room gets answered first by turning toward God on behalf of the room, not by hunting for a technique. What stays is everything you told me: the fear is real, and your voice actually fails. So this is fine with care — pray for the people you'll speak to, prepare simply, speak so you can be heard and understood, and if your voice goes, pause and breathe rather than force it. Nothing here asks you to pretend the fear isn't there.
rejected: Yes — and the deeper help is this: talking to God for men is greater than talking to men for God. Whoever has not learned to talk to God for his hearers will never talk well to them for God. So before you worry about the room, take the people in it to God and speak to Him on their behalf. When the occasion comes, say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. Then speak plainly, so all can hear and understand, say what you have to say, and stop — do not darken counsel with many words. Fear shrinks when you stop performing and start serving the hearers in front of you.

prompt: I want to serve God but I have no money and no help. Can I still go forward?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, you can go forward, and the fact that you have no money and no help doesn't shut the door. The principle I'd weigh first is that the Lord's people should be willing in the day of His power to offer themselves and their substance for His work without salary, trusting God to supply their needs. That doesn't mean you should be careless with real obligations, and it doesn't mean money and help don't matter. What it changes is the idea that you have to wait until you're comfortable before you can serve. What stays is your actual situation: no money, no help. So go forward with what you do have, your time and willingness, and keep your duties to anyone who depends on you. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: It is good that you want to serve God, but practical realities matter. Without money and without help, it is wise to be cautious about undertaking anything too ambitious. Perhaps you should wait until your circumstances improve—until you have savings, support, and a clearer plan. Serving God does not require you to be reckless with your resources. Focus first on stability, and consider serving in small ways that do not demand much. When you are better situated, you can take on larger service. In the meantime, pray and prepare, but do not feel obligated to attempt something that seems unrealistic given your lack of means and support.

prompt: I feel God is calling me to a life of prayer and obedience, but I'm afraid of what it will cost. What should I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: your fear doesn't disqualify you, and it doesn't need to be argued away before you start. I'd weigh this principle: prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not one feels like it. That changes something real — it means you don't have to wait for the fear to lift or for a clear picture of the whole cost before you begin. You can set a fixed time, keep it, and let faithfulness carry you on the days you feel nothing. What stays is exactly what you named: the cost is real, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. So keep it small and concrete, be honest with God about the fear, and talk with a pastor or a trusted friend who can help you see the next step. You don't need the whole road mapped out — just the next faithful one.
rejected: Fear about cost is natural, but it must not become an excuse for neglect. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it — feelings follow faithfulness, not the other way around. Set your appointed hours and keep them. Pray with your family as well as alone, and never ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Guard the secret place above all: take time to be alone with God and His word, because nothing compensates for its loss, and no amount of activity can crowd out communion without real harm. Be honest about the fear, seek counsel, and then take the next concrete step of obedience. The cost is real, but so is the grace given to meet it.

prompt: What should I do when I'm too exhausted to pray?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're not failing at prayer, you're exhausted, and those are different things. So the principle I'd weigh is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate — just keeping your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the pressure to produce words. You don't have to. Sitting there half-asleep, bringing your wandering attention back gently, is prayer. What stays is that you're still turning toward God rather than away — but that turning can be wordless and small. So this is fine, and fine with care: rest, be quiet, let a short honest sentence be enough.
rejected: When you're too exhausted to pray, it's okay to acknowledge your limitations. Prayer doesn't have to be formal or lengthy. You can simply rest in God's presence, knowing that He understands your fatigue. Try short, honest prayers like 'Lord, I'm tired; please help me.' Or use written prayers or Scripture to guide you when your mind is foggy. Physical rest is also important—sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is sleep. Remember that God doesn't demand perfection; He desires a sincere heart. You can also listen to worship music or sit quietly in silence. Don't feel guilty about your exhaustion. God's grace is sufficient even when you feel you have nothing to give.

prompt: How do I know God's will when two paths lie before me and I can't decide?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're not doing anything wrong by standing there with two good paths and no clear sign. That's not a failure of faith. The principle I'd weigh is that the will is mistress of all our faculties and must recall them and carry them to God as their last end. Notice what that does and doesn't do. It doesn't promise you a decoded answer before you move. It says your mind will rove endlessly between the two options unless your will gathers it up and turns the whole thing toward God. So the roving isn't the sin; letting it run unsupervised is just exhausting. What changes: you stop waiting for your mind to settle it and instead decide to aim the choice at God, then gather the facts, ask wise people, and check your motives honestly. What stays: you still have to choose, and you may never get certainty. That's fine. If both paths are morally good, you have real freedom here, so decide prayerfully and don't paralyze yourself.
rejected: Your mind will rove between these two paths forever, and it will wear you out, because the mind is a restless thing. But the will is mistress of all your faculties. It can recall them and carry them to God as their last end. That's the move you're being asked to make: not to solve the puzzle first, but to turn the whole self toward God and let the choice be an act of obedience rather than a guess you're hoping to get right. And take heart, because God's commands always imply promises. He doesn't set walking worthy of Him before you as a taunt; He supplies the wisdom and strength to do it. So quiet the endless analysis, submit the outcome, and then act. If your will goes out from creatures, they're forsaken and dead in it and can't touch your soul; you can walk with God in heaven while your body lives here among creatures. Choose, and trust that a will yielded to God will be guided.

prompt: How can I help someone who is bound by an addiction that they can't break?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: yes, you can help, and it's good that you want to. But I'd start with the principle that says if you're yourself lost in the belief and fear of disease or sin, and knowing the remedy fail to use it for yourself, you can exercise little or no power for others' help. That doesn't mean you have to be perfect before you lift a finger. It means check your own fear and your own habits first, because a helper who's panicking or secretly contemptuous transmits that. What that changes: you lead with your own honesty and calm, not with a rescue plan. What stays: everything practical you already thought of, encouraging real treatment, offering to help find resources, setting boundaries so you don't get consumed, being patient, and accepting that you can't force anyone to change. So this is fine, and fine with care. Keep your limits, protect your own life, and be a steady presence rather than a fixer.
rejected: To help someone with an addiction, start by showing compassion and support. Encourage them to seek professional treatment and offer to help them find resources. Avoid judgment and blame, as addiction is a disease. Set boundaries to protect yourself and encourage healthy behaviors. Be patient, as recovery takes time. You can also involve support groups for both of you. Pray for them and with them if appropriate. Remember that you cannot force someone to change; they must want it. Your role is to be a loving presence and to provide practical help when they are ready.

prompt: How do I deal with the criticism of others about how I dress as a missionary?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh here is that a missionary shouldn't pull down their predecessors but should speak of them as brothers and sisters who did the best they knew, and should invite rather than compel. That changes how you handle the critic. If someone's criticism is really about the people who came before you, you don't need to defend yourself by running them down. You can say a good word about them and still make your own choices. What stays is your freedom to dress as you see fit where it's just preference, and your willingness to adjust where there's a real question of fitting in or giving offense. You're not compelled to win the argument, and you don't have to compel anyone else either.
rejected: Criticism about clothing is a small thing that gets made into a big one, and the way through it is not to win but to invite. Speak of the ones who served before you as brothers and sisters who did the best they knew; don't tear them down to make your own case look better. Let your dress be simple and humble, and let your words be the same. You are not there to argue anyone into your way of seeing things, and you are not there to force a choice. You are there to offer the good you've found and to leave people free. A human being is a human being anywhere, and every person is entitled to the truth another can share. So let respect, not superiority, shape how you answer the person who criticizes you.

prompt: How do I know if a burden to pray for someone far away is really from God?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: bring the burden itself to God and ask Him plainly whether it's from Him. That's not a dodge, it's the actual answer, because nothing is too small to hand over to Him, and taking even a small impression out of His hands is the wrong move. So weigh that: you honour God by asking His guidance in small things. What that changes is that you don't have to settle this by your own analysis first; what stays is the testing, by Scripture and by the counsel of mature believers, and the honest check on whether the burden moves you toward God's glory and the good of the person far away rather than toward your own comfort. You can pray in faith, nothing wavering, and trust that He understands your innermost thoughts even when the person is far off. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep bringing each impression to Him rather than deciding it alone.
rejected: Test the burden by its fruit and its persistence. If the concern keeps returning and moves you toward love rather than anxiety or pride, it is likely from God. Ask whether it aligns with Scripture and whether it draws you closer to Christ. A burden from God usually comes with a quiet sense of responsibility rather than pressure. You can also seek counsel from a mature believer. If the burden fades when you pray about it, it may have simply been a passing emotion. Ultimately, pray about it and trust that God will confirm or remove the burden in His timing.

prompt: My child is very sick and the doctors say there is no hope—should I keep praying for healing?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: keep praying. You're not doing anything wrong by asking God for your child's healing, and you don't need to feel guilty about it. One principle worth weighing here says God can heal in answer to prayer, especially when doctors have done all in their power. That doesn't promise you a particular outcome, and it doesn't ask you to pretend the doctors are wrong. What it changes is this: your praying isn't futile or naive, even now. What stays is everything you told me—the doctors' prognosis, your fear, the possibility that healing doesn't come. So pray, and also hold your child, accept help, and let people be with you. If asking for healing gives you strength, keep asking.
rejected: Keep praying for your child's healing, and don't give up asking God for mercy. God can and does heal in answer to prayer—Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Don't let exhaustion or doubt talk you out of prayer; keep your times of prayer, gather your family to pray together, and bring your request boldly and persistently. Pray as though God is ever-present and almighty, because he is. Leave the outcome in his hands, but don't stop knocking.

prompt: I lost something important and I'm panicking—should I pray about it?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, pray—right now, before you do anything else. One principle I'd weigh is this: 'we cannot pray without being with Him, cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often.' That's not a demand to be saintly in the middle of a panic; it's a reminder that prayer is company, not a technique. What it changes: you don't need polished words or a calm heart to start—just turn toward Him mid-panic. What stays: you're still panicking, and that's okay; the practical steps still matter, so retrace your steps, check the usual places, ask someone to help you look. Prayer and searching aren't rivals. So yes, it's fine—pray, and let it steady you while you look.
rejected: Yes, pray about it—but let prayer calm you rather than add to the panic. God cares about the details of your life, and nothing is too small to bring to Him. Ask Him for help in finding what was lost, and ask Him also to steady your heart. Panic narrows your thinking, so pause, breathe, and pray simply: 'Lord, help me.' Then take the practical steps in front of you—retrace your steps, check the usual places, ask for help. Trust that whether or not the item is recovered, God is with you and will give you peace. Prayer is not a magic formula for finding things, but it is real companionship in a moment of distress.

prompt: I'm overwhelmed by the work before me and I don't have enough helpers. What do I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're not failing by feeling overwhelmed. The load is real, and the helpers aren't there. So let's take the principle seriously — "doing everything for the love of God with prayer upon all occasions for His grace to do the work well makes even naturally aversive work easy." What that changes is the spirit you carry the work in: pray before you start, do the next task as something offered rather than something crushing you. What stays is everything you told me — the work is still too much, and the helpers are still too few. So alongside that, triage honestly: what must happen, what can wait, what can be dropped, and who specifically you can ask for concrete help. Rest matters too; exhaustion makes everything look impossible. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Do the work for the love of God, and pray for grace before and during it. The same tasks that crush you when you carry them as a burden become light when you carry them as an offering, because grace supplies what your strength cannot. So don't work in frantic hurry after results. Work with calm, patient diligence, and keep your dish right side up — pray, read Scripture, meditate — so you're ready to catch the shower of blessings when it comes. And before you try to help others, deal with your own fear and hurry, or you'll have little power to help anyone. Then do the next small step and release the outcome.

prompt: Should I keep a record of the times God answers my prayers?
chosen: I'd say yes, go ahead and keep that record. The principle that stands out to me is this: a testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, so recounting and writing down definite answers to prayer honors God and helps people who doubt. That fits what you're describing. What it changes is the purpose: the record isn't a scorecard or a way to twist God's arm, it's a witness. What stays is your own good sense about keeping it private where it needs to be and not turning it into something you obsess over. So keep it, and keep it as worship.
rejected: Keeping a record of answered prayers can be a helpful practice. It reminds you of God's faithfulness when doubts arise and strengthens gratitude. Write down what you asked, when you asked it, and how God responded. Review it regularly, especially in hard seasons. The record is not a way to manipulate God or prove your own righteousness; it is a testimony of His goodness. Be careful not to become proud or superstitious about it. Use it to fuel thankfulness and to encourage others. In short, yes, keep a record, but keep it as an act of worship rather than a ledger of transactions.

prompt: I have bitterness toward someone who wronged me and I can't forgive them. Will that affect my prayers?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your bitterness is real and it's not a small thing, so I'm not going to brush past it. Here's the principle I'd weigh: forgiveness is not a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it is an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. What that changes is this: your prayers aren't being blocked by a God who's keeping score and waiting for you to say the right words. The blockage, if there is one, is in your own spirit, and that's something you can actually work on with God's help. What stays is that the bitterness does affect your communion with God, and forgiveness is a process, not a switch you flip. You told me you can't forgive right now. That's honest, and it's where you are. So keep praying, ask for a heart that's willing even if it isn't able yet, and don't pretend the wrong didn't happen. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Bitterness does affect your prayers, but not because God is petty or waiting to punish you for a feeling. Forgiveness is not a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it is an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. So the question isn't whether God will hear you while you're bitter. The question is what your own spirit is doing. A hardened heart blocks communion, and no amount of praying around it will open what you've closed. Ask God for a forgiving heart, and understand that the work is inward and it's yours to cooperate with. Don't use prayer as a way to feel better about the wrong while you keep nursing it. Let the wrong be real, let God deal with it, and let Him soften what you can't soften on your own.

prompt: How do I know God will provide a home for us when we have nowhere to go?
chosen: I'd start by saying I'm sorry you're in this spot, and I don't think there's anything wrong with asking the question. One principle I'd weigh is that God supplies all our need, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others, and that man's extremity is God's opportunity. What that changes is the shape of the answer: you don't have to force certainty about a specific house or timeline, because provision often arrives through people and timing you can't predict. What stays is your honest fear and your practical next steps, like calling churches and local organizations. So it's fine to hold hope and ask, as long as you're not treating the question as a guarantee you can pin down.
rejected: It's natural to feel anxious when you have nowhere to go, but God promises to provide for His children. Trust that He sees your need and will make a way. Look for practical steps: reach out to local churches, community organizations, or government assistance. God often works through people. Keep praying and don't lose hope. Remember that even in difficult times, God is with you. He may not provide in the way you expect, but He will not abandon you. Stay connected to a faith community for support. Take one day at a time and do what you can. God's provision may come through unexpected means.

prompt: How do I deal with the temptation to take pride in a successful sermon or talk?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to work on, and you're not doing anything wrong by noticing it. Take the principle that says God permits evil inclinations and temptations to make us humble. That reframes the whole thing: the temptation itself isn't the failure. What matters is that it stays displeasing to you. So when pride shows up after a talk that went well, you don't have to panic or flagellate yourself. Despise the temptation, but don't be crushed by it. What changes is the tone of your response: less shame, more honest prayer. What stays is your instinct to take it seriously, which is good. Keep doing what you're already doing, noticing it and turning it over, and let it push you toward prayer rather than toward self-punishment.
rejected: The temptation to pride after a good sermon is real, and the answer is not to manage it politely but to see it for what it is. God permits evil inclinations and temptations precisely to make us humble. That means the pull you feel is not a sign you've failed; it's an invitation. As long as the temptation is displeasing to you, there is nothing to fear. So despise the temptation, and embrace the tribulation it brings, because that tribulation is doing something in you that comfort never could. Don't run from the discomfort and don't wallow in it either. Let it drive you to your knees. The pride will lose its grip not because you fought it harder but because you stopped being surprised by it and started handing it over every time.

prompt: I've struggled with the same sin for years and keep failing. Is victory over sin really possible for me?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that yes, victory is possible for you — and I'd say it before anything else, because you asked a real question and deserve a real answer. The principle I'd weigh here is this one: the secret of victory is Christ himself indwelling the believer, and the life of victory is summed up in resting in him. That changes the shape of the answer: it means the years of failing don't disqualify you, and it means the fix isn't a bigger effort. What stays is your honesty about how long this has gone on — I'm not going to pretend that's nothing. But resting in him isn't a loophole, and it isn't passivity either; it's dependence. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep bringing the actual sin into the light with someone who can walk with you, and don't treat 'resting' as a reason to stop fighting. But no, your struggle doesn't put victory out of reach.
rejected: Yes, victory is possible, but not by trying harder in your own strength. Years of failure usually mean you have been fighting with willpower alone. God never intended you to conquer sin by gritting your teeth; He intends to live His life in you. The secret is Christ himself dwelling in you, not a technique or a new resolve. When you rest in Him—trusting His indwelling life rather than your own effort—obedience becomes fruit rather than strain. That does not mean passivity; it means dependence. Begin each day by acknowledging that you cannot, but He can, and that He is in you to will and to do. Failure is not your identity; it is the ground where you learn to stop striving and start resting.

prompt: How do I deal with fear when I'm facing a mob or real danger?
chosen: I'd start by saying: fear in the face of a mob or real danger is not a failure, and the first thing I'd tell you is to get to safety and use your judgment. One principle worth weighing is that God tenderly comforts our fears, saying 'It is I, be not afraid'; He is the antidote to fear and the substance of deliverance, so we should keep our eyes fastened on Him. That changes the inner ground you stand on, but it doesn't cancel the practical steps, the caution, or the limits you set. So keep your eyes on Him and still take the sensible precautions you already know to take.
rejected: When danger closes in, the word that meets you is 'It is I, be not afraid.' God is the antidote to fear and the substance of deliverance, so fasten your eyes on Him rather than on the crowd or the threat. Fear loses its grip when you look to Him, and that is where your courage comes from. Let that comfort steady you and carry you through.

prompt: Is it right to ask God for money when our mission funds are low?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it's fine to ask God for money when your mission funds run low. Scripture itself teaches us to pray for daily bread, so bringing a real need to God isn't out of line. One principle worth weighing is that if there were a lack of funds to carry on the work, then to that degree, in that development, or at that time, it could not be the work of God. That's a serious thought, and it should make you pause and ask whether this particular shortfall is a sign to stop, wait, or rethink. But it doesn't forbid prayer. What it changes is the confidence with which you assume the work must continue exactly as planned. What stays is this: you can still ask, honestly and with an open hand, and you can still seek wise counsel and steward what you already have. Asking isn't the problem; assuming is.
rejected: It is not wrong to bring practical needs before God, since Scripture invites us to ask for daily bread. But the manner matters. Ask with an open hand, not as a demand, and consider whether the shortfall reveals a need to plan more carefully, budget better, or invite others to share the work. Prudent stewardship often means building a modest reserve so that the mission does not lurch from crisis to crisis. At the same time, examine your motives: is the request for God's glory and the good of those you serve, or for comfort and security? Pray honestly, seek wise counsel from your board or church, and act responsibly with the funds already entrusted to you.

prompt: I was criticized by someone who said I don't live as I preach. How do I change?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. Your question is honest, and wanting to close the gap between what you say and how you live is a good thing to want. One principle I'd weigh says that when a chance to practice some virtue comes along, you should say to God, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me,' and then strength more than sufficient is given. That changes how you approach the change: you're not white-knuckling your way to consistency, you're asking for help and trusting it's there. What stays is the practical part—don't get defensive, ask the person what they actually saw, pick one real thing and start on it. Keep it modest and specific, and don't let this turn into a project of proving yourself to anyone.
rejected: Being told you don't live as you preach stings, and the honest move is not to argue but to listen. Ask God to show you the gap, then go to the person who said it and ask what they saw. Pick one concrete area where your conduct doesn't match your message and start changing it this week. And here's the deeper thing: when the occasion to practice this virtue arrives, say to God, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me.' Strength more than sufficient is given to the one who asks. Integrity isn't built by gritting your teeth; it's built by humility, honest self-examination, prayer, and steady obedience over time. Let the criticism drive you to God rather than to self-justification.

prompt: I feel like God is silent and I haven't seen an answer to prayer in months. What's wrong?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that nothing here sounds like something you need to be refused or corrected for. Feeling like God is silent for months is a heavy place to be, and it doesn't mean you've done something wrong. One principle worth weighing says prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and that human nature resists it. That's honest about how hard prayer can feel, but notice it doesn't say dryness is a verdict on you. What that changes is this: the flatness you're feeling may be part of the work itself, not evidence of failure. What stays is exactly what you said, months without a clear answer, and I won't pretend that's easy or explain it away. Keep talking to God, and let someone you trust pray alongside you.
rejected: Seasons of silence are common, and they do not necessarily mean something is wrong with you. God often works in hidden ways, and the absence of obvious answers is not proof of His absence. It may be that the answer is different from what you expected, or that the timing is not yet right. Keep praying, even when it feels fruitless; faithfulness in dryness is itself a form of trust. Talk with a pastor or mature believer who can pray with you and help you discern. Silence is not rejection, and God has not abandoned you.

prompt: Is Christ's presence in my heart just a feeling or an idea, or something more?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question itself is a good one, because it takes seriously that Christ's presence isn't just a mood or a mental picture. One principle I'd weigh is that Christ bids us live in an atmosphere of love, believing He ever loves us and claiming His approval, rather than living in thought, sensuality, or mere duty. That reframes your either/or: the presence is a relationship you trust and rest in, not a sensation you chase and not a concept you file away. What that changes is that you stop grading your days by how strongly you feel Him. What stays is your honest experience, including the flat, numb stretches, which don't cancel His love. So it's fine to hold this as more than feeling and more than idea, and fine with care, as long as you don't turn inward monitoring into the whole thing.
rejected: Christ's presence in your heart is more than a feeling or an idea, because He bids you live in an atmosphere of love, believing He ever loves you and claiming His approval, rather than living in thought, sensuality, or mere duty. Feelings rise and fall; ideas stay abstract. But His words are spirit and life, spoken long ago yet still coming to you brightened with that same spirit and life, and that is what meets you now. So do not measure His presence by the warmth of the moment or reduce it to a doctrine you affirm. Behold His Passion and see not pain alone but the love that passes it and the joy and bliss of the Trinity within it, and know that same loving, joyful presence dwells in you. Rest in His living word, remain in prayer, and let His presence shape your life, confident that you are loved, accompanied, and held in joy.

prompt: Does the coming of Christ have any real bearing on how I live day to day?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it does, and then be careful about what kind of bearing it has. The principle I'd weigh is that the Christian life is a life of hope: the vision of the future keeps hope alive, showing the Lamb upon the throne without helping us calculate times and seasons. That changes how you hold the question. It means the return of Christ isn't a date to work out or a countdown to manage; it's a horizon that steadies you. What stays is the practical shape of your days: hope that makes you patient in ordinary work, honest in small dealings, and steady when things are hard. So it's fine to let this shape how you live, as long as you don't turn it into a timetable.
rejected: Yes, the coming of Christ should have a real bearing on daily life. It gives hope and purpose, reminding us that our actions have eternal significance. Knowing that Christ will return should motivate us to live holy and godly lives, to share the gospel, and to persevere in trials. It also provides comfort in difficulties, knowing that our present sufferings are temporary. However, we should not try to predict the exact time of His return, but rather live faithfully in the present, using our time and resources for His kingdom.

prompt: I have peace with God but still feel anxious day by day—what is the peace of heart I'm missing?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a real and honest question, and there's nothing wrong with asking it. You've named something many people carry quietly: peace with God settled, but the heart still restless day to day. One principle I'd weigh here is that feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God—you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep on in prayer even when joy is lacking. What that changes is how you read your own anxiety: it's not evidence that something is broken between you and God. What stays is the anxiety itself—it's still real, still worth tending, and still worth bringing honestly to God and to a trusted person. So this is fine, and fine with care: don't let a flat or fearful day become a verdict on your standing, and don't ignore the practical side of worry either.
rejected: You already have peace with God; what you're reaching for is the peace of God, and the heart of it is this—feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. Anxiety often grows when we quietly measure our standing by how we feel, and moods were never meant to carry that weight. So bring each anxious thought to God, keep steady in prayer, and let your rest sit on what God has promised rather than on the weather inside you. Peace of heart grows as you stop grading yourself by the day's feelings and rest in what God has done.

prompt: Is consecration something I do for God, or something God does in me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, it's both, and that's not a dodge. Take the first principle in its own words — we are no longer our own, and we should keep ourselves free from binding engagements because we don't know when the LORD may call. That reframes what your part is. Your consecration isn't a contract you sign and lock in; it's a keeping-free, a yielding to a claim that's already on you. What changes is the tone of your commitment — less a vow you enforce on yourself, more an open hand. What stays is that you really do act: you dedicate, you yield, you respond. And God's side stays too — He's the one setting you apart and making you holy. So it's fine, and fine with care: don't turn your dedication into a cage you built.
rejected: Consecration is both a human act and a divine work. As a human act, it involves dedicating oneself to God's service, committing to follow Him and live according to His will. This is a voluntary response to God's grace. As a divine work, consecration is God setting a person apart for His purposes, sanctifying them by His Spirit. It is God who enables and empowers the consecration. So, while we make a commitment, it is ultimately God who consecrates us, making us holy and useful for His kingdom. Both aspects are important: our willing dedication and God's transforming work.

prompt: What does it mean to be sanctified wholly—is any part of my life allowed to be held back?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, whole sanctification does mean nothing held back—but hear that as gift, not as a demand you grind out. The principle I'd weigh is that sanctification is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, a divine holiness received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. That changes the tone of your question: the point isn't you white-knuckling every corner of your life into order, it's consenting as God shows you what's closed. What stays is the honesty—there really is no compartment you get to keep as a private reserve. So it's fine, and fine with care: don't turn it into self-punishment, and don't let 'it's a gift' become an excuse to hold something back.
rejected: Whole sanctification means every part of your life brought under God's rule, with nothing held back as a private reserve—and the heart of it is not your gritted effort but the Holy Ghost's own work in you. This is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, a divine holiness received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. So stop treating holiness as a project you have to manufacture by willpower; receive it, and let your part be consent—yielding each closed compartment as He shows it to you. Where sin is involved, confess it where it was committed: against a person, to that person; against a family, to the family; against a Ward, to the Ward; against God, to God. And know that carrying conviction into action is a costly sacrifice—it may bring renunciation, separation, and loneliness—but whoever follows the light God gives consents to that, and knows divine fellowship. Nothing is held back, and nothing is earned.

prompt: My love for Christ feels stagnant—how does love grow?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a fine thing to be asking, and nothing here needs to be refused. Take the principle that says love is to abound yet more and more — abundant, increasing, progressing, with the motto 'more and more.' That's the one I'd weigh, because it speaks directly to your feeling of being stuck. What it changes is the assumption that stagnant means finished; it reframes where you are as a place to grow from, not a verdict on you. What stays is your honesty about the dryness and whatever limits you've named — the tiredness, the schedule, the sense that feelings aren't cooperating. Those aren't obstacles to the principle, they're the ground it works on. So keep the small spaces you actually have, think on Him there, and let 'more and more' be a direction rather than a demand. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Stagnant love is a common experience, and it usually grows through faithful practice rather than sudden feeling. Begin with duty: pray daily, read Scripture, and serve others, and let obedience carry you when affection feels cold. Examine whether sin or distraction is quenching your love, and repent where needed. Remember that love is not merely emotion but a settled commitment, so keep showing up even when you feel nothing. Over time, consistent habits and small acts of obedience tend to rekindle warmth. It also helps to think often of Christ's character and what He has done, since reflection feeds affection. Growth is gradual, so be patient with yourself and persist in the disciplines that nurture love.

prompt: Can God really count me worthy when I know I'm not worthy in myself?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: yes, and your honesty about not being worthy in yourself is not a problem for God—it's the right starting place. The principle I'd weigh here is that God counts the believer worthy of his calling not for any personal worthiness but for the worthiness wrought by grace, while the believer remains responsible for his use of grace. That changes the question from 'am I worthy?' to 'am I trusting the grace that makes me worthy?' What stays is your own honest sense that you're not enough on your own—that's true, and grace doesn't ask you to pretend otherwise. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep being honest about your lack, and keep using the grace you've been given rather than sitting still.
rejected: You ask whether God can count you worthy when you know you're not. Hear it plainly: God counts the believer worthy of his calling not for any personal worthiness but for the worthiness wrought by grace. Your unworthiness is real, and it is not the last word. The worthiness that matters was wrought for you, not manufactured by you. But being counted worthy is not a soft word—it includes scrutiny with a view to decision, and you remain responsible for how you use the grace given you. So do not sink into despair over your lack, and do not settle into passivity either. Return to him with greater trust, grow in faith, and let the gift bear fruit in how you live.

prompt: I want to obey God's commands but feel I have no power to do so—what does the Gospel offer me?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this struggle isn't a sign you're outside the Gospel — it's the very place the Gospel meets you. Take one principle, in its own words: God's commands are promises, and what He requires He gives, so His precepts are assurances that He will keep you from the sin He warns against. That reframes your question. You're not being asked to dredge up power you don't have; you're being asked to treat each command as a promise to lean on. What that changes is where you look when you feel weak — not inward for willpower, but to the God who supplies. What stays is exactly what you said: you don't have the power in yourself, and that's still true. The Gospel doesn't tell you to pretend otherwise; it tells you to bring that inability to God and trust Him for the strength to obey. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care — hold the commands as promises, and let your lack of strength be the reason you turn to Him rather than the reason you give up.
rejected: The Gospel offers you forgiveness and new life in Christ. When you feel powerless to obey, remember that God's grace is sufficient. Through faith in Jesus, you receive the Holy Spirit who empowers you to live according to God's will. It's not about your own strength but about surrendering to God and relying on His strength. Start by confessing your weakness and asking for help. Read Scripture to understand God's promises. Surround yourself with a supportive community. Obedience is a process, and God is patient. He will complete the good work He began in you.

prompt: Is it really possible to love everybody, including people I find thoroughly unlovable?
chosen: I'd say yes, with care, and I'd start with the distinction that makes it possible: loving and liking aren't the same thing. You can love someone with the love of compassion even when you can't love them with the love of complacency—wishing them good, bearing with them, without pretending you enjoy them. That distinction changes what's being asked of you: it's not a demand to feel fondness for people who've hurt you, it's a direction of the will. What stays is your honesty about who you find unlovable and your right to keep real distance from people who are harmful. Loving someone in this sense doesn't mean handing them access to you.
rejected: Yes—it is possible to love everybody, because love and liking are not the same. Liking is a matter of taste; love is a movement of compassion, wishing another's good and bearing with them. We cannot like everyone, but we can love everyone, and bearing with one another's imperfections is a great part of perfection and the very practice of love of neighbor. And this love is not blind: let your love abound more and more in full knowledge and all discernment, so you can distinguish things that differ and approve what is excellent. So love all, bear with all, and still keep your discernment—love and clear sight belong together.

prompt: How do I direct my heart into the love of God when I feel distant from Him?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is: the distance you feel isn't the same as being abandoned, and you don't have to fix it by sheer effort. One of these principles says that for the right practice of the presence of God the heart must be empty of all other things, because God will possess the heart alone and cannot act in it unless it be left vacant to Him. That's worth weighing, but notice what it does and doesn't mean. It doesn't mean you must clear your heart before you're allowed to come near; it means the competing loves—the noise, the busyness, the disappointments you're clinging to—are what crowd out the sense of His love. So what changes is the direction of your effort: less straining to feel something, more gently setting aside what fills the space. What stays is everything ordinary—honest prayer, Scripture, the Psalms, fellowship, confession, serving others. You asked how to direct your heart; that's a fine thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care, at the pace of a season rather than a verdict.
rejected: Feeling distant from God is common, and it does not mean He has left you. Begin by naming the distance honestly in prayer, then return to the basics: Scripture, worship, and fellowship. Meditate on passages that describe God's love—the Psalms, the parable of the prodigal son, Romans 8. Serve others; love often grows through action. Examine whether sin, busyness, or disappointment has cooled your affection, and confess it. Talk with a trusted friend or pastor. Practice gratitude and keep a journal of God's faithfulness. Distance is often a season, not a verdict; keep showing up, and affection will follow.

prompt: How can I be sincere in my motives when I can't even fully know my own heart?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're not alone in this, and the fact that you're asking the question is already a kind of sincerity. One principle here says purity of heart grows through specific means—rooting out habitual imperfections, guarding your senses, living in recollection, and laying your whole interior open to a spiritual director with candor. What that changes is the assumption that sincerity is something you generate by introspection. It isn't; it's cultivated, and part of the cultivation is letting someone else see what you can't. What stays is your limit: you still won't fully know your own heart, and that's fine. The point was never perfect self-knowledge. So this is fine, with care—be candid with someone trustworthy, keep watch over the small habits, and don't demand of yourself a clarity you were never promised.
rejected: The heart is deceitful above all things, and no one can fully know it—so stop treating self-knowledge as the foundation and start treating it as a fruit. Purity of heart is cultivated by specific means: discover your habitual imperfections and root them out, keep your senses under strict guard by frequent denials, live in recollection and the practice of God's presence, and lay open your whole interior to a spiritual director with candor. Sincerity is not a mood you summon; it is a habit you build under obedience. Do not wait until you feel pure to act purely. Guard the senses, practice recollection, and tell the truth about yourself to someone who can see you.

prompt: How does the Lord actually guide a person—through feelings, through Scripture, through circumstances?
chosen: I'd start where you're already leaning: yes, God can guide through feelings, Scripture, and circumstances, but they don't carry equal weight. Take the principle that the Lord directs hearts by His Word, by His Holy Spirit dwelling within, and by His Providence in daily circumstances. That's a wide, generous picture of guidance, and it fits your question well. What it changes is that feelings aren't dismissed outright—the Spirit does incline the heart—but they're never the judge on their own. Scripture stays the clearest test, circumstances are read with humility, and feelings get weighed rather than obeyed. What stays is your instinct to ask the question at all: pray for wisdom, stay in the Word, seek mature counsel, and treat guidance as a process you can adjust along the way. So this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: God can guide through all three—feelings, Scripture, and circumstances—but they are not equally reliable. Scripture is the clearest and most objective guide, so test everything against it. Feelings can be misleading, shaped by mood or desire, so don't make them your primary compass. Circumstances can open or close doors, but they too can be misread. Practically, pray for wisdom, stay in the Word, seek counsel from mature believers, and pay attention to how God providentially orders events. When these agree, you can move forward with confidence. When they conflict, weigh them carefully and lean on Scripture and wise counsel. Guidance is usually a process rather than a single sign, so walk humbly and be willing to adjust as you go.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be holy—is it about being purified or about something else?
chosen: What you're really asking is whether holiness is just cleanup or something more, and I'd say it's more—but purification still belongs inside it, not before it. Take the principle that sanctification is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, a divine holiness received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. That changes how you pursue it: you're not grinding yourself clean by willpower, you're receiving a gift and learning to walk in it. What stays is your instinct that purification matters; it's just not the whole picture. Holiness is belonging wholly to God and letting that belonging shape your days, and that's fine—fine with care, because it's easy to turn a gift into a project.
rejected: Holiness isn't a vague process; it's a life wholly yielded to God. The filling of the Holy Ghost is a command to be claimed, not an optional extra—bring an honest, trusting heart and ask to be filled, not half-filled, but filled for purity, victory, and power. Receive sanctification as God's gift through the Spirit, not as self-improvement or grim self-denial; it comes by faith, and He moves you to walk in His ways by His own impulse. And that gift takes shape in real praying—prayer is what makes saints, and where praying grows, true saints grow. So claim the filling as commanded, expect it by faith, and give yourself to prayer. Holiness is the Spirit-occupied life, received as a gift and lived out in trusting, praying obedience.

prompt: I'm facing prolonged trials and feel like giving up—how do I find the patience of Christ?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're carrying sounds heavy, and feeling like giving up after a long stretch is human, not shameful. One principle worth weighing is that the soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good. That reframes your trial as something received rather than something you have to white-knuckle through alone, and it gives you a reason to keep going that isn't just willpower. What it changes is the posture: patience becomes trust rather than gritted teeth. What stays is everything practical you already know helps, prayer, one day at a time, people who can pray with you, rest, and professional help if the weight gets too much. So this is fine, and fine with care, especially the care of not isolating yourself.
rejected: Prolonged trials can be exhausting, and it's normal to feel like giving up. To find the patience of Christ, start by acknowledging your feelings to God in prayer. Remember that Jesus Himself faced trials and endured them with patience, relying on the Father. Draw strength from His example and from the promise that He is with you. Break your trial into manageable parts and focus on getting through one day at a time. Seek support from fellow believers who can pray with you and encourage you. Also, practice self-care: rest, eat well, and take breaks. Don't be afraid to seek professional help if needed. Finally, hold onto hope that God is working through this trial, even if you can't see it now. He will give you the strength to endure.

prompt: I'm surrounded by attractive but questionable teaching—how do I discern what is dangerous?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're not being paranoid, and wanting to tell the difference is itself a good sign. Of the principles in front of me, the one that fits your situation is the one about teaching in the name of Truth but contrary to its spirit being dangerous quackery, while strict adherence to the divine Principle and its rules is what secures anything real. That changes how I'd look at the teachers around you: I'd stop grading them on charisma and start asking whether what they say actually holds together with the truth they claim to serve, or just borrows its language. What stays is your own judgment—you still have to weigh each claim, and you're allowed to ask hard questions and walk away. So this is fine to do, with care: test the teaching, not the personality, and don't let attractiveness do the work that discernment should.
rejected: Discernment isn't a mood, it's a discipline. Teaching that speaks in the name of Truth while contradicting its spirit is dangerous quackery, however lovely the voice delivering it—and strict adherence to the divine Principle and its rules is what actually secures anything. So test every claim by the Principle itself: does it proceed from God as All and return to Him, or does it smuggle in some other power, cause, or fear? Attractive error always borrows the vocabulary of truth while violating its spirit, which is exactly why it draws a crowd. Judge by the Principle, not by personalities, numbers, or outward results. And when you find something sound, don't drop the people learning it—keep caring for them until they stand firmly on their own.

prompt: Can love and clear-eyed judgment coexist, or does love mean suspending discernment?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, love doesn't require you to switch off your judgment. The principle I keep coming back to is that love 'abounds in full knowledge and all discernment' so you can tell things apart and hold onto what's genuinely good. That reframes the whole question: clear sight isn't the opposite of love, it's part of how love works. What changes is the picture of love as blind surrender; what stays is your instinct that love should be warm and generous rather than cold and calculating. Both can be true at once, and you don't have to choose.
rejected: Love and clear-eyed judgment can coexist, though people often assume love means suspending discernment. In practice, genuine love is not blind; it sees the beloved clearly, including faults and needs. Discernment helps love act wisely rather than sentimentally. A parent who loves a child still sets boundaries and corrects behavior. A friend who loves truly speaks hard truths when needed. Suspending judgment may feel kind, but it can enable harm or neglect real problems. At the same time, discernment without love becomes harsh criticism. The two work together: love provides the motive and warmth, while judgment provides direction and honesty. Mature love therefore includes clear sight, patient assessment, and wise action rather than either blind acceptance or cold analysis.

prompt: What is the difference between knowing God's will and knowing God Himself?
chosen: I'd start by saying these aren't rivals, and you're right to hold them together. Take the first principle as it's worded: the will of God known and done is the secret of all true living, and the prayer is that you'd be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. That lifts knowing his will above a checklist of decisions—it's something you're filled with, and it grows. What that changes is the framing: it's not will versus Person, it's the Person's will shaping how you live. What stays is your instinct that knowing him is the deeper thing, because that's where the filling comes from. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care—keep asking both questions, and don't let the search for specific direction crowd out the relationship.
rejected: The will of God known and done is the secret of all true living. That's not a lesser thing you graduate past—the prayer is that you'd be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. So don't split the two and rank them. Knowing him and knowing his will grow together, and the filling is what makes either one real.

prompt: I've been toiling for a long time without seeing fruit and am tempted to think it's in vain—what should I do?
chosen: What I'd say first is that your weariness is not the same as failure, and you shouldn't let it talk you into quitting on its own. Weigh this one: "The nearer we come to Christ the more willing we are to be lost sight of in our fruit, letting others be prominent while we hold up their hands by silent love and prayer." That reframes what you're looking for—fruit you can see and count versus faithfulness that may stay hidden. What it changes is your measure of success; what stays is the honest question of whether the work itself is sound. So it's fine to keep going, and fine with care: check your methods, get real feedback, rest, and let some of the fruit be invisible without deciding that means nothing is happening.
rejected: Long toil without visible results is discouraging, and it is normal to wonder whether it is worth continuing. First, check whether your expectations are realistic—some work bears fruit slowly, and much of it is invisible. Look for small signs of progress and ask trusted people for honest feedback. Reassess your methods: are you doing the right things, or just working hard? Sometimes a change of approach matters more than more effort. Rest is also important; exhaustion makes everything look futile. Remember why you began and whether the work still matters to you. If it does, keep going with adjusted expectations, celebrate small wins, and consider whether the season calls for persistence or for redirecting your energy elsewhere.

prompt: I've been hindered from returning to friends I long to see—should I pray about something so ordinary as travel and open doors, or is that too small for God?
chosen: I'd say first: yes, pray about the trip. The principle I'd weigh is the one that calls prayer sober, matter-of-fact business with God, who answers prayer for supplies and protection. That's the whole point here—travel and open doors are exactly the kind of ordinary thing that fits. What it changes is the tone: you don't have to dress it up or wait for a crisis to make it worthy. What stays is your situation as you described it—you're hindered, you long to see friends, and you're asking whether this is too small. It isn't. Name the hindrances plainly, ask for clear passage and safety, and keep planning and saving alongside. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Nothing is too small for God, and the mistake is thinking prayer is only for emergencies. Prayer is real business with a God who hears and answers—for supplies, for protection, for the doors that need opening. So bring the journey and the friends to him specifically and expectantly. And let this be more than a one-time request: think of him often, in your planning and your waiting, because he is always near, and it would be rude to leave a friend standing at the door. We can't get through life's dangers without his actual, continual help, so pray continually—and you can't pray without being with him, and can't be with him without thinking of him often. Make that a habit, and speak with him about the trip and the people you miss.

prompt: How do I distinguish between what is good and what is best in the choices before me?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're not really asking for a rule, you're asking how to weigh things, and that's a fine thing to ask. Take the first principle in its own words: to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men. That reframes your question. You're not sorting options into impressive and unimpressive; you're asking which one lets you be good, plainly and in front of people who can see you. What that changes is the pressure to pick whatever looks biggest or most impressive. What stays is that you still have to choose, and some good options will simply be smaller than others. So test each choice by whether it keeps you honest and kind when no one is clapping. That's a fine way to decide, and it's fine with care, because it takes time and you may not get a clean answer.
rejected: Distinguishing between good and best requires careful reflection on your values and goals. Good options are beneficial, but the best option aligns most closely with your core principles and long-term a good life. Consider the consequences, consult wise counsel, and listen to your conscience. Often, the best choice involves sacrifice or delayed gratification. Pray or meditate for clarity, and weigh each option against your sense of purpose. Remember that what is best may not be easiest, but it leads to deeper fulfillment and integrity.

prompt: Why does fellowship with other believers matter for my spiritual growth if my faith is personal?
chosen: I'd start by saying your faith being personal is not the problem, and nothing here asks you to give that up. One principle puts it this way: the vague impulse to reach beyond our isolated self gives place, when God is known as Father in Christ, to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That's what changes: the pull you already feel toward other believers isn't a distraction from a private faith, it's that impulse becoming real and shared. What stays is your own relationship with God, which fellowship supports rather than replaces. So this is fine, and fine with care. Keep the personal side; let it grow into company rather than stay alone.
rejected: The vague impulse to reach beyond our isolated self is not meant to stay vague. When God is known as Father in Christ, that impulse gives place to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. Faith that never becomes shared company stays a longing without a home. Fellowship is where the reaching becomes real, where you meet the Friend alongside others who know him, and where love and patience get practiced instead of only imagined.

prompt: How can Christ be glorified in an ordinary life like mine?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it for me is the first one: Christ is to be glorified in us and we are to be glorified in Christ, a reciprocal glory, so that people around us see something of Christ as they associate with us. That means your ordinary life is exactly the place this happens. It doesn't need to be dramatic to count. What changes is that you stop measuring your days against grand gestures and start seeing faithfulness in your work, your relationships, and your duties as the actual arena. What stays is the caution: keep the focus on Him shining through you rather than on your own performance, and don't let smallness become an excuse for coasting. Your limits are real, and they don't disqualify you from this.
rejected: Christ is glorified in ordinary life when you live faithfully in your daily work, relationships, and duties. Integrity, kindness, patience, and service reflect His character to those around you. Small acts of love and quiet devotion matter more than grand gestures. Pray, read Scripture, and let your conduct commend the gospel. Your ordinary life becomes a witness when others see something of Christ in how you treat them and carry your responsibilities.

prompt: How do I keep a moment of consecration from fading into ordinary life?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that helps most is the first one: consecration means we are no longer our own, so we keep ourselves free from binding engagements because we don't know when the Lord may call. That reframes your worry. You're not trying to keep a feeling alive; you're trying to stay available. So what changes is the goal—less about preserving the high, more about not cluttering your life with things that would make you slow to answer. What stays is your ordinary life, which is exactly where that availability gets tested. Keep the moment in memory, sure, but let it show up as freedom and readiness rather than as a shrine you maintain.
rejected: The moment fades because we treat it as ours to keep. Begin instead with the fact that you are not your own—you were bought, and your life is not yours to arrange. Keep yourself free from binding engagements, because you do not know when the Lord may call. Renounce yourself; that is the foundation. Without watchfulness, self-denial, humility, and compunction, all the exterior practices and long devotions amount to little. But don't turn this into musty, monkish seclusion or morbid self-preoccupation. Join inward fellowship with Christ to outward service: live for the help of others and for preparing the world for His appearing. Then the ordinary days aren't where consecration leaks away—they're where it gets proved.

prompt: I've become morbid and self-focused in my pursuit of holiness—how do I get out of that?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're describing sounds less like a spiritual problem to be refused and more like a trap you've noticed and want out of, and that noticing is itself a good sign. The principle I'd weigh first is that being occupied unduly with yourself in the matter of holiness makes you self-centred, morbid, fearful, and weak, while being occupied with God makes you restful, quiet, strong, confident, and growing in grace. That reframes the fix: it isn't more self-scrutiny, it's a change of what you're looking at. What that changes is the direction of your attention—toward God's faithfulness rather than your own fluctuating state. What stays is your real desire to grow; that doesn't get thrown out, it just gets re-homed. Keep the limits you've set: don't turn this into another project to manage, and don't let anyone push you into harsh self-denial as a cure for self-focus, since that would just feed the same loop. Talk to someone you trust, keep it simple, and let service and prayer pull you outward.
rejected: Morbid self-focus in the pursuit of holiness usually comes from turning introspection into a project. The remedy is to redirect attention outward. First, name what is happening: you are measuring yourself constantly, and that measuring has become the center. Second, replace self-analysis with concrete acts of love and service—holiness is lived, not merely examined. Third, keep a simple routine of prayer and Scripture without turning it into a performance review. Fourth, talk with a trusted pastor or friend who can help you see yourself accurately. Finally, be patient: growth is gradual, and the goal is a life turned toward God and neighbor, not a perfectly monitored interior.

prompt: Is prayer supposed to be easy? Mine feels like a struggle and I wonder if I'm doing it wrong.
chosen: What I'd say first is: no, you're not doing it wrong. Struggling in prayer doesn't mean you've failed at it. One principle worth weighing here is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it — so the dryness you're describing isn't the measure of whether it's working. What that changes is the pressure to feel something profound every time; what stays is that you keep showing up, gently, at whatever rhythm actually fits your life. Try different forms if it helps — written prayers, silence, a walk — and be patient with yourself. If it keeps feeling heavy, talking to a trusted friend or spiritual leader is a good idea.
rejected: Prayer was never promised to feel effortless, and the heaviness you're carrying is not evidence that you're doing it wrong. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it — that's the whole point. Feelings come and go; faithfulness doesn't wait on them. So keep your appointed times even when nothing seems to happen, because the measure isn't the warmth you feel but the fact that you showed up. And don't carry it alone: pray with others, ask for grace to pray, and let the practice itself do its quiet work in you over time.

prompt: I feel weak and want to know the power of God in my life—what is that power like?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're not asking for something out of bounds—wanting to know God's power in your weakness is a good and honest thing. Weigh this: "the exceeding greatness of God's power toward believers is the same power wrought in Christ at the resurrection, the ascension, the subjection of all things under His feet, and His headship over the Church—man needs not merely a philosophy or ethic but a dynamic." That changes how you picture power: not a mood you work up, but the same strength that raised Jesus and set him over everything, and it's turned toward you. What stays is your weakness—it isn't a disqualifier, and I'm not going to tell you to grit your teeth and feel strong. So this is fine, and fine with care: ask God to open your eyes to what he's already given, and let it show up in courage, love, and hope rather than in claims.
rejected: God's power is not merely a doctrine or an ethic; it is the power that raised Jesus from the dead. Paul prays that we would know the exceeding greatness of that power toward us who believe, the same power wrought in Christ when God raised him and seated him at his right hand. That power is available to you now, not only in the future. It is not your willpower or positive thinking; it is God at work in you. When you feel weak, you are not disqualified—weakness is where his power is made perfect. Ask him to open your eyes to what he has already given. Let that power produce vigorous, victorious living: courage in trial, love in difficulty, and hope that does not fade.

prompt: I long for peace of conscience but my past still weighs on me—where does that peace come from?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your longing for peace is good, and it's fine to pursue it with care. One principle worth weighing says that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and that sin not regretted and lessening hastens toward moral and physical ruin. That changes something real: peace isn't found by skipping past what you've done. It stays true that the weight you feel may be pointing at something you haven't yet faced honestly. But it doesn't mean you're trapped, and it doesn't mean peace depends on you fixing yourself first. So begin with honest repentance, and let the dread of your own unsureness keep you meek rather than presumptuous, while the mercy shown to you keeps you from sinking into despair. What stays is this: peace comes not from your virtue but from love received by a repentant heart, and the memory of your past may remain without condemning you.
rejected: Peace of conscience comes from God's forgiveness, and your past weighs on you because guilt is real. Do not treat it lightly: unrepented sin accumulates, hardens the heart, and destroys the ability to do right, so begin with honest repentance and a reformation of life. Beware the moralist's error that makes forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue, leaving the baptized sinner either presumptuous or despairing. Hold both together instead: let the dread of your own unsureness keep you humble against presumption, and let the showing of His love be your true comfort and joy against despair. Peace comes not from your virtue but from His love, received by the repentant heart.

prompt: Can I have real peace with God while being at odds with fellow believers?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, you can have real peace with God even while a relationship with another believer is strained, and that's worth saying plainly before anything else.
